school-c12-maths-b.title: Class 12 Mathematics — Part B (Ch 7–13 + Revision)
school-c12-maths-b.description: Class 12 Maths chapter by chapter: integrals, areas, differential equations, vectors, 3D geometry, linear programming and probability, plus formula sheets and mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Integrals
courses.summary: Indefinite integrals, substitution, trigonometric identities, special integrals, partial fractions, integration by parts, definite integrals, the fundamental theorem and properties of definite integrals.
outcomes: Learners can integrate standard functions and add the constant correctly
Learners can choose substitution, partial fractions or parts as appropriate
Learners can evaluate definite integrals using the fundamental theorem
Learners can use properties of definite integrals to simplify hard integrals

lessons.title: Integration as anti-differentiation

scenes.text: Kiran's cycle computer shows speed v(t) at every second but has lost the distance record.
Reversing differentiation — integration — rebuilds the distance function from the speed.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
F is an **antiderivative** of f if F′(x) = f(x). The **indefinite integral** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant (because derivatives of constants are zero).

Properties: ∫[f ± g]dx = ∫f dx ± ∫g dx; ∫k f dx = k∫f dx.

steps.title: Standard integrals
steps.body:
- ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, n ≠ −1;  ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x| + C
- ∫eˣdx = eˣ + C;  ∫aˣdx = aˣ/ln a + C
- ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C;  ∫cos x dx = sin x + C
- ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C;  ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x + C
- ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C;  ∫cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C
- ∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + C;  ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C

steps.title: Solved: ∫(x³ + 2x − 5)dx
steps.body: x⁴/4 + x² − 5x + C.

steps.title: Solved: ∫(x² + 1)/x dx
steps.body: Split: ∫x dx + ∫(1/x)dx = x²/2 + ln|x| + C.

steps.title: Solved: ∫(2 sin x + 3 sec²x − 4eˣ)dx
steps.body: −2 cos x + 3 tan x − 4eˣ + C.

steps.title: Solved: find f if f′(x) = 4x³ − 3 and f(1) = 5
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting **+ C** in indefinite integrals.
- Using xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) for n = −1 (use ln|x|).
- Integrating a quotient by dividing integrals: ∫(f/g) ≠ ∫f / ∫g.

activity.prompt: Match each integrand with its integral (+ C)

quiz.why: By the power rule ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), so ∫x⁵dx = x⁶/6 + C.
The power rule fails for n = −1. The derivative of ln|x| is 1/x, so ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x| + C.
d/dx cot x = −cosec²x, so ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x + C.
∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C, so ∫2ˣ dx = 2ˣ/ln 2 + C.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Integration by substitution and trigonometric identities

scenes.text: Neha sees ∫2x cos(x²)dx and notices 2x is the derivative of x².
Putting t = x² turns it into ∫cos t dt — substitution is the chain rule run backwards.

steps.title: Substitution
steps.body:
If the integrand contains g(x) and g′(x), put t = g(x), dt = g′(x)dx. After integrating in t, substitute back.

Key results: ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C; ∫[f(x)]ⁿf′(x)dx = [f(x)]ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C.

steps.title: Integrals of tan, cot, sec, cosec
steps.body:
- ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C
- ∫cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C
- ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
- ∫cosec x dx = ln|cosec x − cot x| + C

steps.title: Solved: ∫2x cos(x²)dx
steps.body: t = x², dt = 2x dx ⇒ ∫cos t dt = sin t + C = **sin(x²) + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫(ln x)/x dx
steps.body: t = ln x, dt = dx/x ⇒ ∫t dt = t²/2 + C = **(ln x)²/2 + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫sin²x dx (identity)
steps.body: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 ⇒ ∫ = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C.

steps.title: Solved: ∫e^(tan⁻¹x)/(1 + x²) dx
steps.body: t = tan⁻¹x, dt = dx/(1 + x²) ⇒ ∫eᵗdt = **e^(tan⁻¹x) + C**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing the variable but leaving a stray x in the integral.
- Forgetting to replace dx by dt/g′(x).
- ∫sin²x dx ≠ sin³x/3 — use the half-angle identity.

activity.prompt: Complete using ∫f′/f = ln|f|.

quiz.why: With t = 3x, dt = 3dx, so ∫cos 3x dx = (1/3) sin 3x + C.
∫tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + C, which equals ln|sec x| + C.
The numerator 2x is the derivative of 1 + x², so ∫f′/f dx = ln(1 + x²) + C.
cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, so the integral is x/2 + (sin 2x)/4 + C.
With t = sin x, dt = cos x dx, so the integral is t²/2 = sin²x/2 + C. Other forms differ only by a constant.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Special integrals and partial fractions

scenes.text: Rohan's integrals keep looking like 1/(x² + something). He builds a toolkit of six standard forms.
For rational functions with factorable denominators, he breaks them into simpler fractions first.

steps.title: Six special integrals
steps.body:
- ∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + C
- ∫dx/(x² − a²) = (1/2a)ln|(x − a)/(x + a)| + C
- ∫dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a)ln|(a + x)/(a − x)| + C
- ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
- ∫dx/√(x² + a²) = ln|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
- ∫dx/√(x² − a²) = ln|x + √(x² − a²)| + C

steps.title: Solved: ∫dx/(x² + 4x + 13)
steps.body:
Complete the square: x² + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)² + 9.

∫dx/((x + 2)² + 3²) = **(1/3)tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C**.

steps.title: Partial fractions
steps.body:
For a **proper** rational function (degree of numerator < denominator):

- (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b)
- (px + q)/(x − a)² = A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²
- (px² + qx + r)/((x − a)(x² + bx + c)) = A/(x − a) + (Bx + C)/(x² + bx + c)

If improper, divide first.

steps.title: Solved: ∫dx/(x² − 9)
steps.body: Using the second formula with a = 3: (1/6)ln|(x − 3)/(x + 3)| + C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using partial fractions on an improper fraction without dividing first.
- Mixing up ∫dx/(x² − a²) and ∫dx/(a² − x²) — the log arguments are reciprocal-like; memorise carefully.
- Forgetting the 1/a factor in the tan⁻¹ formula.

activity.prompt: Match the integral with its result (+ C)

quiz.why: ∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + C. With a = 4 this is (1/4)tan⁻¹(x/4) + C.
∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. With a = 3 it is sin⁻¹(x/3) + C.
Write 1/((x+1)(x+2)) = A/(x+1) + B/(x+2). Cover-up gives A = 1 and B = −1.

quiz.q: x² + 6x + 10 written by completing the square

quiz.why: The numerator has degree 3, higher than the denominator's 2, so the fraction is improper. Divide first, then use partial fractions.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Integration by parts

scenes.text: ∫x eˣ dx has no obvious substitution. Ishaan remembers the product rule for derivatives.
Rearranged, it gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du — integration by parts.

steps.title: Formula and ILATE
steps.body:
∫u·v dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′·∫v dx]dx.

Choose u (the function to differentiate) by the order **ILATE**: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.

steps.title: Solved: ∫x eˣ dx
steps.body: u = x, v = eˣ: x eˣ − ∫1·eˣdx = **eˣ(x − 1) + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫x cos x dx
steps.body: u = x: x sin x − ∫sin x dx = **x sin x + cos x + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫ln x dx
steps.body: Write as ∫ln x·1 dx, u = ln x: x ln x − ∫x·(1/x)dx = **x ln x − x + C**.

steps.title: Two special results
steps.body:
- ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)]dx = eˣf(x) + C. Example: ∫eˣ(sin x + cos x)dx = eˣ sin x + C.
- ∫√(a² − x²)dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
- ∫√(x² + a²)dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2)ln|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
- ∫√(x² − a²)dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2)ln|x + √(x² − a²)| + C

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing u = eˣ in ∫x eˣ dx — the new integral becomes harder.
- Sign slip in the second term (it is **minus** ∫).
- Forgetting that ∫ln x dx needs the hidden factor 1.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to evaluate ∫x sin x dx
items: Choose u = x (algebraic) and v = sin x
Simplify: −x cos x + sin x + C

quiz.q: By ILATE, in ∫x² ln x dx choose u =
quiz.why: By ILATE, a logarithmic function comes before an algebraic one, so u = ln x and dv = x² dx.
By parts with u = x: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C.
∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)]dx = eˣ f(x) + C. Here f = 1/x and f′ = −1/x², so the result is eˣ/x + C.
By parts with u = ln x and dv = 1·dx: ∫ln x dx = x ln x − ∫1 dx = x ln x − x + C.
The standard formula ∫√(a² − x²)dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C with a = 2 gives (x/2)√(4 − x²) + 2 sin⁻¹(x/2) + C.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

scenes.text: A rain gauge records rainfall *rate* r(t) mm/hour. The total rain between 2 pm and 5 pm is the area under the rate graph.
The fundamental theorem says: find any antiderivative F, then the total is F(5) − F(2).

steps.title: Fundamental theorems
steps.body:
- **First**: if A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt, then A′(x) = f(x).
- **Second**: if F′ = f on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a).

The constant C cancels, so it is not written. Geometrically, ∫ₐᵇ f dx is the signed area between the curve and the x-axis (as the limit of a sum of thin rectangle areas).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- After substitution, keeping the old x-limits.
- Writing F(a) − F(b) instead of F(b) − F(a).
- Treating a definite integral as always positive: it is a *signed* area.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫₁³ (2x + 1) dx.

quiz.why: ∫₀¹ x³dx = [x⁴/4]₀¹ = 1/4.
∫₁ᵉ (1/x)dx = [ln x]₁ᵉ = ln e − ln 1 = 1 − 0 = 1.
∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = −cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2.
By the first fundamental theorem of calculus, d/dx ∫₀ˣ f(t)dt = f(x), so the answer is x².
∫₀^(π/4) sec²x dx = [tan x]₀^(π/4) = 1 − 0 = 1.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Properties of definite integrals

scenes.text: Ananya faces ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx in a test. Direct integration looks horrible.
Using ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx, she adds two versions and the answer π/4 drops out in three lines.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- P0: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t)dt
- P1: ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦₐ f;  ∫ₐₐ f = 0
- P2: ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫꜀ᵇ f
- P3: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x)dx
- P4: ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx
- P5: ∫₀²ᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f(2a − x) = f(x); = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x)
- P6: ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f is even; = 0 if f is odd

steps.title: Solved: I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx
steps.body:
By P4, I = ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx.

Add: 2I = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2 ⇒ **I = π/4**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx and ∫₋₁¹ x² dx
steps.body: x³ is odd ⇒ 0. x² is even ⇒ 2∫₀¹ x² dx = 2/3.

steps.title: Solved: ∫₋₁² |x| dx (P2)
steps.body: Split at 0: ∫₋₁⁰ (−x)dx + ∫₀² x dx = 1/2 + 2 = **5/2**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫₋π/2^π/2 sin⁷x dx
steps.body: sin⁷x is odd ⇒ **0** (no integration needed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying P6 without checking even/odd correctly (e.g. x³ + 1 is neither).
- Forgetting to split at the point where |f| changes sign.
- Using P4 on limits that don't start at 0 — use P3 instead.

statements.s: ∫₋₂² x⁵ dx = 0
∫₋₁¹ |x| dx = 0
∫₀^π sin x dx = 2∫₀^(π/2) sin x dx
∫ₐᵇ f dx = ∫ᵦₐ f dx

quiz.why: x³ is odd and cos x is even, so x³cos x is odd. The integral over [−3, 3] is 0.
Using ∫₀^a f(x)dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x)dx, I = ∫ √cos/(√cos+√sin), so 2I = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2 and I = π/4.
x² + 1 is even, so ∫₋₁¹ = 2∫₀¹ (x² + 1)dx = 2(1/3 + 1) = 8/3.
The graph of |x − 1| on [0, 2] is two triangles, each with base 1 and height 1, so area = 2 × ½ = 1.
For an odd function, the area on the left of 0 cancels the area on the right, so ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x)dx = 0.

questions.why: d/dx tan x = sec²x, so ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C.

questions.why: ∫₀¹ 2x dx = [x²]₀¹ = 1.

questions.why: ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)]dx = eˣ f(x) + C. With f = sin x and f′ = cos x, the answer is eˣ sin x + C.

questions.why: x⁵ is an odd function, so its integral over a symmetric interval [−1, 1] is 0.

options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Integration reverses differentiation, and since d/dx ln|x| = 1/x, R explains A.

questions.why: With t = ln x, dt = dx/x, so the integral is ∫t dt = t²/2 = (ln x)²/2 + C.

options: x sin x + cos x + C
x sin x − cos x + C
questions.why: By parts with u = x: ∫x cos x dx = x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.

questions.q: Case: water flows into a tank at r(t) = 3t² + 2 litres/min. Water added from t = 0 to t = 2 min is
questions.why: Water added is the integral of the rate: ∫₀² (3t² + 2)dt = [t³ + 2t]₀² = 8 + 4 = 12 litres.

questions.why: Using the property ∫₀^a f(x)dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x)dx, I = ∫cos/(sin+cos). Adding gives 2I = π/2, so I = π/4.
x² + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)² + 9, so the integral is (1/3)tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C.

questions.q: ∫₋₁² |x| dx =
questions.why: Split at 0: ∫₋₁⁰ (−x)dx = 1/2 and ∫₀² x dx = 2. The total is 1/2 + 2 = 5/2.

questions.q: ∫₀^π x sin x dx =
questions.why: By parts: ∫x sin x dx = −x cos x + sin x. From 0 to π: (−π(−1) + 0) − 0 = π.

questions.q: ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx =
questions.why: By parts, ∫x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1). From 0 to 1: e(1 − 1) − e⁰(0 − 1) = 0 + 1 = 1.

questions.q: ∫√(x² + 9)dx contains which term?
questions.why: The standard formula is ∫√(x² + a²)dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2) ln|x + √(x² + a²)| + C. With a² = 9, the log term has coefficient 9/2.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Application of Integrals
courses.summary: Finding areas under simple curves — lines, parabolas, circles and ellipses — with vertical and horizontal strips, plus practice on regions between a line and a curve.
outcomes: Learners can set up area integrals with the correct strip and limits
Learners can find areas bounded by parabolas, circles and ellipses
Learners can handle sign changes and symmetry
Learners can find the area between a line and a curve

lessons.title: Area under a simple curve

scenes.text: A muralist paints the region under an arch shaped like y = 4 − x² above the floor (x-axis).
To buy the right amount of paint she needs the exact area — a definite integral of thin vertical strips.

steps.title: Vertical and horizontal strips
steps.body:
Area bounded by y = f(x) ≥ 0, the x-axis and x = a, x = b: **A = ∫ₐᵇ y dx**.

Area bounded by x = g(y) ≥ 0, the y-axis and y = c, y = d: **A = ∫꜀ᵈ x dy**.

If the curve lies **below** the axis, the integral is negative — take its absolute value. If it crosses the axis, split the integral.

steps.title: Solved: area under the arch y = 4 − x² above the x-axis
steps.body: Roots: x = ±2. A = ∫₋₂² (4 − x²)dx = 2∫₀² (4 − x²)dx = 2[4x − x³/3]₀² = 2(8 − 8/3) = **32/3 sq units**.

steps.title: Solved: area between x = y², the y-axis, y = 0 to y = 2
steps.body: Horizontal strips: A = ∫₀² y² dy = **8/3 sq units**.

steps.title: Solved: area bounded by y = sin x and the x-axis from 0 to 2π
steps.body: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2 and ∫_π^2π sin x dx = −2. Area = 2 + |−2| = **4 sq units** (not 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Integrating straight across a sign change and getting a cancelled (too small) area.
- Using dx when the region is described by x = g(y).
- Forgetting units: 'sq units'.

steps.title: Always sketch
steps.body: A rough sketch shows which strip to use, the limits and whether symmetry can halve the work.

activity.prompt: Area bounded by y = x², the x-axis and x = 0 to x = 3 (sq units).

quiz.q: Area under y = x from 0 to 2
quiz.why: Area = ∫₀² x dx = [x²/2]₀² = 2.

quiz.q: Area under y = 3 from x = 1 to x = 4
quiz.why: The area is a rectangle of height 3 and width 4 − 1 = 3, so 9.

quiz.q: Area bounded by y = cos x and x-axis from 0 to π
quiz.why: cos x is positive on [0, π/2] and negative on [π/2, π]. Taking each area as positive gives 1 + 1 = 2.

quiz.q: Region given by x = g(y) uses
quiz.why: When the curve is given as x in terms of y, use horizontal strips and integrate with respect to y.

quiz.q: Area under y = eˣ from 0 to 1
quiz.why: Area = ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = [eˣ]₀¹ = e − 1.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Area of regions bounded by a parabola

scenes.text: A dish's cross-section is the parabola y² = 4x. Engineers need the flat area of the region cut off by the line x = 3.
Symmetry about the x-axis halves the work: compute the upper half and double it.

steps.title: Standard parabolas
steps.body: y² = 4ax opens right (symmetric about x-axis); x² = 4ay opens up (symmetric about y-axis). Use symmetry: area = 2 × area of one half.

steps.title: Solved: area bounded by y² = 4x and x = 3
Solved: area bounded by x² = 4y, y = 2 and y = 4 in the first quadrant
Solved: area bounded by y² = 9x, x = 2, x = 4 and the x-axis in the first quadrant
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using y² = 4x directly as y = 4x.
- Forgetting to double when the region is on both sides of the axis.
- Mixing up x^(3/2) evaluation: 4^(3/2) = 8, 2^(3/2) = 2√2.

activity.prompt: Area bounded by y² = x and the line x = 4 (both halves), in sq units (decimal).

quiz.why: Replacing y by −y leaves y² = 4ax unchanged, so the parabola is symmetric about the x-axis.

quiz.q: Area bounded by x² = y and y = 1
quiz.why: The region is symmetric about the y-axis, so area = 2∫₀¹ √y dy = 2 × (2/3) = 4/3.

quiz.q: Area bounded by y² = 4x and x = 1
quiz.why: The area is symmetric about the x-axis: 2∫₀¹ 2√x dx = 4 × (2/3) = 8/3.
Taking the positive root of y² = 4x gives the upper half, y = 2√x.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Area of circles and ellipses

scenes.text: A stadium's elliptical field is x²/16 + y²/9 = 1 (in tens of metres). The groundskeeper wants its exact area for seeding.
Integration (or the formula πab it produces) gives 12π square units = about 3770 m².

steps.title: Using ∫√(a² − x²)dx
steps.body: ∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²)dx = [(x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a)]₀ᵃ = (a²/2)(π/2) = **πa²/4**.

steps.title: Solved: area of circle x² + y² = a²
steps.body: By symmetry, A = 4∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²)dx = 4·πa²/4 = **πa²**.

steps.title: Solved: area of ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1
steps.body:
Upper half y = (b/a)√(a² − x²).

A = 4(b/a)∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²)dx = 4(b/a)(πa²/4) = **πab**.

For x²/16 + y²/9 = 1: π·4·3 = 12π sq units.

steps.title: Solved: area of the circle x² + y² = 16 in the first quadrant between x = 0 and x = 2
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing sin⁻¹(1) = 1 instead of π/2.
- For ellipses, confusing which of a, b goes with x.
- Forgetting the factor 4 for the full figure.

activity.prompt: Area of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/4 = 1 (sq units, decimal, use π = 3.1416).

quiz.why: The area of a circle of radius a is πa², so for radius 3 it is 9π.

quiz.q: Area of ellipse with a = 5, b = 2
quiz.why: The area of an ellipse with semi-axes a and b is πab. With a = 5 and b = 2 it is 10π.
∫₀³ √(9 − x²)dx is the area of a quarter of a circle of radius 3, which is πa²/4 = 9π/4.

courses.summary: Order and degree, general and particular solutions, and solving first-order equations by separation of variables, the homogeneous substitution and the integrating factor.

lessons.title: Order, degree and solutions

scenes.text: A cup of tea cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter it is than the room. That sentence is a differential equation.
Before solving one, we classify it: order, degree, and what counts as a solution.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- A **differential equation (DE)** involves derivatives of an unknown function.
- **Order** = order of the highest derivative present.
- **Degree** = power of the highest-order derivative, *only when the DE is a polynomial in its derivatives*; otherwise degree is **not defined**.
- **General solution**: contains as many arbitrary constants as the order. **Particular solution**: constants fixed by given conditions.

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- y‴ + 2y″ + y′ = 0 → order 3, degree 1.
- (y″)² + (y′)³ = x → order 2, degree 2.
- y″ + sin(y′) = 0 → order 2, degree **not defined** (sin of a derivative is not polynomial).
- (dy/dx)⁴ + 3y = 0 → order 1, degree 4.

steps.title: Solved: verify y = eˣ + 1 solves y″ − y′ = 0
steps.body: y′ = eˣ, y″ = eˣ ⇒ y″ − y′ = 0 ✔

steps.title: Solved: verify y = A cos x + B sin x solves y″ + y = 0
steps.body: y″ = −A cos x − B sin x = −y ⇒ y″ + y = 0 ✔. Two constants for a 2nd-order DE — a general solution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the degree from a lower-order derivative's power.
- Giving a degree when the DE contains sin(y′), e^(y′), etc.
- Confusing order with the number of terms.

activity.prompt: Match each DE with its order and degree

quiz.why: The highest derivative in y″ + 5(y′)⁴ = 0 is y″, so the order is 2.
The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative. y″ is squared, so the degree is 2.

quiz.q: Number of arbitrary constants in the general solution of a 3rd-order DE
quiz.why: The general solution of an n-th order DE has n independent arbitrary constants, so a 3rd-order one has 3.
The equation y′ + e^(y′) = x is not a polynomial in y′, so its degree is not defined.

quiz.q: y = Ce^(2x) is the general solution of
quiz.why: From y = Ce^(2x), y′ = 2Ce^(2x) = 2y. So y = Ce^(2x) solves y′ = 2y.

lessons.title: Variables separable method

scenes.text: A colony grows at a rate proportional to its size: dN/dt = kN.
Money in an account with continuous interest obeys the same law. Separating N and t solves both.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: If dy/dx = f(x)g(y), separate: dy/g(y) = f(x)dx, then integrate both sides: ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx + C.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²)
steps.body: dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²) ⇒ **tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + C**.

steps.title: Solved: dN/dt = kN
steps.body: dN/N = k dt ⇒ ln|N| = kt + C ⇒ **N = N₀eᵏᵗ** (N₀ = value at t = 0).

steps.title: Doubling time
steps.body: Money at 5% p.a. compounded continuously: dP/dt = 0.05P ⇒ P = P₀e^(0.05t). It doubles when e^(0.05t) = 2, t = ln 2/0.05 ≈ **13.9 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the constant C, or adding a constant on both sides separately (one is enough).
- Dividing by g(y) without noting g(y) ≠ 0.
- Writing ln|y| = x² + C then y = eˣ² + C (wrong) — exponentiate everything: y = Ae^(x²).

activity.prompt: Money doubles under continuous growth at 10% per year. Using ln 2 ≈ 0.693, how many years?

quiz.why: Separate: dy/y = dx, so ln|y| = x + c and y = Ceˣ.
Separating variables gives y dy = x dx. Integrating, y²/2 = x²/2 + c, so y² − x² = C.
e^(x+y) = eˣ eʸ, so dy/dx = eˣeʸ. Separating, e⁻ʸ dy = eˣ dx.
Integrate directly: ∫sec²x dx = tan x, so y = tan x + C.
Integrating gives y = x² + C. With y(0) = 3, C = 3, so y = x² + 3.

lessons.title: Homogeneous differential equations

scenes.text: Some equations look the same whether you measure in metres or centimetres — only the ratio y/x matters.
For these homogeneous equations, putting y = vx turns them into separable ones.

steps.title: Definition and method
steps.body:
F(x, y) is **homogeneous of degree n** if F(λx, λy) = λⁿF(x, y). A DE dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous if F is homogeneous of degree 0 (i.e. a function of y/x).

Method: put **y = vx**, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, separate v and x, integrate, replace v = y/x.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = (x + y)/x
steps.body:
y = vx: v + x v′ = 1 + v ⇒ x dv/dx = 1 ⇒ dv = dx/x ⇒ v = ln|x| + C.

**y = x ln|x| + Cx**.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = y/x + tan(y/x)
steps.body: v + x v′ = v + tan v ⇒ cot v dv = dx/x ⇒ ln|sin v| = ln|x| + c ⇒ **sin(y/x) = Cx**.

steps.title: Solved: test homogeneity of F(x, y) = (x² + y²)/(xy)
steps.body: F(λx, λy) = λ²(x² + y²)/(λ²xy) = λ⁰F ⇒ homogeneous of degree 0 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the extra 'v' when writing dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
- Calling (x + y + 1)/x homogeneous — the constant 1 breaks it.
- Leaving the answer in v.

activity.prompt: Is the DE dy/dx = F(x, y) homogeneous?

quiz.why: For a homogeneous DE the standard substitution is y = vx, so the equation is in v and x only.
If y = vx, by the product rule dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.

quiz.q: Degree of homogeneity of x² + xy
quiz.why: Replacing x, y by λx, λy gives λ²x² + λ²xy = λ²(x² + xy), so the degree is 2.
Put y = vx: v + x dv/dx = 1 + v, so dv = dx/x and v = ln|x| + C. So y = x ln|x| + Cx.
x³ + y² has terms of degree 3 and 2, so scaling by λ does not give a single power of λ. It is not homogeneous.

lessons.title: Linear differential equations

story.title: The tank with inflow and leak

scenes.text: Salt water flows into a tank while mixed water drains out. The salt amount S obeys dS/dt + kS = q.
This is a first-order linear DE. An integrating factor turns the left side into one neat derivative.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Form: **dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x)**.

1. Integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx).
2. Solution: y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.

(Similarly dx/dy + P₁(y)x = Q₁(y) uses IF = e^(∫P₁dy).)

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx + y = eˣ
steps.body: IF = eˣ. y eˣ = ∫e²ˣdx = e²ˣ/2 + C ⇒ **y = eˣ/2 + Ce⁻ˣ**.

steps.title: Solved: x dy/dx + 2y = x² (x ≠ 0)
steps.body:
Divide by x: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x. IF = e^(2 ln x) = x².

yx² = ∫x³dx = x⁴/4 + C ⇒ **y = x²/4 + C/x²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not dividing by the coefficient of dy/dx before reading P.
- Writing IF = ∫P dx (forgetting the exponential).
- e^(ln x) = x, e^(−ln x) = 1/x, e^(2 ln x) = x² — simplify carefully.

activity.prompt: Find the integrating factor.

quiz.why: For dy/dx + Py = Q the integrating factor is e^(∫P dx). Here P = 2, so IF = e²ˣ.
P = −1/x, so IF = e^(∫−1/x dx) = e^(−ln x) = 1/x.

quiz.q: IF of dy/dx + y tan x = sec x
quiz.why: P = tan x, so IF = e^(∫tan x dx) = e^(ln sec x) = sec x.
The solution of a linear DE is y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.
IF = eˣ, so y eˣ = ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C. So y = 1 + Ce⁻ˣ.

lessons.title: Vectors: basics, types and components

scenes.text: A treasure map says: walk 3 km east, then 4 km north. Distance alone is not enough — direction matters.
Quantities with both size and direction are vectors. The straight-line shortcut is 5 km on a definite bearing.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
A **vector** has magnitude and direction; a **scalar** has magnitude only. Position vector of P(x, y, z): OP = x î + y ĵ + z k̂, |OP| = √(x² + y² + z²).

Types: **zero** vector, **unit** vector (magnitude 1), **co-initial**, **collinear** (parallel), **equal** (same magnitude and direction), **negative** of a vector.

steps.title: Direction cosines
steps.body: If r = aî + bĵ + ck̂ makes angles α, β, γ with the axes, l = cos α = a/|r|, m = b/|r|, n = c/|r|, and l² + m² + n² = 1. a, b, c are **direction ratios**.

steps.title: Solved: r = 2î − 3ĵ + 6k̂
steps.body: |r| = √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. Unit vector r̂ = (2î − 3ĵ + 6k̂)/7. Direction cosines 2/7, −3/7, 6/7.

steps.title: Solved: vector joining A(2, −1, 3) to B(5, 3, 3)
Solved: find a vector of magnitude 9 in the direction of î + 2ĵ − 2k̂
steps.body: |v| = 3, unit vector (î + 2ĵ − 2k̂)/3. Required vector = 3î + 6ĵ − 6k̂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- AB = (position of B) − (position of A), not A − B.
- Calling two vectors equal just because magnitudes match.
- Forgetting to divide by the magnitude for a unit vector.

quiz.why: Vectors with the same magnitude and direction are equal vectors.

lessons.title: Addition, scalar multiples and section formula

scenes.text: Two tugboats pull a ship with forces in different directions. The ship moves along their sum.
Vector addition follows the triangle (or parallelogram) law — and the same algebra splits a segment in a given ratio.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Triangle law: AB + BC = AC. Parallelogram law gives the same result.
- a + b = b + a; (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
- In components: add matching components. λa scales the magnitude by |λ| and reverses direction if λ < 0.
- a and b are collinear ⇔ b = λa for some scalar λ (component ratios equal).

steps.title: Section formula
steps.body:
Point R dividing PQ (position vectors a, b) in ratio m : n:

- internally: r = (mb + na)/(m + n)
- externally: r = (mb − na)/(m − n)
- midpoint: (a + b)/2

steps.title: Solved: are A(1, 2, 3), B(2, 3, 4), C(4, 5, 6) collinear?
steps.body: AB = î + ĵ + k̂, AC = 3î + 3ĵ + 3k̂ = 3AB ⇒ parallel with a common point ⇒ **collinear**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping m and n in the section formula (m goes with the far end b).
- Using '+' in external division.
- Adding magnitudes instead of vectors: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.

4î + 6ĵ = 2(2î + 3ĵ), so one is a scalar multiple of the other, and they are collinear (parallel).

Work = F · d = |F||d| cos θ — the dot product measures 'how much of one vector lies along another'.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
a · b = |a||b| cos θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π). In components: a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.

- a · b = b · a; a · a = |a|²
- a ⊥ b ⇔ a · b = 0 (non-zero vectors)
- î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1, î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0
- Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b|; projection vector = ((a · b)/|b|²) b

lessons.title: Cross (vector) product and areas

scenes.text: A mechanic pushes a spanner. The turning effect (torque) points along the bolt — perpendicular to both the spanner and the push.
That perpendicular vector is the cross product, and its size equals the area of a parallelogram.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector perpendicular to both (right-hand rule).

- a × b = −(b × a) (not commutative); a × a = 0
- a ∥ b ⇔ a × b = 0
- î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ
- Determinant form: a × b = |î ĵ k̂; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃|
- Area of parallelogram with sides a, b = |a × b|; triangle = ½|a × b|; parallelogram with diagonals d₁, d₂ = ½|d₁ × d₂|

steps.title: Solved: area of triangle A(1, 1, 1), B(1, 2, 3), C(2, 3, 1)
steps.body:
AB = ĵ + 2k̂, AC = î + 2ĵ.

AB × AC = î(0 − 4) − ĵ(0 − 2) + k̂(0 − 1) = −4î + 2ĵ − k̂, magnitude √21.

Area = **√21/2 sq units**.

steps.title: Solved: unit vector perpendicular to a and b above
steps.body: (−7î + 5ĵ − k̂)/(5√3) (and its negative).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign on the ĵ-component of the determinant.
- Using a × b = b × a.
- Taking |a × b| as the triangle's area (it is the parallelogram's — halve it).

quiz.why: î × ĵ = k̂, and reversing the order changes the sign, so ĵ × î = −k̂.
a × a has magnitude |a||a| sin 0 = 0, so it is the zero vector.

lessons.title: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line

scenes.text: A drone flies in a straight line from launch pad P(−2, 4, −5) to rooftop Q(1, 2, 3).
The direction of that path is captured by three numbers — direction ratios — and their normalised versions, direction cosines.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For a line making angles α, β, γ with the x, y, z axes: l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ, with **l² + m² + n² = 1**.

Any numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n are **direction ratios**; then l = ±a/√(a² + b² + c²), etc.

Direction ratios of the line through (x₁, y₁, z₁) and (x₂, y₂, z₂): x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁.

steps.body: DRs of AB: −3, −5, −3. DRs of BC: 6, 10, 6 = −2 × (−3, −5, −3). Proportional with common point B ⇒ collinear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating DRs as DCs without normalising.
- Forgetting l² + m² + n² = 1 when one DC is unknown (two possible signs).
- Thinking 90°, 60°, 30° can be the angles with the three axes (cos² sum ≠ 1).

**Parallel lines** r = a₁ + λb, r = a₂ + μb:

lessons.title: Formulating a linear programming problem

scenes.text: A carpenter makes tables (profit ₹30 each) and chairs (₹20 each). Wood and labour hours are limited.
How many of each maximises profit? First, translate the story into an objective function and constraints.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Decision variables**: the quantities we choose (x, y ≥ 0).
- **Objective function**: Z = ax + by to maximise or minimise.
- **Constraints**: linear inequalities from limited resources, plus **non-negativity** x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
- **Feasible region**: points satisfying all constraints; each such point is a feasible solution; the best one is the **optimal solution**.

steps.title: Solved: carpenter
steps.body:
A table needs 2 units of wood and 1 hour; a chair 1 unit of wood and 2 hours. Available: 40 units of wood, 50 hours.

Let x tables, y chairs. Maximise **Z = 30x + 20y** subject to 2x + y ≤ 40, x + 2y ≤ 50, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Solved: diet problem
steps.body:
Food P costs ₹4/unit with 3 units of vitamin A and 1 of B; food Q costs ₹6/unit with 1 of A and 2 of B. Need at least 6 of A and 4 of B.

Minimise **Z = 4x + 6y** subject to 3x + y ≥ 6, x + 2y ≥ 4, x, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ≥ for a resource limit (limits are usually ≤; requirements are ≥).
- Forgetting non-negativity constraints.
- Mixing up which coefficient goes with which variable — make a small table first.

steps.title: Make a table
steps.body: Rows = products, columns = resources + profit. Each column of resources becomes one constraint; the profit column becomes Z.

quiz.why: In a linear programming problem, the objective function to be maximised or minimised is linear in the variables.

lessons.title: Graphical method: corner point theorem

scenes.text: Shading all the carpenter's constraints on graph paper gives a polygon-shaped feasible region.
The best plan is always at a corner — just test each corner in Z.

steps.title: Corner point theorem
steps.body:
If the feasible region is **bounded**, Z = ax + by has both a maximum and a minimum, and each occurs at a **corner point**.

Method: 1) draw each constraint line, shade the correct side; 2) find corner points (solve pairs of lines); 3) evaluate Z at each; 4) pick the largest/smallest. If two adjacent corners give the same optimum, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.

steps.title: Solved: carpenter (max Z = 30x + 20y)
steps.body:
Lines 2x + y = 40 and x + 2y = 50 meet where x = 10, y = 20.

Corners: (0, 0) → 0; (20, 0) → 600; (0, 25) → 500; (10, 20) → 300 + 400 = **700**.

Make 10 tables and 20 chairs; maximum profit ₹700.

lessons.title: Unbounded regions and minimisation

scenes.text: For the diet problem the feasible region stretches away to infinity — you can always buy more food.
A minimum may still exist, but we must check it with an extra half-plane test.

steps.title: Rule for unbounded regions
steps.body:
Find the candidate value M at the corners.

- For a **minimum** candidate m: draw ax + by < m. If this open half-plane has **no point in common** with the feasible region, m is the minimum; otherwise no minimum.
- For a **maximum** candidate M: draw ax + by > M; if no common point, M is the maximum; otherwise Z has no maximum.

steps.title: Solved: min Z = 3x + 5y, x + 3y ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 2, x, y ≥ 0
steps.body:
Corners: (3, 0) → 9; (0, 2) → 10; intersection of x + 3y = 3 and x + y = 2: y = 1/2, x = 3/2 → 4.5 + 2.5 = **7**.

The region 3x + 5y < 7 lies below the corner (3/2, 1/2) and meets no feasible point ⇒ minimum **7** at (3/2, 1/2).

steps.title: Solved: diet min Z = 4x + 6y, 3x + y ≥ 6, x + 2y ≥ 4
steps.body:
Corners: (0, 6) → 36; (4, 0) → 16; intersection: from 3x + y = 6 and x + 2y = 4: x = 8/5, y = 6/5 → 6.4 + 7.2 = 13.6.

Half-plane 4x + 6y < 13.6 has no feasible point ⇒ minimum cost **₹13.60** at (1.6, 1.2).

steps.title: Solved: max Z = x + y on the same unbounded region
steps.body: Z grows without limit (e.g. (100, 0) is feasible, Z = 100) ⇒ **no maximum**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring the smallest corner value the minimum without the half-plane check.
- Claiming a maximum exists on an unbounded region just because corners give finite values.
- Arithmetic errors at the intersection corner.

lessons.title: Conditional probability

scenes.text: Two coins are tossed to decide batting order. Someone peeks and says 'at least one is a head'.
Now what is the chance both are heads? New information shrinks the sample space — that's conditional probability.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
For events E, F with P(F) > 0: **P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F)**.

Properties: P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1; P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F); P(A ∪ B|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P(A ∩ B|F).

steps.title: Solved: two coins, at least one head
steps.body:
S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. F = at least one head = {HH, HT, TH}, E = both heads = {HH}.

P(E|F) = (1/4)/(3/4) = **1/3** (not 1/2!).

lessons.title: Multiplication theorem and independent events

scenes.text: A jar has 10 black and 5 red marbles. Two are drawn one after another without replacement.
The chance both are black uses the multiplication rule with conditional probabilities.

steps.title: Multiplication theorem
steps.body: **P(E ∩ F) = P(E)·P(F|E) = P(F)·P(E|F)**. For three events: P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F|E)P(G|E ∩ F).

steps.title: Independence
steps.body:
E and F are **independent** if P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) (equivalently P(E|F) = P(E)). If E, F are independent, so are E and F′, E′ and F, E′ and F′.

Independent ≠ mutually exclusive: exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are always **dependent**.

steps.title: Solved: two students attempt a problem
steps.body:
P(A solves) = 1/2, P(B solves) = 1/3, independently.

P(solved) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − (1/2)(2/3) = **2/3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying probabilities of dependent events without conditioning.
- Assuming 'mutually exclusive' means 'independent'.
- Forgetting the complement trick for 'at least one'.

lessons.title: Total probability and Bayes' theorem

scenes.text: A test for a rare condition (1% of people) is 90% accurate on those who have it, but gives 5% false positives.
Aarav tests positive. Bayes' theorem shows his actual chance of having it is only about 15% — the base rate matters!

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
If E₁, …, Eₙ partition S (mutually exclusive, exhaustive, each P(Eᵢ) > 0) and A is any event:

- **Total probability**: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)
- **Bayes**: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ)

P(Eᵢ) are **prior** probabilities; P(Eᵢ|A) are **posterior** probabilities.

lessons.title: Random variables, probability distributions and mean

scenes.text: At a school fair, a game pays ₹10 for a six on a die and nothing otherwise; it costs ₹2 to play.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A **random variable** X assigns a real number to each outcome. Its **probability distribution** lists values xᵢ with pᵢ = P(X = xᵢ), where pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1.

**Mean (expectation)**: μ = E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ.

*Extension*: variance Var(X) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ − μ², standard deviation = √Var(X).

lessons.title: Knockout and league fixtures with numericals

scenes.text: 11 teams register for a football tournament and the organiser must prepare a draw.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**Knockout (single elimination):**
- Matches = **N − 1** (each match eliminates one team).
- Byes = (next power of 2) − N. Rounds = exponent of that power of 2.
- Teams in the first round = N − byes.

**League (round robin):**
- Single league matches = **N(N − 1) ÷ 2**; double league = N(N − 1).
- Rounds: N − 1 if N even; N if N odd.
Byes are given to avoid unequal rounds; they are placed in the lower half first (NCERT convention varies slightly by case; follow the rule of your board).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · knockout
steps.body: N = 11. Next power of 2 is 16 → byes = 16 − 11 = **5**. Matches = 11 − 1 = **10**. Rounds = log₂16 = **4**. First-round teams = 11 − 5 = 6 → 3 first-round matches.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · league
steps.body: N = 8. Single league = 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = **28 matches**; rounds = 7. Double league = **56**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to halve in the league formula.
- Using the previous power of 2 for byes.

steps.title: Nutrients
steps.body:
- **Macronutrients:** carbohydrates (main fuel, 4 kcal/g), proteins (repair and growth, 4 kcal/g), fats (concentrated energy, 9 kcal/g).
- **Micronutrients:** vitamins and minerals (iron for oxygen transport, calcium for bones).
- **Water**, **fibre**.
- **Balanced diet:** all nutrients in right proportion and quantity for age, sex, activity. Typical split for athletes: carbohydrates roughly half or more of energy, protein about 10–20%, fat about 20–35%.
- Indian examples: whole grains, pulses, milk products, vegetables, fruit, nuts; limit sugar, salt, trans fats.

steps.title: Solved example · energy
steps.body:
A snack has 40 g carbohydrate, 10 g protein, 5 g fat.
- Carbs: 40 × 4 = 160 kcal
- Protein: 10 × 4 = 40 kcal
- Fat: 5 × 9 = 45 kcal
- Total = **245 kcal**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 4 kcal for fat (it is 9).
- Believing athletes need only protein.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- Water regulates temperature, carries nutrients and removes wastes. Sweat loses water and electrolytes (sodium, potassium).
- Signs of dehydration: thirst, dark urine, headache, dizziness, fatigue.
- Drink fluids regularly before, during and after exercise; for most school-level activity water is enough; long hot sessions may need electrolytes.
- **Pre-event:** carbohydrate-rich meal 2–3 hours before, low in fat and fibre. **During:** fluids; quick carbohydrates in long events. **Post-event:** carbohydrates plus protein and fluids to restore glycogen and repair muscle.
- Avoid trying new foods on match day.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Abrasion:** scraped skin. **Laceration:** torn/cut skin. **Contusion:** bruise from direct blow. **Puncture:** deep narrow wound.
- **Sprain:** injury to a **ligament** (bone-to-bone). **Strain:** injury to a **muscle or tendon** (muscle-to-bone). Grades 1–3.
- **Causes:** poor warm-up, fatigue, faulty technique, unsafe ground or equipment, overtraining.
- **RICE:** Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation (PRICE adds Protection).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Twisted ankle with swelling and pain, can bear partial weight: likely sprain. Action: stop play, rest, apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes, compress with a bandage, elevate; seek medical help if severe pain, deformity, or inability to bear weight.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting ice directly on skin.
- Confusing sprain (ligament) with strain (muscle/tendon).
- Returning to play too early. This is general first-aid education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Fractures
steps.body:
A **fracture** is a break in a bone. Types: **simple/closed** (skin intact), **compound/open** (bone through skin), **greenstick** (incomplete, in children), **comminuted** (several pieces), **stress fracture** (tiny crack from repetitive load). **Dislocation:** bone displaced from joint.
Signs: severe pain, swelling, deformity, inability to move, tenderness.
First aid: keep still, **do not straighten or push the bone back**, immobilise the joint above and below with a splint or sling, cover open wounds with a clean cloth, control bleeding by pressing around it, treat for shock, **call 112 / go to hospital**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Forearm fracture suspected: support the arm in a sling, splint with a rolled newspaper or board padded with cloth, check fingers for colour and warmth, arrange transport. Do not give food or drink if surgery may be needed.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Trying to realign the bone. Only trained professionals should do that.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Biomechanics and Sports

scenes.text: A sprinter pushes back against the blocks and the blocks push her forward.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
**Biomechanics** applies mechanics to human movement.
1. **Inertia:** a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a net force acts (a football stays until kicked).
2. **F = m × a:** acceleration is proportional to force and inversely to mass.
3. **Action–reaction:** every action has an equal and opposite reaction (jumping pushes ground down, ground pushes you up).
Other: **momentum = mass × velocity**; **impulse = force × time**; speed = distance ÷ time.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A 0.45 kg football accelerates at 40 m/s² when kicked. F = 0.45 × 40 = **18 N**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A 60 kg sprinter runs at 10 m/s: momentum = 60 × 10 = **600 kg·m/s**. A runner covering 100 m in 12.5 s has speed 100 ÷ 12.5 = **8 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using grams instead of kg in F = ma.

scenes.text: When you stand on your toes, your foot acts like a lever.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Lever:** rigid bar turning about a **fulcrum** with effort and load.
- **First class:** fulcrum between effort and load (neck nodding).
- **Second class:** load between fulcrum and effort (calf raise on toes).
- **Third class:** effort between fulcrum and load (biceps curl) — most common in the body; gives speed and range.
**Equilibrium:** static (at rest) and dynamic. Stability rises with a lower centre of gravity, wider base, greater mass and keeping the line of gravity within the base.
**Friction:** opposes motion; helpful for grip (spikes), harmful in joints (reduced by synovial fluid).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Why does a wrestler crouch low and spread feet? Lowers the centre of gravity and widens the base → better stability against being pushed.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling the elbow in biceps curl a second-class lever; it is third class.

Anatomical terms: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, rotation, circumduction. Planes: sagittal, frontal, transverse.

lessons.title: Electric charge and its properties

scenes.text: On a dry winter evening Riya pulls off her woollen sweater and hears tiny crackles in the dark.
She even sees faint sparks. Her little brother asks: is the sweater full of lightning?
Riya realises friction has moved electrons between the wool and her shirt — the sweater and shirt now carry equal and opposite charge.

steps.title: What charge is
steps.body:
Electric charge is a basic property of matter that makes it feel electric forces. There are two kinds, called **positive** and **negative** (names given by Benjamin Franklin). **Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.**

When two bodies are rubbed, electrons move from one to the other. The body that loses electrons becomes positive; the one that gains becomes negative. Mass changes are negligible (an electron is only 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg). SI unit of charge: **coulomb (C)**.

steps.title: Conductors, insulators and charging by induction
steps.body:
- **Conductors** (metals, the human body, earth) let charge move freely.
- **Insulators** (glass, plastic, rubber) hold charge where it is placed.
- **Charging by induction:** bring a charged rod near a neutral metal sphere, earth the far side, remove the earth connection, then remove the rod. The sphere keeps a charge *opposite* to the rod, with no contact.
- A charged body attracts a neutral light object (paper bits) because it induces opposite charge on the near side.

steps.title: Three basic properties
steps.body:
- **Additivity:** total charge is the algebraic sum: +3 μC, −5 μC and +1 μC together make −1 μC.
- **Conservation:** charge can neither be created nor destroyed in an isolated system, only transferred. (In pair production a γ-photon creates an electron and a positron — net charge still zero.)
- **Quantisation:** every free charge is an integer multiple of e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C: **q = ne**, n = 0, ±1, ±2, …

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** How many electrons must be removed from a neutral body to give it +1 μC?
- n = q/e = 1×10⁻⁶ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹
- n = **6.25×10¹²** electrons.

**Ex 2.** Can a body carry 2.4×10⁻¹⁹ C?
- n = 2.4×10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5
- n must be an integer, so **no**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying protons move during rubbing — only electrons move in solids.
- Forgetting that quantisation is invisible at large scales: 1 μC already contains trillions of e, so charge looks continuous.
- Mixing up induction (no contact, opposite charge) with conduction (contact, same sign charge).

statements.s: A body becomes positively charged by gaining protons.
statements.why: It loses electrons; protons stay locked in nuclei.

statements.s: Charge 4.8×10⁻¹⁹ C is possible on an isolated body.
In charging by induction the body gets the same sign of charge as the inducing rod.
Total charge of an isolated system stays constant.

quiz.q: The SI unit of charge is
quiz.why: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb. 1 C is the charge carried by a current of 1 A in 1 s.

quiz.q: The smallest free charge observed is
quiz.why: Charge comes in whole multiples of e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, the charge of an electron or proton, so this is the smallest free charge.

quiz.q: A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive because
quiz.why: Rubbing transfers electrons. Glass loses electrons to silk, so glass is left positive and silk negative.
Charge must be an integer multiple of e (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C). 8.0×10⁻²⁰ C is half of e, so it is not possible.

quiz.q: A neutral paper bit is attracted by a charged comb because
options: the comb induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper
quiz.why: The charged comb induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper, which is closer than the like charge on the far side. So the attraction is stronger than the repulsion.

lessons.title: Coulomb's law and superposition

scenes.text: In the physics lab two charged balloons hang from threads and push each other apart.
Kabir moves them twice as close; the threads swing out far more — not double, but four times the force.
His teacher says: that is the inverse-square law Coulomb measured in 1785 with a torsion balance.

steps.title: Coulomb's law
steps.body:
The force between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by r in vacuum:

**F = k q₁q₂ / r²**, with k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻²

ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻² is the permittivity of free space. The force acts along the line joining the charges; repulsive for like charges, attractive for unlike.

**Vector form:** F₂₁ (force on q₂ by q₁) = k q₁q₂ r̂₂₁ / r², where r̂₂₁ points from q₁ to q₂. Note F₁₂ = −F₂₁ (Newton's third law).

steps.title: In a medium
steps.body: In a medium of permittivity ε = Kε₀ the force becomes **F = q₁q₂ / (4πε₀K r²)**, i.e. reduced K times. K (dielectric constant or relative permittivity εᵣ) is 1 for vacuum, ≈ 1.0006 for air and about 80 for water.

steps.title: Superposition principle
steps.body:
The force on a charge due to several charges is the **vector sum** of the forces due to each one taken alone — each pair interaction is unaffected by the others.

**F₁ = F₁₂ + F₁₃ + … + F₁ₙ**

Add vectors by components, or use the parallelogram rule: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Charges 2 μC and 3 μC are 30 cm apart in air. Force?
- F = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶)(3×10⁻⁶) / (0.3)²
- = 9×10⁹ × 6×10⁻¹² / 0.09 = **0.6 N (repulsive)**.
- In oil of K = 3 the same pair feels 0.6/3 = **0.2 N**.

**Ex 2.** Three equal charges q sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. Net force on one?
- Each of the other two pushes with F = kq²/a²; the angle between the two forces is 60°.
- R = √(F² + F² + 2F² cos 60°) = √3 F
- **F_net = √3 kq²/a²**, directed along the bisector, away from the triangle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert μC to C (×10⁻⁶) and cm to m.
- Adding forces as numbers instead of vectors.
- Using the medium formula with K multiplied instead of divided.
- Applying Coulomb's law directly to large charged bodies that are not point-like.

steps.title: JEE shortcut
steps.body: For a charge placed between two like charges q₁ and q₂ (distance d apart) to be in equilibrium, it must sit at x = d√q₁/(√q₁ + √q₂) from q₁. For unlike charges the null point lies outside, nearer the smaller charge.

quiz.why: The force varies as 1/r². Halving the distance makes the force (1/(1/2))² = 4 times larger.

quiz.why: In Coulomb's law k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻².

lessons.title: Electric field, field lines and the dipole

scenes.text: Ananya imagines every point around a charge carrying an arrow that says: a positive test charge here would be pushed this way, this hard.
That map of arrows is the electric field.
In a microwave oven, water molecules — tiny dipoles — twist back and forth in such a field, and that motion heats the food.

steps.title: Electric field
steps.body:
**E = F/q₀** (force per unit positive test charge, q₀ → 0). Unit N/C (= V/m).

Field of a point charge: **E = kq/r²**, radially outward for +q, inward for −q. Fields from many charges add as vectors (superposition).

**Field lines:** start on + charges and end on − charges (or infinity); never cross (field has one direction at a point); crowded where the field is strong; never form closed loops in electrostatics; are perpendicular to a conductor's surface.

steps.title: Electric dipole and its field
steps.body:
A dipole is a pair +q and −q separated by 2a. **Dipole moment p = q × 2a**, a vector from −q to +q, unit C m.

**On the axis** at distance r from the centre:
E = kq[1/(r−a)² − 1/(r+a)²] = k(4qar)/(r²−a²)² = 2kpr/(r²−a²)²
For r ≫ a: **E_axial = 2kp/r³**, along p.

**On the equatorial line:** the two fields have equal magnitude kq/(r²+a²); their components along the line cancel and those parallel to the axis add:
E = 2kq·a/(r²+a²)^(3/2) = kp/(r²+a²)^(3/2)
For r ≫ a: **E_eq = kp/r³**, opposite to p. So E_axial = 2 E_eq at equal distances. A dipole field falls as 1/r³.

steps.title: Dipole in a uniform field
steps.body:
The forces +qE and −qE are equal and opposite, so **net force = 0**, but they form a couple:

**τ = pE sin θ**, vector form **τ = p × E**.

The torque turns the dipole to align p with E (θ = 0 is stable equilibrium, θ = 180° unstable). In a non-uniform field there is also a net force.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Field 20 cm from a 4 μC charge:
- E = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁶ / (0.2)² = **9×10⁵ N/C**, away from the charge.

**Ex 2.** Charges ±10 μC are 2 mm apart. (a) p = 10×10⁻⁶ × 2×10⁻³ = **2×10⁻⁸ C m**. (b) Equatorial field at 10 cm: E = kp/r³ = 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁸ / 10⁻³ = **1.8×10⁵ N/C**; axial field at 10 cm = **3.6×10⁵ N/C**. (c) In a uniform field 5×10⁴ N/C at 30°: τ = 2×10⁻⁸ × 5×10⁴ × 0.5 = **5×10⁻⁴ N m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing p from + to −: it points from −q to +q.
- Using 1/r² for a dipole at large distance — it is 1/r³.
- Saying a dipole in a uniform field moves: it only rotates.
- Letting field lines cross or start in empty space.

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its expression (r ≫ a).

quiz.q: The SI unit of electric field is
quiz.why: Electric field is force per unit charge, so its unit is N/C, which is also V/m.

options: the field at a point has a unique direction
quiz.why: If two field lines crossed, the field at the crossing point would have two directions, which is impossible. So they never cross.

quiz.q: The direction of a dipole moment is
quiz.why: By convention the dipole moment p points from the negative charge to the positive charge.

quiz.q: At the same large distance, axial field : equatorial field =
quiz.why: Axial field = 2kp/r³ and equatorial field = kp/r³, so the ratio is 2 : 1.

quiz.q: A dipole in a uniform field experiences
quiz.why: In a uniform field the two forces on a dipole are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple that gives torque pE sin θ.

quiz.q: Torque on a dipole is maximum when the angle between p and E is
quiz.why: Torque = pE sin θ, which is maximum when sin θ = 1, that is at 90°.

lessons.title: Electric flux and Gauss's law

scenes.text: Dev holds a hoop in a steady breeze. Facing the wind, lots of air goes through; turned sideways, none.
Electric flux works the same way — it measures how much field passes through a surface, depending on its tilt.
Gauss found something beautiful: for any closed surface, the total flux depends only on the charge inside.

steps.title: Electric flux
steps.body:
For a small area ΔS with outward normal: **ΔΦ = E·ΔS = E ΔS cos θ**. Total flux Φ = ∮ E·dS. Unit N m² C⁻¹ (= V m). Flux is a scalar.

For a closed surface, outward flux is positive, inward flux negative.

steps.title: Continuous charge distributions
steps.body:
- Linear charge density **λ = dq/dl** (C/m) — wires, rings.
- Surface charge density **σ = dq/dS** (C/m²) — sheets, conductor surfaces.
- Volume charge density **ρ = dq/dV** (C/m³).
The field is found by adding contributions k dq/r² as vectors (integration).

steps.title: Gauss's law
steps.body:
**Φ = ∮ E·dS = q_enclosed / ε₀**

- Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux (lines entering also leave).
- The surface chosen (a *Gaussian surface*) is imaginary and must not pass through a discrete charge.
- The E in the integral is the field due to *all* charges, but only enclosed charge sets the total flux.
- Gauss's law is most useful when symmetry makes E constant over the surface.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A uniform field E = 200 N/C (along x) passes through a 10 cm × 10 cm square whose normal makes 60° with x.
- Φ = EA cos θ = 200 × 0.01 × 0.5 = **1 N m²/C**.

**Ex 2.** A 1 μC charge is at the centre of a cube.
- Total flux = q/ε₀ = 10⁻⁶ / 8.854×10⁻¹² ≈ **1.13×10⁵ N m²/C**.
- By symmetry each of the 6 faces gets **1.88×10⁴ N m²/C**.
- If the charge were moved off-centre (still inside) the total stays 1.13×10⁵, but face values change.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sin θ instead of cos θ: θ is the angle between E and the *normal*, not the surface.
- Thinking the field on the Gaussian surface is due only to enclosed charge.
- Counting a charge outside the surface in q_enclosed.
- For a charge at a cube corner, the flux through the cube is q/(8ε₀) (only 1/8 is enclosed).

activity.prompt: Complete Gauss's law statements.
activity.text: Total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed divided by ___. A charge outside the surface gives a net flux of ___. A charge at the centre of a cube sends 1/___ of the total flux through each face.

quiz.why: Flux is E·S, a dot product, so it is a scalar.

quiz.q: A surface encloses charges +3 μC and −3 μC. The net flux is
quiz.why: By Gauss's law flux = (net enclosed charge)/ε₀. +3 μC and −3 μC add up to zero, so the net flux is zero.

quiz.q: If the radius of a Gaussian sphere around a point charge is doubled, the flux
quiz.why: By Gauss's law, flux depends only on the enclosed charge, not on the size of the surface, so it stays the same.
Flux = E × area, so its unit is (N/C) × m², which is N m² C⁻¹.

quiz.q: A charge q is at the corner of a cube. Flux through the cube is
quiz.why: Eight such cubes meeting at a point surround the charge completely, so each cube gets one eighth of q/ε₀, that is q/8ε₀.

lessons.title: Applications of Gauss's law

story.title: Why the car is safe in lightning

scenes.text: Ishaan's family is driving through a thunderstorm when lightning strikes nearby.
His father calmly says the metal body of a car shields them.
Gauss's law explains it: charge on a closed conductor sits on the outside, and the field inside the cavity is zero.

steps.title: Infinite straight line charge (λ)
steps.body:
Take a coaxial cylinder of radius r and length l. E is radial, so flux through the flat ends is zero; curved surface: E·2πrl.

E·2πrl = λl/ε₀ ⇒ **E = λ/(2πε₀ r) = 2kλ/r**, radial. E ∝ 1/r.

steps.title: Infinite plane sheet (σ)
steps.body:
Take a cylinder (pillbox) of cross-section A piercing the sheet. Flux through the curved side is zero; each flat face gives EA.

2EA = σA/ε₀ ⇒ **E = σ/(2ε₀)**, independent of distance.

Two parallel sheets with +σ and −σ: fields add between them, **E = σ/ε₀**, and cancel outside (this is the parallel-plate capacitor).

steps.title: Thin spherical shell (charge q, radius R)
steps.body:
- **Outside (r > R):** Gaussian sphere of radius r: E·4πr² = q/ε₀ ⇒ **E = kq/r²** — as if all charge were at the centre.
- **On the surface:** E = kq/R² = σ/ε₀.
- **Inside (r < R):** no enclosed charge ⇒ **E = 0**.
The same zero-field result explains electrostatic shielding.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A long wire carries λ = 2 μC/m. Field at 10 cm?
- E = 2kλ/r = 2 × 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶ / 0.1 = **3.6×10⁵ N/C**.

**Ex 2.** A large sheet has σ = 8.85×10⁻¹⁰ C/m².
- E = σ/(2ε₀) = 8.85×10⁻¹⁰ / (2 × 8.85×10⁻¹²) = **50 N/C**.
- Between two such oppositely charged plates: σ/ε₀ = **100 N/C**; outside: 0.

**Ex 3.** A shell of radius 10 cm has 3 μC. Field at 5 cm is **0**; at 20 cm: 9×10⁹ × 3×10⁻⁶/0.04 = **6.75×10⁵ N/C**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ/ε₀ for a single isolated sheet (that is for a conductor surface or two plates).
- Thinking E inside a charged shell is non-zero 'because charge is nearby'.
- Forgetting the 2 in E = λ/(2πε₀r).

steps.title: Where you meet this
steps.body: Sensitive electronics are wrapped in metal cages (Faraday cages); coaxial TV cables use an outer conductor to shield the signal; the plate-charge result underlies every capacitor in your phone.

activity.prompt: How does E vary with distance r?

quiz.q: Field due to an infinite sheet of charge
quiz.why: For an infinite plane sheet E = σ/2ε₀, with no dependence on distance, since the field lines are parallel.

quiz.q: Field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is
quiz.why: A Gaussian surface inside a charged shell encloses no charge, so by Gauss's law the field inside is zero.

quiz.q: For an infinite line charge, if r is tripled, E becomes
quiz.why: For an infinite line charge E ∝ 1/r. If r is tripled, E becomes one third.

quiz.q: Field between two large oppositely charged parallel plates is
quiz.why: Each plate gives σ/2ε₀. Between oppositely charged plates the two fields point the same way and add to σ/ε₀.

options: field inside a conductor cavity being zero
quiz.why: Inside a conductor's cavity the field is zero, so the region is protected from outside fields. This is electrostatic shielding.

questions.q: Which property makes charge look continuous in everyday life?

questions.why: The charge e is tiny compared with everyday charges (even 1 μC is about 6×10¹² e), so charge appears to flow continuously.

questions.q: The force between two charges is F. Each charge is doubled and distance doubled. New force:
questions.why: F ∝ q₁q₂/r². Doubling both charges gives ×4 and doubling distance gives ÷4, so the force is unchanged at F.

questions.q: Electric field lines are
questions.why: In equilibrium there is no tangential field on a conductor's surface, so field lines meet it at right angles.

questions.q: Assertion: A dipole in a uniform field has zero net force. Reason: the forces on its two charges are equal and opposite.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. In a uniform field, the forces on the two charges are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero and there is only a couple.

questions.why: A dipole has equal and opposite charges, so the net enclosed charge is zero and by Gauss's law the flux is zero.

questions.why: For zero field, k·9/x² = k·4/(50 − x)², so 3/x = 2/(50 − x), giving x = 30 cm from the 9 μC charge.

The field at 1 m on the axis of a short dipole is 4 N/C. Field at 2 m on its equatorial line:
questions.why: Axial field 2kp/r³ = 4 at r = 1 m gives kp = 2. Equatorial at r = 2 m is kp/r³ = 2/8 = 0.25 N/C.

questions.why: For balance qE = mg, so q = (3.2×10⁻¹⁵ × 10)/10⁵ = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C. Dividing by e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C gives 2 excess electrons.

questions.why: A charge at the centre has total flux q/ε₀. By symmetry the 6 faces share it equally, so each gets q/6ε₀.

Assertion: The field due to an infinite plane sheet does not depend on distance. Reason: field lines from the sheet are parallel and uniform.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. The field lines of an infinite sheet are parallel and equally spaced, so the field is uniform and independent of distance.

questions.q: Three charges +q each sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle. Field at the centroid is
questions.why: At the centroid the three fields have equal magnitude and are 120° apart, so their vector sum is zero.

questions.q: A uniform field E = 3î + 4ĵ N/C passes through a 2 m² area lying in the y–z plane. Flux:
questions.why: The area in the y–z plane has its normal along x, so only Eₓ counts: Φ = 3 × 2 = 6 N m²/C.

questions.q: Two identical small spheres carry 6 μC and −2 μC. They touch and are returned to the same separation. The ratio new force/old force is
questions.why: On touching, the charges share equally: (6 − 2)/2 = +2 μC each. F′/F = (2 × 2)/(6 × 2) = 1/3, and the force is now repulsive.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
courses.summary: Electric potential and potential difference, potential of a point charge, dipole and system of charges, equipotential surfaces, potential energy, conductors and dielectrics, capacitors and their combinations, and energy stored — with derivations and numericals. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can calculate potential due to point charges, dipoles and systems of charges.
Learners can relate E and V (E = −dV/dr) and describe equipotential surfaces.
Learners can derive C = ε₀A/d and the effect of a dielectric.
Learners can solve series/parallel capacitor networks and energy-sharing problems.

lessons.title: Electric potential and potential difference

scenes.text: Meher pushes a shopping cart up a ramp; it gains gravitational potential energy.
Pushing a positive charge towards another positive charge is similar: you do work against the repulsion, and energy is stored.
'Volts' on a battery measure exactly this — work done per unit charge.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Electrostatic force is **conservative**: the work done in moving a charge between two points does not depend on the path.

**Potential at a point:** V = W/q — the work done by an external agent in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point *without acceleration*. Unit **volt** (1 V = 1 J/C). Scalar.

**Potential difference:** V_B − V_A = W_AB/q.

steps.title: Potential due to a point charge
steps.body:
Bring a unit charge from ∞ to r against the field kq/r'²:
V = −∫(∞→r) kq/r'² dr' = **kq/r**.
Positive for +q, negative for −q; falls as 1/r (field falls as 1/r²).

steps.title: Dipole and system of charges
steps.body:
**Dipole:** at distance r (r ≫ a) at angle θ from the axis, **V = kp cos θ / r²**.
- On the axis (θ = 0): V = kp/r².
- On the equatorial line (θ = 90°): **V = 0** (but E ≠ 0!).

**System of charges:** potentials add as scalars: V = k Σ qᵢ/rᵢ.

**Uniformly charged shell:** V = kq/r outside, and V = kq/R (constant) everywhere inside.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Potential 9 cm from a 4×10⁻⁷ C charge, and work to bring 2×10⁻⁹ C there from infinity.
- V = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁷ / 0.09 = **4×10⁴ V**.
- W = qV = 2×10⁻⁹ × 4×10⁴ = **8×10⁻⁵ J**.

**Ex 2.** +4 μC and −1 μC are 15 cm apart. Where on the line is V = 0?
- Between them, x from +4 μC: 4/x = 1/(15 − x) ⇒ x = **12 cm**.
- Outside, beyond −1 μC: 4/x = 1/(x − 15) ⇒ x = **20 cm** (5 cm beyond the smaller charge).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding potentials as vectors — potential is a scalar; keep the sign of each charge.
- Thinking V = 0 means E = 0 (dipole equatorial line: V = 0, E ≠ 0).
- Thinking E = 0 means V = 0 (inside a shell: E = 0, V = kq/R).

activity.prompt: Find the potential (in volts) at the centre of a square of side 2√2 m with charges +2 μC, +2 μC, −1 μC and +1 μC at its corners. (Each corner is 2 m from the centre.)

quiz.why: Potential is work per unit charge, which is a scalar.
A volt is a joule per coulomb, since potential is energy per unit charge.

quiz.q: Potential on the equatorial line of a dipole is
quiz.why: On the equatorial line the potentials of +q and −q cancel, so the potential is zero.

quiz.q: Potential due to a point charge varies as
quiz.why: For a point charge V = kq/r, so potential varies as 1/r.

quiz.q: Inside a charged conducting sphere the potential is
options: constant, equal to the surface value
quiz.why: The field inside a conductor is zero, so there is no potential difference there, and the potential stays constant at the surface value.

lessons.title: Equipotential surfaces and potential energy

story.title: Contour lines on a hill map

scenes.text: On a trekking map, Arjun sees contour lines joining points of equal height.
Walking along a contour costs no effort against gravity; climbing straight across contours is steepest.
Equipotential surfaces are the contour lines of electricity, and the field always points 'straight downhill'.

steps.title: Equipotential surfaces
steps.body:
A surface on which V is the same everywhere.
- No work is done in moving a charge along it.
- **E is always perpendicular** to an equipotential surface.
- Point charge: concentric spheres. Uniform field: parallel planes perpendicular to E.
- Closely spaced surfaces mean a strong field.
- Two equipotentials never intersect.

steps.title: Relation between E and V
steps.body: **E = −dV/dr** — the field points in the direction of steepest *decrease* of potential, and its magnitude is the potential gradient. For a uniform field: **E = V/d**. Unit V/m = N/C.

steps.title: Potential energy of charges
steps.body:
- **Two charges:** U = kq₁q₂/r₁₂ (work to assemble them from infinity). Negative for unlike charges (bound system).
- **Three charges:** U = k(q₁q₂/r₁₂ + q₂q₃/r₂₃ + q₁q₃/r₁₃).
- **Single charge in external potential V:** U = qV.
- **Dipole in a uniform field:** U(θ) = −pE cos θ (zero at θ = 90°). Work to rotate from θ₁ to θ₂: W = pE(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂). From 0° to 180°: W = 2pE.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** U for +2 μC and −3 μC at 10 cm:
- U = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶)(−3×10⁻⁶)/0.1 = **−0.54 J** (0.54 J must be supplied to separate them fully).

**Ex 2.** A dipole p = 2×10⁻⁸ C m is in E = 5×10⁴ N/C. Work to turn it from aligned to anti-aligned:
- W = pE(cos 0° − cos 180°) = 2pE = **2×10⁻³ J**.

**Ex 3.** V = 5x² volts (x in m). Field at x = 2 m:
- E = −dV/dx = −10x = **−20 V/m** (points towards −x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign in E = −dV/dr.
- Counting each pair twice in the three-charge energy formula.
- Writing U = pE cos θ (the sign is negative; minimum energy is at θ = 0).

statements.s: Electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.
statements.why: Otherwise work would be done moving along the surface.

statements.s: Work is needed to move a charge along an equipotential surface.
A dipole has minimum potential energy when aligned with the field.
Two equipotential surfaces can intersect.
statements.why: A point cannot have two values of potential.

quiz.q: E and V are related by
quiz.why: The electric field is the negative gradient of potential: E = −dV/dr.

quiz.q: Equipotential surfaces of a point charge are
quiz.why: V = kq/r depends only on distance from the charge, so surfaces of equal V are concentric spheres.

quiz.q: Potential energy of two unlike charges is
quiz.why: Potential energy U = kq₁q₂/r. For unlike charges q₁q₂ is negative, so U is negative.

quiz.q: Work done to rotate a dipole from 0° to 180° in field E is
quiz.why: Energy is U = −pE cos θ. Going from 0° to 180° changes it from −pE to +pE, so the work done is 2pE.

quiz.q: A uniform field of 500 V/m exists between plates 4 mm apart. The p.d. is
quiz.why: For a uniform field V = Ed = 500 × 0.004 = 2 V.

lessons.title: Conductors and dielectrics in electric fields

scenes.text: Zoya rubs a ruler and holds it near a stream of tap water; the stream bends towards it.
Water molecules are permanent dipoles; they line up and get pulled into the stronger field.
Materials respond to fields in two very different ways — conductors move charge freely, dielectrics only polarise.

steps.title: Electrostatics of conductors
steps.body:
1. **E = 0 inside** the material of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
2. Just outside, **E is normal** to the surface and E = σ/ε₀.
3. **Excess charge resides only on the surface.**
4. **Potential is constant** throughout the volume and on the surface.
5. Charge density is higher at sharp points (this is why lightning conductors are pointed).
6. **Electrostatic shielding:** a cavity inside a conductor (with no charge in it) has zero field.

steps.title: Dielectrics and polarisation
steps.body:
Dielectrics are insulators that get **polarised** in a field.
- **Non-polar molecules** (O₂, H₂, CO₂): centres of + and − charge coincide; a field *induces* dipoles.
- **Polar molecules** (H₂O, HCl): permanent dipoles, randomly oriented, which *align* in a field.

**Polarisation P** = dipole moment per unit volume = χₑ E (for linear isotropic dielectrics). Bound surface charges reduce the field inside: **E = E₀/K**, with **K = 1 + χₑ** (in suitable units).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm has 2 μC. (a) Field at the centre: **0**. (b) Potential at the centre: kq/R = 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶/0.1 = **1.8×10⁵ V**. (c) Surface charge density: σ = q/4πR² = 2×10⁻⁶/(4π × 0.01) ≈ **1.6×10⁻⁵ C/m²**.

**Ex 2.** A field of 1000 V/m acts across a slab of K = 4 placed between plates (no air gap). Field inside the slab: E = 1000/4 = **250 V/m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the field inside a conductor is zero even while current flows — the result is for electrostatics only.
- Thinking dielectrics conduct; they only shift charge slightly within molecules.
- Forgetting that the potential inside a conductor is not zero, only constant.

steps.title: Real-world links
steps.body: Pointed lightning rods, earthing of appliances, the antistatic bags electronics ship in, and the high-K ceramics used in tiny capacitors all come from these ideas.

activity.prompt: Sort each molecule: polar or non-polar?

quiz.q: Excess charge on a conductor resides
quiz.why: Like charges repel each other and move as far apart as they can, so the excess charge sits on the outer surface of a conductor.

quiz.q: Field just outside a charged conductor is
quiz.why: Just outside a charged conductor the field is σ/ε₀ and normal to the surface. A tangential component would make surface charges move.

quiz.q: A dielectric placed in a field reduces the field inside to
quiz.why: Bound charges in the dielectric set up an opposing field, so the net field inside is reduced to E₀/K.
CO₂ is linear and symmetric, so the dipole moments of its two C=O bonds cancel and it is non-polar. H₂O, NH₃ and HCl are polar.

quiz.q: Charge density on an irregular conductor is greatest at
quiz.why: Charge density is higher where the radius of curvature is smaller, which is at sharp points.

lessons.title: Capacitors and their combinations

scenes.text: Nisha's old camera whines for a few seconds before the flash is ready.
During the whine a capacitor slowly fills with charge from the small battery.
Then it dumps all that energy in a millisecond — a burst no battery could give directly.

steps.title: Capacitance
steps.body: A capacitor = two conductors separated by an insulator. **C = Q/V**. Unit **farad** (1 F = 1 C/V); practical units μF, nF, pF. C depends only on geometry and the medium, not on Q or V.

steps.title: Parallel-plate capacitor (derivation)
steps.body:
Plates of area A, separation d, charges ±Q, σ = Q/A.
- Field between plates: E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A) (fields outside cancel).
- p.d.: V = Ed = Qd/(ε₀A).
- **C = Q/V = ε₀A/d**.

With a dielectric filling the gap: **C = Kε₀A/d = KC₀**.
With a slab of thickness t (< d): **C = ε₀A/(d − t + t/K)**; a metal slab (K → ∞) gives ε₀A/(d − t).

steps.title: Combinations
steps.body:
- **Series** (same Q on each): V = V₁ + V₂ + … ⇒ **1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …** (result smaller than the smallest).
- **Parallel** (same V across each): Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + … ⇒ **C = C₁ + C₂ + …**
For two in series: C = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A = 6×10⁻³ m², d = 3 mm (air).
- C = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 6×10⁻³ / 3×10⁻³ = **1.77×10⁻¹¹ F ≈ 17.7 pF**.
- With mica (K = 6) filling the gap: **106 pF**.

**Ex 2.** 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF across 12 V.
- Series: 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 ⇒ **C = 1 μF**; Q = 12 μC on each; V across 2 μF = 6 V, 3 μF = 4 V, 6 μF = 2 V.
- Parallel: C = **11 μF**; total Q = 132 μC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the resistor formulas the wrong way round: capacitors in *parallel* add directly.
- Assuming equal voltage on series capacitors — it is equal *charge*.
- Forgetting to convert mm to m and cm² to m² in C = ε₀A/d.

steps.title: Battery connected or not?
steps.body: When a dielectric is inserted: **battery connected** ⇒ V fixed, C, Q and U increase K times. **Battery disconnected** ⇒ Q fixed, C up K times, V and U fall K times.

quiz.q: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is
quiz.why: For a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d, from E = σ/ε₀ and V = Ed.

quiz.q: If plate separation is doubled (battery removed), capacitance
quiz.why: C = ε₀A/d, so C ∝ 1/d, and doubling the separation halves the capacitance.

quiz.q: Equivalent of two 6 μF capacitors in series is
quiz.why: In series 1/C = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so C = 3 μF.

quiz.q: In a series combination each capacitor has the same
quiz.why: In series the same charge flows through every capacitor, so each carries the same charge.

quiz.q: Filling the gap with a dielectric K = 5 changes C₀ to
quiz.why: A dielectric of constant K multiplies the capacitance by K, so C = 5C₀.

quiz.q: A metal slab of thickness d/2 is inserted into a parallel-plate capacitor of gap d. C becomes
quiz.why: A metal slab of thickness t makes the effective gap d − t = d/2, so C = ε₀A/(d/2) = 2C₀.

lessons.title: Energy stored in a capacitor

scenes.text: Kunal connects a full water tank to an empty one with a pipe; water flows until the levels match.
Some energy is lost as the water sloshes and churns.
Connecting a charged capacitor to an uncharged one is the same — charge shares and some energy is lost as heat.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
While charging, at an instant the charge is q and p.d. q/C. Work to add dq: dW = (q/C) dq.
W = ∫₀^Q (q/C) dq = Q²/2C.

**U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV**.

steps.title: Energy density
steps.body:
For a parallel-plate capacitor: U = ½CV² = ½(ε₀A/d)(Ed)² = ½ε₀E² × (Ad).
Volume between plates = Ad, so the **energy density u = ½ε₀E²** (J/m³). In a dielectric: u = ½Kε₀E². Energy is stored *in the field*.

steps.title: Sharing of charge
steps.body:
Two capacitors C₁ (at V₁) and C₂ (at V₂) joined positive to positive:
- Common potential **V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂)** (charge conserved).
- **Energy lost = C₁C₂(V₁ − V₂)² / 2(C₁ + C₂)** — dissipated as heat and radiation in the wires. Energy is never gained.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 12 pF capacitor is charged to 50 V.
- U = ½ × 12×10⁻¹² × 50² = **1.5×10⁻⁸ J**.

**Ex 2.** A 2 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is connected to an uncharged 2 μF capacitor.
- Common V = (2×100 + 0)/4 = **50 V**.
- Initial U = ½ × 2×10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.01 J; final U = ½ × 4×10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 0.005 J.
- **Loss = 0.005 J** (half!). Check with formula: (2×2/2×4) × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.005 J ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using U = ½QV with the final V but initial Q.
- Expecting energy to be conserved when capacitors share charge.
- For a capacitor charged by a battery, the battery supplies QV but only ½QV is stored — the other half is lost in the circuit resistance.

bands.text: Up to 20 V: U = ½CV² ≤ 2 mJ — tiny.
At 50 V: U = 12.5 mJ. Doubling V quadruples energy.
At 100 V: U = 50 mJ — 25 times the 20 V value, because U ∝ V².

quiz.q: Energy stored in a capacitor is
quiz.why: The energy stored is U = ½CV², which equals Q²/2C and ½QV.

quiz.q: Energy density of an electric field in vacuum is
quiz.why: The energy per unit volume of an electric field in vacuum is ½ε₀E².

quiz.q: Doubling the charge on a capacitor makes its energy
quiz.why: U = Q²/2C, so U ∝ Q². Doubling the charge makes the energy four times.

quiz.q: When two capacitors share charge, total energy
quiz.why: When two capacitors share charge, current flows between them and some energy is lost as heat, so the total energy decreases.

Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can derive I = neAv_d and ρ = m/(ne²τ).
