lessons.title: Current, drift velocity and mobility

scenes.text: Aarav flips a switch and the bulb glows instantly, yet he reads that electrons in the wire crawl at less than a millimetre per second.
His teacher compares it to a packed metro tube: push one person in at one end and someone pops out at the other at once.
The signal (the field) travels near light speed; the electrons themselves just drift.

steps.title: Electric current
steps.body:
**I = dq/dt**; unit ampere (A) = C/s. Current is a scalar (it obeys algebraic, not vector, addition) even though it has a direction convention: conventional current flows from + to −, opposite to electron flow.

**Current density j = I/A** (A/m²), a vector along E.

steps.title: Drift velocity — derivation
steps.body:
Free electrons move randomly (≈10⁵ m/s) with zero average velocity. Apply a field E: each electron accelerates a = −eE/m between collisions. The average time between collisions is the **relaxation time τ**.

**v_d = −eEτ/m** (opposite to E).

In time Δt, electrons in a length v_dΔt of the wire (cross-section A, n electrons per m³) cross a section:
Δq = neAv_dΔt ⇒ **I = neAv_d**.

steps.title: Ohm's law from the microscopic picture
steps.body:
j = I/A = nev_d = ne(eEτ/m) = (ne²τ/m)E.
So **j = σE** with conductivity **σ = ne²τ/m** and resistivity **ρ = m/(ne²τ)**. Since E = V/l and j = I/A, this gives V = (ρl/A) I = IR — Ohm's law.

**Mobility μ = v_d/E = eτ/m** (m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A copper wire of cross-section 1.0×10⁻⁷ m² carries 1.5 A; n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³.
- v_d = I/(neA) = 1.5 / (8.5×10²⁸ × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0×10⁻⁷)
- = 1.5/1360 ≈ **1.1×10⁻³ m/s** (about 1 mm/s).

**Ex 2.** Relaxation time in copper (ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω m):
- τ = m/(ne²ρ) = 9.1×10⁻³¹ / (8.5×10²⁸ × 2.56×10⁻³⁸ × 1.7×10⁻⁸)
- ≈ **2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing drift speed (~mm/s) with thermal speed (~10⁵ m/s) or signal speed (~10⁸ m/s).
- Calling current a vector because it has a direction.
- Forgetting that for a given current, v_d is larger where the wire is thinner (v_d ∝ 1/A).

activity.prompt: A wire of cross-section 2×10⁻⁶ m² carries 3.2 A. If n = 1×10²⁹ m⁻³, find the drift speed in mm/s.

quiz.why: Electrons are negatively charged, so they drift opposite to the electric field.

quiz.q: I = neAv_d. If the area is halved for the same current, v_d
quiz.why: I = neAv_d, so for the same current v_d ∝ 1/A. Halving the area doubles the drift velocity.
ρ = m/(ne²τ), so resistivity depends on the number density of electrons and the relaxation time, not on length or area.
Mobility μ = v_d/E, the drift velocity per unit electric field.

quiz.q: Electric current is a scalar because
options: it does not follow vector addition laws
quiz.why: Current has direction along the wire, but it does not obey the vector addition rule. Currents at a junction add algebraically, so it is a scalar.

lessons.title: Ohm's law, resistivity and temperature

scenes.text: Kavya's toaster draws a big current for the first second, then settles down.
As the nichrome coil heats up its resistance rises, so the current falls a little.
Resistance depends on temperature — and in some materials it even drops on heating.

steps.title: Ohm's law and resistance
steps.body:
At constant temperature and physical conditions, **V = IR**. Unit ohm (Ω).

**R = ρl/A** where ρ (Ω m) is resistivity — a property of the material. Conductivity σ = 1/ρ.

**Non-ohmic devices** (diodes, thyristors, water voltameter, gallium arsenide) show non-linear or one-way V–I graphs, or more than one V for the same I.

steps.title: Effect of stretching a wire
steps.body: Volume stays constant (Al = constant). If length becomes n times, area becomes 1/n times, so **R becomes n² times**. If radius is halved (same volume), length is 4 times and R becomes 16 times.

steps.title: Temperature dependence
steps.body:
For metals: **ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]**, α > 0 (τ falls as ions vibrate more). Nichrome has a very small α and high ρ — ideal for heaters; manganin and constantan for standard resistors.

For **semiconductors** α < 0: ρ falls with temperature because n increases faster than τ decreases. Insulators: ρ very high.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A coil has 2.1 Ω at 27 °C and 2.7 Ω at 100 °C. Find α.
- α = (R₂ − R₁)/(R₁ΔT) = 0.6/(2.1 × 73)
- ≈ **3.9×10⁻³ °C⁻¹**.

**Ex 2.** A 1 m wire of 4 Ω is stretched to 3 m (volume constant).
- R' = n²R = 9 × 4 = **36 Ω**; resistivity is unchanged (same material).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking resistivity changes when a wire is stretched — resistance changes, resistivity does not.
- Treating every device as ohmic.
- Using α in R = R₀(1 + αΔT) with ΔT in kelvin vs °C — any is fine since it is a *difference*.

statements.s: Resistivity of copper increases on heating.
Doubling the length of a wire by stretching doubles its resistance.
statements.why: Area also halves, so R becomes 4 times.

statements.s: Resistivity of silicon decreases with temperature.
A diode obeys Ohm's law.
statements.why: Its V–I graph is non-linear and one-directional.

quiz.q: Resistivity of a wire depends on
quiz.why: Resistivity is a property of the material and changes with temperature, but not with length or area.

quiz.q: A wire's length is tripled by stretching. Its resistance becomes
quiz.why: Stretching to 3 times the length makes the area 1/3. So R ∝ l/A rises by 3 × 3 = 9 times.

quiz.q: Nichrome is used in heaters because it has
options: high resistivity and high melting point
quiz.why: Nichrome has high resistivity and a high melting point, so it gets very hot without melting or oxidising.

quiz.q: For semiconductors the temperature coefficient of resistivity is
quiz.why: In semiconductors more charge carriers are freed as temperature rises, so resistivity falls, giving a negative temperature coefficient.

quiz.q: The SI unit of resistivity is
quiz.why: ρ = RA/l, so the unit is ohm × m²/m = ohm metre (Ω m).

lessons.title: Combinations of resistors and electrical power

scenes.text: When Sahil switches off his room's fan, the kitchen light stays on.
Home appliances are connected in parallel so each gets the full 230 V and works independently.
And the electricity bill counts kilowatt-hours — energy, not power.

steps.title: Series and parallel
steps.body:
- **Series:** same current; **R = R₁ + R₂ + …**
- **Parallel:** same voltage; **1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …**; two in parallel: R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
- n equal resistors R: series nR, parallel R/n.

steps.title: Electrical power and energy
steps.body:
Energy dissipated when charge q falls through V: W = qV = VIt.

**P = VI = I²R = V²/R** (watt). In series (same I) the larger R dissipates more power; in parallel (same V) the smaller R dissipates more.

1 kWh (1 'unit') = 3.6×10⁶ J. Power loss in transmission lines, I²R, is reduced by transmitting at high voltage (low current).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V.
- R = V²/P = 220²/100 = **484 Ω**.
- On 110 V: P = 110²/484 = **25 W** (a quarter — P ∝ V² for fixed R).

**Ex 2.** 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel across 6 V.
- 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 ⇒ **R = 1 Ω**; total I = 6 A.
- Currents: 3 A, 2 A, 1 A; powers 18 W, 12 W, 6 W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P = I²R and P = V²/R and concluding opposite things — check which quantity is common.
- Forgetting that a bulb's rated values give its resistance, which stays (roughly) the same on other voltages.
- Adding parallel resistances directly.

steps.title: Two bulbs in series
steps.body: Two bulbs 60 W and 100 W (same rated voltage) in series: the **60 W bulb glows brighter** because it has the larger resistance and the same current flows through both.

activity.prompt: A 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω is connected to 12 V. Find the current from the source (A).

quiz.q: Equivalent of three 9 Ω resistors in parallel is
quiz.why: n equal resistors in parallel give R/n = 9/3 = 3 Ω.

quiz.q: A heater of 1000 W runs for 2 hours. Energy used:
quiz.why: Energy = power × time = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh.

quiz.q: In a parallel combination, which resistor dissipates the most power?
quiz.why: In parallel all have the same voltage, so P = V²/R is largest for the smallest resistance.

quiz.q: Power lines use high voltage to
quiz.why: For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current, which reduces the I²R heat loss in the lines.

lessons.title: Cells, emf and internal resistance

story.title: The car that would not start

scenes.text: On a cold morning, Rohan's dad turns the key; the dashboard lights dim sharply and the engine just clicks.
The battery's emf is still about 12 V, but its internal resistance has grown in the cold.
When the starter motor demands a huge current, most of the voltage is lost inside the battery itself.

steps.title: emf and terminal voltage
steps.body:
**emf (ε)**: the p.d. across a cell's terminals when no current flows — work done by the cell per unit charge.

With current I through external R and internal resistance r:
- **I = ε/(R + r)**
- Terminal voltage **V = ε − Ir** (discharging); **V = ε + Ir** while being charged.
- Short circuit (R = 0): I_max = ε/r.

steps.title: Combinations of cells
steps.body:
- **n identical cells in series:** ε_eq = nε, r_eq = nr ⇒ I = nε/(R + nr).
- **Two cells in parallel:** ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂), r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂).
- **n identical cells in parallel:** ε_eq = ε, r_eq = r/n.
- A cell connected the wrong way in series subtracts its emf but still adds its r.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking terminal voltage equal to emf when current flows.
- Forgetting the internal resistance of reversed cells.
- Using V = ε − Ir while the battery is being *charged* (it is ε + Ir).

steps.title: Graph trick
steps.body: A V–I graph for a cell is a straight line: the **y-intercept = ε** and the **slope = −r**. The x-intercept is the short-circuit current ε/r.

activity.prompt: A cell's terminal voltage is 2.2 V when no current flows and 1.8 V when it supplies current through a 5 Ω resistor. Find its internal resistance (Ω).

quiz.q: When a cell is being charged, terminal voltage is
quiz.why: While charging, current flows into the positive terminal against the emf, so the terminal voltage is V = ε + Ir.

quiz.q: Short-circuit current of a cell is
quiz.why: With R = 0 the whole emf drives current through the internal resistance: I = ε/r.

quiz.q: n identical cells in parallel have internal resistance
quiz.why: Identical cells in parallel combine like parallel resistors, so r_eq = r/n.

quiz.q: On a V–I graph of a cell, the slope gives
quiz.why: V = ε − Ir, so a graph of V against I has slope −r.

quiz.q: emf of a cell is measured best when
quiz.why: When no current flows, there is no drop across the internal resistance, so the terminal voltage equals the emf.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone bridge

scenes.text: Mehak is repairing a toy whose circuit has two batteries and loops that cannot be split into simple series and parallel parts.
She writes two rules on paper: what flows into a point flows out, and around any loop the voltage rises and drops cancel.
With three equations she finds every current — Kirchhoff's rules work for any circuit.

steps.title: Kirchhoff's rules
steps.body:
1. **Junction rule (KCL):** ΣI at a junction = 0 (current in = current out) — conservation of charge.
2. **Loop rule (KVL):** Σ(ΔV) around any closed loop = 0 — conservation of energy.

**Sign conventions:** going across a resistor *with* the assumed current: −IR; against: +IR. Going across a cell from − to +: +ε; from + to −: −ε. If a current comes out negative, its true direction is opposite to the assumed one.

steps.title: Wheatstone bridge
steps.body:
Four resistors P, Q (one arm), R, S (other arm), a galvanometer across the middle and a cell across the ends. When the galvanometer shows no deflection, the bridge is **balanced**:

**P/Q = R/S**

Derivation: with I_g = 0, the same current I₁ flows in P and Q, and I₂ in R and S; the two midpoints are at equal potential, so I₁P = I₂R and I₁Q = I₂S. Dividing gives the condition. The galvanometer and the cell can be swapped without disturbing balance. The meter bridge is a practical form of this circuit.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A loop has a 12 V cell, a 4 V cell opposing it, and resistors 2 Ω and 6 Ω in series (ignore internal resistances).
- KVL: 12 − 4 − 2I − 6I = 0 ⇒ **I = 1 A**.

**Ex 2.** At a junction 3 A and 2 A enter, 4 A leaves along one wire. The fourth wire carries **1 A out**.

**Ex 3.** Bridge: P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω, R = 15 Ω. Balance needs S = QR/P = **30 Ω**. In a balanced bridge the galvanometer branch can be removed, so equivalent resistance = (10 + 20) ∥ (15 + 30) = 30×45/75 = **18 Ω**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing sign conventions halfway through a loop.
- Thinking a negative current answer means a mistake — it just means the direction was assumed wrongly.
- Forgetting that a balanced bridge's middle resistor carries no current and can be ignored.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to solve a circuit with Kirchhoff's rules.
items: Mark an assumed current direction in every branch
Apply the junction rule at enough junctions
Apply the loop rule with consistent signs
Interpret negative answers as reversed currents

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule follows from conservation of
quiz.why: The junction rule says charge entering a junction equals charge leaving it, which is conservation of charge.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule follows from conservation of
quiz.why: The loop rule says the net work done on a charge around a closed loop is zero, which is conservation of energy.
A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S, when the two midpoints are at the same potential.

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge the current through the galvanometer is
quiz.why: At balance the two midpoints are at equal potential, so no current flows through the galvanometer.

quiz.q: Four 2 Ω resistors form a balanced bridge with a 2 Ω galvanometer branch. Equivalent resistance between the ends:
quiz.why: The bridge is balanced, so the galvanometer branch carries no current. Two (2 + 2) = 4 Ω paths in parallel give 2 Ω.

questions.why: Current density j = I/A, so its unit is A/m².

questions.why: Electrons drift very slowly, only about a millimetre per second or less (10⁻³ to 10⁻⁴ m/s).

questions.why: The 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (R = V²/P). In series the current is the same, so P = I²R is greater for the 60 W bulb, which glows brighter.

questions.why: Both are true. A rise in temperature shortens the relaxation time τ, and since ρ = m/(ne²τ), resistivity and hence resistance rise.

Five identical resistors of R in parallel have equivalent
questions.why: Five identical resistors in parallel give R/5.

questions.why: The two diametrically opposite points divide the circle into two halves of 5 Ω each. In parallel they give 2.5 Ω.

questions.q: The resistance of a wire is R. Its radius is halved by stretching (volume constant). New resistance:
questions.why: Halving the radius quarters the area. Volume is constant, so the length becomes 4 times. R ∝ l/A rises by 4 × 4 = 16.

questions.why: Total emf = 6 × 2 = 12 V and total internal resistance = 6 × 0.5 = 3 Ω. I = 12/(9 + 3) = 1 A.

questions.why: With one cell reversed, the emfs oppose and cancel, so the net emf is zero and so is the current.

lessons.title: Magnetic force and the motion of charges

scenes.text: On a rare night, sky-watchers in Ladakh photograph a faint red glow — an aurora.
Charged particles from the Sun spiral along Earth's magnetic field lines towards the poles.
A magnetic force bends a moving charge but never speeds it up — that is why the particles corkscrew instead of crashing straight in.

steps.title: Lorentz force
steps.body:
For a charge q moving with velocity v in fields E and B:

**F = q[E + v × B]**

Magnetic part: **F = qvB sin θ**, perpendicular to both v and B (right-hand rule; reverse it for negative charges).
- No force if v = 0 or v ∥ B.
- Being perpendicular to v, the magnetic force **does no work**: speed and kinetic energy stay constant.
- Unit of B: **tesla** (1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹); 1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ T.

steps.title: Circular and helical motion
steps.body:
If v ⊥ B: qvB = mv²/r ⇒ **r = mv/(qB)**, **ω = qB/m**, **T = 2πm/(qB)** — the period does not depend on speed.

If v makes angle θ with B: the component v cos θ is unaffected, v sin θ gives circular motion ⇒ a **helix** with radius r = mv sin θ/(qB) and **pitch p = v cos θ × T = 2πmv cos θ/(qB)**.

steps.title: Velocity selector
steps.body: Cross E and B at right angles, both perpendicular to v. Electric force qE and magnetic force qvB oppose. Particles pass undeflected when **v = E/B**, regardless of charge or mass.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A proton (m = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 2×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to B = 0.1 T.
- r = mv/(qB) = (1.67×10⁻²⁷ × 2×10⁶)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) ≈ **0.21 m**.

**Ex 2.** An electron at 3×10⁷ m/s moves at 30° to B = 6×10⁻⁴ T.
- F = evB sin θ = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 3×10⁷ × 6×10⁻⁴ × 0.5 = **1.44×10⁻¹⁵ N**.

**Ex 3.** E = 3×10⁴ V/m and B = 0.02 T are crossed. Undeflected speed v = E/B = **1.5×10⁶ m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the right-hand rule for an electron without reversing the direction.
- Thinking the magnetic force can change the speed of a particle.
- Using v instead of v sin θ for the radius of a helix.

activity.prompt: An α-particle (q = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 6.4×10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 1×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T. Find the radius of its path in cm.

quiz.q: The magnetic force on a charge moving parallel to B is
quiz.why: F = qvB sin θ, and for motion parallel to B, θ = 0, so the force is zero.

quiz.q: Work done by a magnetic force on a moving charge is
quiz.why: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work on the charge.

quiz.q: Time period of a charged particle in a uniform B is
quiz.why: T = 2πm/qB, which does not depend on the speed or radius of the circular path.
1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ tesla, so 1 tesla = 10⁴ gauss.

quiz.q: In a velocity selector undeflected particles have v =
quiz.why: Particles go straight when the electric and magnetic forces balance: qE = qvB, so v = E/B.

quiz.q: If the speed of a charged particle in a uniform B is doubled, its radius
quiz.why: r = mv/qB, so r ∝ v. Doubling the speed doubles the radius.

lessons.title: Biot–Savart law and the circular loop

scenes.text: Tanvi opens an old doorbell and finds a coil of copper wire wound round an iron core.
Every tiny piece of the wire makes a small magnetic field; added together they make a strong field at the centre.
Biot and Savart worked out how much each little piece contributes.

steps.title: Biot–Savart law
steps.body:
The field dB at a point at distance r from a current element I dl:

**dB = (μ₀/4π) × I dl sin θ / r²**, vector form dB = (μ₀/4π) I (dl × r̂)/r²

μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ (permeability of free space). dB is perpendicular to both dl and r. Compare: Coulomb's law has a source scalar q; Biot–Savart has a vector source I dl, and the field is zero along the line of the element (θ = 0).

steps.title: Field on the axis of a circular loop (derivation)
steps.body:
Loop radius R, current I, point P on the axis at distance x. Each element dl is ⊥ to the line joining it to P (length √(R² + x²)), so dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl/(R² + x²).

Components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs; components along the axis add: dB cos φ with cos φ = R/√(R² + x²).

B = (μ₀ I R/4π(R² + x²)^(3/2)) ∮dl = **μ₀ I R² / [2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]**

- At the centre (x = 0): **B = μ₀I/(2R)**; for N turns, μ₀NI/(2R).
- Direction by the right-hand thumb rule (curl fingers with current; thumb gives B).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A coil of 100 turns, radius 10 cm, carries 1 A.
- B at centre = μ₀NI/(2R) = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 100 × 1/(0.2) = **6.28×10⁻⁴ T**.

**Ex 2.** Same coil, point on the axis at x = R = 10 cm.
- B = μ₀NIR²/[2(2R²)^(3/2)] = B_centre/(2√2) ≈ **2.2×10⁻⁴ T**.

**Ex 3.** A semicircular arc of radius R carrying I: B at centre = μ₀I/(4R) (half of a full loop).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using μ₀I/(2πR) (straight wire) for a loop centre — the loop is μ₀I/(2R).
- Forgetting the 3/2 power on the axis.
- Not multiplying by the number of turns N.

steps.title: A loop is a magnetic dipole
steps.body: Far along the axis (x ≫ R): B ≈ μ₀IR²/(2x³) = (μ₀/4π)(2m/x³) with **m = IπR² = IA** — exactly like the axial field of an electric dipole. The face where current appears anticlockwise acts as a north pole.

activity.prompt: Complete the results.
activity.text: Field at the centre of a loop of radius R is μ₀I/(___R). The permeability of free space is 4π×10^___ T m/A. Along the line of the current element itself the field is ___.

quiz.q: The field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns is
quiz.why: The field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns is B = μ₀NI/2R.

quiz.q: Biot–Savart law gives dB proportional to
quiz.why: In the Biot–Savart law, dB ∝ Idl sin θ/r², so it falls as the inverse square of distance.

quiz.q: If the radius of a loop is doubled at the same current, B at centre
quiz.why: B = μ₀I/2R at the centre, so doubling the radius at the same current halves B.

quiz.q: Far along the axis, a current loop behaves like
quiz.why: Far from the loop, along its axis, B ∝ m/x³ like a bar magnet, so the loop behaves as a magnetic dipole.

quiz.q: The direction of B at the centre of a loop is given by
quiz.why: The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of B at the centre: curl the fingers in the direction of current and the thumb shows the field.

lessons.title: Ampère's circuital law: wire and solenoid

scenes.text: Grandpa Ravi is nervous before his MRI scan; the technician explains the huge ring is a solenoid.
Superconducting wire carries a large current through thousands of turns, making a strong, uniform field inside.
Ampère's law tells us that field: μ₀ times turns per metre times current.

steps.title: Ampère's circuital law
steps.body:
**∮ B·dl = μ₀ I_enclosed**

The line integral of B around any closed loop (an *Amperian loop*) equals μ₀ times the net current threading it. Sign by the right-hand rule. Like Gauss's law, it is most useful when symmetry makes B constant along the loop.

steps.title: Long straight wire
steps.body:
Take a circle of radius r centred on the wire. B is tangential and constant in magnitude:
B × 2πr = μ₀I ⇒ **B = μ₀I/(2πr)**. Field lines are concentric circles (right-hand thumb rule).

steps.title: Long solenoid
steps.body:
n = N/L turns per metre. Inside, B is uniform and along the axis; outside ≈ 0. Take a rectangular loop with one side l inside:
B l = μ₀ (n l) I ⇒ **B = μ₀nI**.
At the ends of a long solenoid B ≈ μ₀nI/2. With a core of relative permeability μᵣ, B = μ₀μᵣnI.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A long wire carries 35 A. Field at 20 cm:
- B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2×10⁻⁷ × 35/0.2 = **3.5×10⁻⁵ T**.

**Ex 2.** A solenoid 0.5 m long has 500 turns and carries 5 A.
- n = 500/0.5 = 1000 m⁻¹
- B = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 5 = **6.28×10⁻³ T** inside.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total turns N instead of turns per unit length n in B = μ₀nI.
- Including currents outside the Amperian loop.
- Thinking B is zero inside a wire — for a thick wire of radius a it rises as μ₀Ir/(2πa²) inside.

activity.prompt: Which formula gives the field?

quiz.why: Ampère's circuital law states that the line integral of B around a closed loop is μ₀ times the current enclosed.

quiz.q: The field inside a long solenoid is
quiz.why: Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform and equals μ₀nI.

quiz.q: Field at the end of a long solenoid is about
quiz.why: At the end of a long solenoid the field is half that at the centre, μ₀nI/2.

quiz.q: Field due to a long wire at distance r varies as
quiz.why: For a long straight wire B = μ₀I/2πr, so B varies as 1/r.

quiz.q: Field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are
quiz.why: By the right-hand thumb rule the field lines around a straight wire are concentric circles.

lessons.title: Force between currents and torque on a loop

story.title: The electric motor in a mixer

scenes.text: Isha's mixer-grinder whirs into life — inside, coils of wire spin between magnets.
Each side of a current loop is pushed in opposite directions by the magnetic field, creating a turning effect.
That torque on a current loop is the heart of every DC motor and every analogue meter.

steps.title: Force on a conductor
steps.body: A straight conductor of length l carrying I in field B: **F = I(l × B)**, magnitude **BIl sin θ** (Fleming's left-hand rule).

steps.title: Two parallel currents
steps.body:
Wire a produces B_a = μ₀I_a/(2πd) at wire b. Force per unit length on b:
**f = μ₀I_aI_b/(2πd)**
- **Like (parallel) currents attract; opposite currents repel** (opposite of charges!).
- Historically the ampere was defined as the current that gives 2×10⁻⁷ N/m between wires 1 m apart; since 2019 the SI defines the ampere by fixing e = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C, and the old relation remains true in practice.

steps.title: Torque on a rectangular loop
steps.body:
Loop of N turns, area A, current I in uniform B; θ = angle between B and the loop's normal (area vector).
- Net force = 0.
- Torque **τ = NIAB sin θ**, vector form **τ = m × B** with **magnetic moment m = NIA** (A m²).
- Potential energy U = −m·B. Stable equilibrium when m ∥ B.

**Electron orbit as a dipole:** an electron circling at speed v in radius r has μ = evr/2 = (e/2mₑ)L. For the lowest Bohr orbit μ_B ≈ 9.27×10⁻²⁴ A m² (Bohr magneton).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 3 A in the same direction.
- f = 2×10⁻⁷ × 5 × 3/0.1 = **3×10⁻⁵ N/m, attractive**.

**Ex 2.** A coil of 50 turns, area 5×10⁻³ m², carries 2 A in B = 0.2 T with its plane parallel to B (θ = 90° between normal and B).
- τ = NIAB = 50 × 2 × 5×10⁻³ × 0.2 = **0.1 N m** (maximum).
- m = NIA = **0.5 A m²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the angle between B and the *plane* of the coil instead of its *normal* in τ = NIAB sin θ.
- Saying parallel currents repel.
- Expecting a net force on a closed loop in a *uniform* field.

statements.s: Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract.
statements.why: Each lies in the other's field and the force points inward.

statements.s: A current loop in a uniform field feels a net force.
statements.why: Forces on opposite sides cancel; only torque remains.

statements.s: Torque on a coil is maximum when its plane is parallel to B.
statements.why: Then the normal is ⊥ B, sin 90° = 1.

statements.s: Magnetic moment of a coil is NIA.

quiz.q: Force per unit length between two long parallel wires is
quiz.why: The force per unit length between two long parallel wires is f = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd.
Magnetic moment m = NIA, so its unit is ampere metre squared (A m²).

quiz.q: Torque on a coil is zero when the angle between m and B is
quiz.why: Torque = mB sin θ is zero when θ = 0°, as the moment is along the field.
Parallel wires with currents in the opposite directions repel each other, while those in the same direction attract.

lessons.title: Moving-coil galvanometer, ammeter and voltmeter

story.title: Building a meter in the lab

scenes.text: In the practical exam, Varun is handed a galvanometer that reads only 3 mA full-scale and is asked to measure 3 A.
He adds a tiny resistance in parallel — a shunt — so most of the current bypasses the coil.
Later, with a large resistance in series, the same galvanometer becomes a voltmeter.

steps.title: How the galvanometer works
steps.body:
A rectangular coil (N turns, area A) hangs in a **radial magnetic field** from curved pole pieces and a soft-iron core, so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B (sin θ = 1).
- Deflecting torque NIAB is balanced by the spring's restoring torque kφ:
**NIAB = kφ ⇒ φ = (NAB/k) I** — a linear scale.
- **Current sensitivity** φ/I = NAB/k.
- **Voltage sensitivity** φ/V = NAB/(kG), G = coil resistance.
Doubling N doubles current sensitivity but also doubles G, so voltage sensitivity is unchanged.

steps.title: Conversion
steps.body:
- **Ammeter:** small **shunt S in parallel**: I_g G = (I − I_g)S ⇒ **S = I_g G/(I − I_g)**. Ammeter resistance is tiny; it is joined in series; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance.
- **Voltmeter:** large **R in series**: V = I_g(G + R) ⇒ **R = V/I_g − G**. Joined in parallel; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
A galvanometer has G = 12 Ω and full-scale current 3 mA.

**Ex 1. Ammeter 0–3 A:**
- S = (3×10⁻³ × 12)/(3 − 0.003) ≈ **0.012 Ω** in parallel.

**Ex 2. Voltmeter 0–18 V:**
- R = 18/(3×10⁻³) − 12 = 6000 − 12 = **5988 Ω** in series.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the shunt in series or the multiplier in parallel.
- Forgetting that a galvanometer alone cannot measure large currents — the coil would burn.
- Thinking higher current sensitivity always means higher voltage sensitivity.

activity.prompt: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full deflection for 2 mA. What series resistance (Ω) converts it into a voltmeter of range 0–10 V?

quiz.q: The radial field in a galvanometer ensures
options: the coil's plane is always parallel to B, so the scale is linear
quiz.why: A radial field keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to B, so the torque depends only on current and the deflection is proportional to current, giving a linear scale.

quiz.q: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, connect
quiz.why: An ammeter has a low-resistance shunt connected in parallel with the galvanometer, so most current bypasses it.
An ideal voltmeter draws no current from the circuit, so its resistance is infinite.

quiz.q: Current sensitivity of a galvanometer is
quiz.why: Current sensitivity is deflection per unit current: φ/I = NAB/k.

quiz.q: If N is doubled, voltage sensitivity
quiz.why: Voltage sensitivity = NAB/(kG). Doubling N also doubles the resistance G of the coil, so the ratio is unchanged.

options: Both true; reason does not explain

An electron and a proton enter a uniform B with equal speeds perpendicular to it. Which statement is correct?
options: Electron's radius is smaller and it curves the opposite way

Case: A galvanometer (G = 100 Ω, I_g = 1 mA) is converted into an ammeter of 0–1 A. The shunt is about

Assertion: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. Reason: A voltmeter has a very high resistance, so it draws very little current.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true, but it is placed in parallel because it must measure the p.d. across the component; its high resistance is why it barely disturbs the circuit.

questions.why: The wire is perpendicular to the field, so F = BIl = 0.1 × 5 × 2 = 1 N.

questions.q: The magnetic moment of an electron in a circular orbit of radius r with speed v is
questions.why: I = e/T = ev/2πr and area = πr², so μ = I × πr² = evr/2.

questions.q: Case: In a velocity selector, B = 0.05 T. For ions of speed 4×10⁵ m/s to pass straight, E must be
questions.why: For undeflected motion qE = qvB, so E = vB = 4×10⁵ × 0.05 = 2×10⁴ V/m.

questions.q: A long wire of radius a carries current I uniformly. Field at r = a/2 inside equals
questions.why: Inside a wire B = μ₀Ir/(2πa²). At r = a/2 this is μ₀I/(4πa).

questions.q: To make a galvanometer of G = 25 Ω, I_g = 4 mA into a voltmeter of 0–20 V, the series resistance needed is
questions.why: For a voltmeter, R_series = V/I_g − G = 20/0.004 − 25 = 5000 − 25 = 4975 Ω.

lessons.title: The bar magnet and its field

scenes.text: Little Anaya snaps a fridge magnet in two, hoping to get one north piece and one south piece.
Each half still has both a north and a south pole.
Her sister explains: a magnet behaves like a tiny solenoid — cutting a solenoid just gives two shorter solenoids.

steps.title: Field lines of a bar magnet
steps.body:
- Field lines form **continuous closed loops**: outside from N to S, inside from S to N.
- Tangent at a point gives the direction of B; density gives strength.
- Lines never intersect.
- Isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) have never been found: breaking a magnet always gives two dipoles.

steps.title: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
steps.body:
A finite solenoid's field far away matches a bar magnet's: on its axis B = (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³) with m = NIA. Iron filings show identical patterns. So a bar magnet can be pictured as a solenoid of circulating atomic currents.

**Magnetic dipole fields (far away, r ≫ size):**
- Axial: **B = (μ₀/4π) × 2m/r³**
- Equatorial: **B = (μ₀/4π) × m/r³**, opposite to m
Magnetic moment m points from S to N; unit A m² (or J/T).

steps.title: Dipole in a uniform field
steps.body:
- Torque **τ = m × B**, magnitude mB sin θ.
- Potential energy **U = −m·B = −mB cos θ**: minimum (−mB) when aligned (stable), maximum (+mB) when anti-aligned (unstable).
- A freely suspended magnet (moment of inertia I) given a small twist oscillates with **T = 2π√(I/(mB))** — this is how a compass needle settles.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A short bar magnet has m = 0.4 A m². Field on its axis at 20 cm:
- B = 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 0.4/(0.2)³ = 10⁻⁷ × 0.8/0.008 = **1×10⁻⁵ T**.
- On the equatorial line at 20 cm: **5×10⁻⁶ T**.

**Ex 2.** A magnet of m = 0.32 J/T is at 60° to B = 0.15 T.
- τ = mB sin 60° = 0.32 × 0.15 × 0.866 ≈ **4.2×10⁻² N m**.
- U = −mB cos 60° = **−0.024 J**.
- Work to turn it to anti-aligned from aligned: 2mB = **0.096 J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing field lines inside the magnet from N to S (inside they go S to N).
- Expecting broken pieces to be monopoles.
- Using electric-dipole intuition for U sign: U = −mB cos θ, minimum when aligned.

activity.prompt: A bar magnet of moment 2 A m² is placed at 90° to a uniform field of 0.05 T. Find the torque on it (N m).

quiz.q: Outside a bar magnet, field lines go
quiz.why: Outside a bar magnet field lines go from the north pole to the south pole, and inside they go from S to N.
Magnetic field lines form closed loops because there are no isolated magnetic poles.

quiz.q: Unit of magnetic moment can be written as
quiz.why: U = −mB, so m has the unit of energy per field: J/T (same as A m²).

quiz.q: A magnet is in stable equilibrium when its moment is
quiz.why: A magnet is in stable equilibrium when its moment is parallel to B, where its potential energy is minimum.

quiz.q: Far away, the axial field of a bar magnet varies as

lessons.title: Gauss's law for magnetism

scenes.text: Physicists have built detectors deep underground just to catch a single magnetic monopole.
None has ever been confirmed.
That experimental fact is written as a law: the total magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero.

steps.title: The law
steps.body:
**∮ B·dS = 0** for every closed surface.

As many field lines leave any closed surface as enter it, because magnetic field lines are closed loops and there are no isolated poles. Compare Gauss's law for electricity, ∮E·dS = q/ε₀, where charges act as sources.

steps.title: Electric vs magnetic dipole
steps.body:
| Feature | Electric dipole | Magnetic dipole |
- Moment: p = q(2a) | m = NIA
- Axial field: (1/4πε₀)(2p/r³) | (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³)
- Torque: p × E | m × B
- Energy: −p·E | −m·B
- Sources: + and − charges exist separately | poles never exist separately
The correspondence is p ↔ m, 1/ε₀ ↔ μ₀.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A closed cube sits in a non-uniform magnetic field. Net flux through it = **0** (always).

**Ex 2.** 5×10⁻⁵ Wb of flux enters a closed surface through its left face. Total flux leaving through all other faces = **5×10⁻⁵ Wb**, so that the net is zero.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the flux through an *open* surface (like a coil) must be zero — the law is for *closed* surfaces only.
- Equating zero net flux with zero field.

activity.prompt: Match the electric quantity to its magnetic analogue.

quiz.q: Gauss's law for magnetism says the net magnetic flux through a closed surface is
quiz.why: Gauss's law for magnetism says the net flux through any closed surface is zero, because magnetic poles do not exist singly.

options: magnetic field lines are closed loops
flux through a coil is zero
quiz.why: Since the net flux through any closed surface is zero, every field line that enters also leaves, so field lines form closed loops.
In the dipole field formulas, μ₀/4π takes the place of 1/4πε₀, so μ₀ is the analogue of 1/ε₀.

quiz.q: Flux through the face of a coil in a field
quiz.why: A coil's face is an open surface, not a closed one, so the flux through it can be non-zero.

quiz.q: Net magnetic flux through a closed surface placed around one pole of a long bar magnet is
quiz.why: Gauss's law for magnetism holds for every closed surface: the lines that enter also leave. So the net flux is zero even around one pole.

lessons.title: Magnetisation, H, susceptibility and permeability

scenes.text: Om winds wire round a nail and picks up 3 paper clips; on a plastic pen, the same coil picks up none.
The iron nail adds its own magnetism to the coil's field — it becomes magnetised.
We describe that extra contribution with magnetisation M and the material's susceptibility.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Magnetisation M** = net magnetic moment per unit volume (A/m).
- **Magnetic intensity H**: the part of the field due to free (conduction) currents. For a solenoid H = nI (A/m).
- Total field: **B = μ₀(H + M)**.
- For linear materials **M = χH**, where χ (magnetic susceptibility) is dimensionless.
- So **B = μ₀(1 + χ)H = μ₀μᵣH = μH**, with relative permeability **μᵣ = 1 + χ** and permeability μ = μ₀μᵣ.

steps.title: Signs and sizes of χ
steps.body:
- Diamagnetic: χ small and **negative** (about −10⁻⁵), μᵣ slightly < 1.
- Paramagnetic: χ small and **positive** (10⁻⁵–10⁻³), μᵣ slightly > 1.
- Ferromagnetic: χ **very large and positive** (10²–10⁵), μᵣ ≫ 1, and not constant (depends on H and history).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A solenoid with n = 1000 turns/m and I = 2 A has an iron core with μᵣ = 400.
- H = nI = **2000 A/m**.
- B = μ₀μᵣH = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 400 × 2000 ≈ **1.0 T**.
- χ = μᵣ − 1 = 399; M = χH ≈ **8.0×10⁵ A/m**.

**Ex 2.** A material has χ = −2×10⁻⁵. μᵣ = 1 − 0.00002 = **0.99998** — diamagnetic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing H (A/m) with B (T).
- Forgetting B = μ₀(H + M), not μ₀H + M.
- Treating χ of iron as a fixed number — for ferromagnets it varies.

activity.prompt: Fill in the relations.
activity.text: B = μ₀(H + ___). Relative permeability μᵣ = 1 + ___. For a diamagnetic material χ is ___.

quiz.q: Magnetisation is magnetic moment per unit
quiz.why: Magnetisation M is the net magnetic moment per unit volume.
Susceptibility χ = M/H is a ratio of two quantities with the same unit, so it is dimensionless.

quiz.q: μᵣ for a diamagnetic substance is
quiz.why: For a diamagnetic substance χ is small and negative, so μᵣ = 1 + χ is slightly less than 1.
H has the same unit as M, ampere per metre (A/m).

quiz.q: In B = μ₀μᵣnI, μᵣ = 1000 means the core
quiz.why: A very large μᵣ such as 1000 is typical of a ferromagnetic core.

lessons.title: Dia-, para- and ferromagnetism

scenes.text: Ritika sees a famous photo of a live frog levitating inside a very strong magnet.
Water — and therefore the frog — is diamagnetic, weakly pushed out of strong fields.
Most matter is magnetic in one of three ways; strong magnets just make the weakest kind visible.

steps.title: Diamagnetism
steps.body:
Atoms have no net permanent moment. An applied field induces tiny currents that oppose it (Lenz-like behaviour), so the material is **repelled** and moves from strong to weak field.
- Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water, NaCl, nitrogen (at STP).
- **Superconductors** are perfect diamagnets (χ = −1): they expel fields completely (**Meissner effect**) — used in maglev trains.

steps.title: Paramagnetism
steps.body:
Atoms have permanent moments that point randomly. A field partly aligns them, so the material is **weakly attracted** (moves from weak to strong field).
- Examples: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen (at STP), copper chloride.
- **Curie's law:** M = C(B₀/T), i.e. **χ = Cμ₀/T** — susceptibility falls as temperature rises, because thermal agitation fights alignment.

steps.title: Ferromagnetism
steps.body:
Strong interactions line up atomic moments in small regions called **domains** (about 1 mm across, each containing ~10¹¹ atoms). An applied field makes favourable domains grow and others rotate, giving huge M; the material is **strongly attracted**.
- Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, alnico.
- **Hard ferromagnets** (alnico) keep magnetisation → permanent magnets. **Soft** ferromagnets (soft iron) lose it → electromagnet and transformer cores.
- Above the **Curie temperature** T_c a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic; then χ ∝ 1/(T − T_c). T_c for iron is about 1043 K.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A paramagnetic salt has χ = 2.8×10⁻⁴ at 300 K. At 200 K (Curie's law):
- χ₂ = χ₁ × T₁/T₂ = 2.8×10⁻⁴ × 300/200 = **4.2×10⁻⁴**.

**Ex 2.** A paramagnetic sample shows M = 8 A/m at 4 K in a field B₁. At 16 K in a field 2B₁:
- M ∝ B/T ⇒ M₂ = 8 × (2) × (4/16) = **4 A/m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying diamagnetism only occurs in some materials — it is present in *all*, but masked by para/ferro effects.
- Applying Curie's law to ferromagnets below T_c.
- Mixing up hard (permanent magnet) and soft (core) magnetic materials.

activity.prompt: Classify each material.

A superconductor expels the field completely, so it is a perfect diamagnet with χ = −1.

quiz.why: A permanent magnet needs a material that keeps its magnetism, so a hard ferromagnet like alnico is used.
Gadolinium is ferromagnetic below about 290 K. Bismuth is diamagnetic, and sodium and lead are not ferromagnetic.

courses.summary: Faraday's and Henry's experiments, magnetic flux, Faraday's law, Lenz's law and energy conservation, motional emf, self- and mutual inductance with energy stored, and the AC generator — derivations and graded numericals. outcomes: Learners can calculate magnetic flux and induced emf with Faraday's law.

lessons.title: Faraday's law and magnetic flux

scenes.text: Pranav's grandfather still has a bicycle with a little dynamo pressed against the tyre.
Pedal faster and the headlamp glows brighter; stop and it goes dark.
A magnet spinning near a coil changes the magnetic flux through it — and a changing flux makes an emf. That is Faraday's discovery.

steps.title: The experiments
steps.body:
Faraday and Henry (1830s) found:
- Moving a magnet towards or away from a coil makes a galvanometer deflect; faster motion, bigger deflection; no motion, no deflection.
- Moving the coil instead of the magnet gives the same effect — only *relative* motion matters.
- Switching a current ON or OFF in one coil induces a momentary current in a nearby coil (no motion at all).
Common factor: **change in magnetic flux**.

steps.title: Magnetic flux
steps.body: **Φ_B = B·A = BA cos θ** (θ between B and the normal to the area). For non-uniform fields Φ = ∫B·dA. Unit **weber (Wb)** = T m². Flux can change by changing B, A or θ.

steps.title: Faraday's law
steps.body:
**ε = −N dΦ_B/dt**

The induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage (NΦ). The minus sign is Lenz's law. Induced current I = ε/R and induced charge **Δq = NΔΦ/R** — independent of how fast the change happens.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 100-turn coil's flux per turn falls from 5×10⁻³ Wb to 1×10⁻³ Wb in 0.1 s.
- |ε| = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 4×10⁻³/0.1 = **4 V**.

**Ex 2.** A 10 cm × 10 cm loop (R = 0.5 Ω) is perpendicular to B, which falls at 0.5 T/s.
- ε = A dB/dt = 0.01 × 0.5 = **5×10⁻³ V**.
- I = 5×10⁻³/0.5 = **10 mA**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using B instead of change of flux: a strong *steady* field induces nothing.
- Forgetting cos θ when the coil is tilted.
- Forgetting N for multi-turn coils.

activity.prompt: A 50-turn coil of area 0.02 m² is perpendicular to a field that rises uniformly from 0.1 T to 0.5 T in 0.2 s. Find the induced emf (V).

quiz.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is
quiz.why: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb), equal to T m².
By Faraday's law the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux.

quiz.q: A magnet held still inside a coil induces
quiz.why: A magnet at rest in a coil produces no change of flux, so no emf is induced.

quiz.q: Induced charge in a coil depends on
options: total change of flux and resistance
quiz.why: Charge = I t = (ε/R) t = NΔΦ/R, so it depends on total flux change and resistance, not on the rate.

quiz.q: Flux through a loop is maximum when the angle between B and the normal is
quiz.why: Φ = BA cos θ is maximum when the angle between B and the normal is 0°.

lessons.title: Lenz's law and energy conservation

scenes.text: Diya drops a strong magnet down a copper pipe; it drifts down slowly, as if through honey.
Currents induced in the pipe create fields that oppose the magnet's motion.
If they helped instead, the magnet would speed up for free — breaking energy conservation.

steps.title: Lenz's law
steps.body:
**The induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in flux that produced it.**
- North pole approaching a coil ⇒ the near face of the coil becomes a north pole (repels it); current appears anticlockwise as seen by the magnet.
- North pole receding ⇒ near face becomes south (attracts it back); current clockwise as seen by the magnet.

steps.title: Why — energy conservation
steps.body: Because the induced current opposes the motion, you must do work to push the magnet. That mechanical work is converted into electrical energy and then heat (Joule heating). If the current *aided* the change, energy would be created from nothing. So Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of energy.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A loop lies flat on a table; a bar magnet's south pole is lowered towards it from above. Seen from above, the induced current is **clockwise** (the loop's upper face becomes a south pole to repel the approaching south pole).

**Ex 2.** Current in a long straight wire increases. A rectangular loop lies beside it in the same plane. The induced current in the near side of the loop flows **opposite** to the wire's current (opposing the rise in flux), so the loop is **repelled** from the wire.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the induced field always opposes the magnet's field — it opposes the *change* in flux. If flux is decreasing, the induced field is *along* the original field.
- Forgetting to state from which side you are looking when saying clockwise/anticlockwise.

a.text: The N pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil. What does the near face of the coil become?

choices.label: A north pole
choices.feedback: Right — it repels the approaching N pole.

choices.label: A south pole
choices.feedback: That would attract the magnet and create energy from nothing.

a2.text: Think again: the coil must oppose the motion. Which pole repels an approaching N pole?

choices.label: North

b.text: Now the magnet is pulled away. What does the near face become?

choices.label: South — it tries to pull the magnet back
choices.feedback: Correct — it opposes the decrease in flux.

choices.label: North again
choices.feedback: That would push the magnet away, helping the change.

b2.text: Opposing a receding N pole means attracting it. Which pole attracts N?

choices.label: South

end.text: You have used Lenz's law: the induced current always opposes the change that causes it.

quiz.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of
quiz.why: Lenz's law follows from conservation of energy: if the induced effect helped the change, energy would be created from nothing.

quiz.q: A magnet falls through a copper ring. Its acceleration is
quiz.why: The induced current in the ring opposes the magnet's fall (Lenz's law), so the magnet's acceleration is less than g.

quiz.q: The minus sign in ε = −dΦ/dt represents
quiz.why: The minus sign shows that the induced emf opposes the change of flux, which is Lenz's law.

quiz.q: When the S pole of a magnet approaches a coil, the near face of the coil becomes
quiz.why: The coil must repel the approaching S pole, so the face of the coil near it becomes an S pole.

quiz.q: If flux through a loop is decreasing, the induced field inside the loop is
quiz.why: The induced current opposes the decrease in flux, so its field inside the loop is along the original field.

lessons.title: Motional emf

scenes.text: A passenger notices that metal aircraft wings cut through Earth's magnetic field at high speed.
A tiny voltage appears between the wing tips — a few tenths of a volt.
Any conductor moving through a magnetic field has its electrons pushed sideways: that is motional emf.

steps.title: Derivation: ε = Blv
steps.body:
A rod of length l slides at speed v on rails in a field B perpendicular to the plane. The enclosed area grows at rate lv, so dΦ/dt = Blv ⇒ **ε = Blv**.

Same result from the Lorentz force: each free charge feels qvB along the rod; work per unit charge over length l is vBl.

steps.title: Force and energy
steps.body: With total circuit resistance R: I = Blv/R. The field exerts a retarding force on the rod: **F = BIl = B²l²v/R**. To keep v constant the external agent must supply power P = Fv = **B²l²v²/R**, which equals the Joule heat I²R — energy conservation confirmed.

steps.title: Rotating rod
steps.body: A rod of length l rotating with angular speed ω about one end, perpendicular to B: each element dr moves at ωr, so ε = ∫₀ˡ Bωr dr = **½Bωl²**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 1 m rod moves at 5 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T.
- ε = Blv = 0.5 × 1 × 5 = **2.5 V**.
- If R = 5 Ω: I = 0.5 A, F = BIl = **0.25 N**, power = 1.25 W.

**Ex 2.** A 1 m metal rod rotates at 400 rad/s about one end in B = 0.5 T.
- ε = ½ × 0.5 × 400 × 1² = **100 V** between centre and end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ε = Blv when v is not perpendicular to both B and l (use components).
- Forgetting the ½ for a rotating rod.
- Thinking no force is needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed.

steps.title: Eddy currents in brakes
steps.body: Bulk metal plates moving through fields carry swirling induced currents (eddy currents). They heat and slow the metal — used in electromagnetic brakes of trains, damping in meters and induction furnaces; laminated cores reduce them in transformers.

activity.prompt: A 0.5 m long rod moves at 10 m/s perpendicular to a 0.4 T field, on rails joined by a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current (A).

quiz.q: Motional emf in a rod of length l moving at v ⊥ B is
quiz.why: For a rod of length l moving at speed v perpendicular to B, the motional emf is Blv.

quiz.q: Emf across a rod rotating about one end is
quiz.why: A rod of length l rotating at ω has speed ωr at distance r. Integrating Bωr dr from 0 to l gives ½Bωl².

quiz.q: The retarding force on a sliding rod (circuit resistance R) is
quiz.why: The current is I = Blv/R, so the magnetic force on the rod is BIl = B²l²v/R, opposing the motion.

quiz.q: If a rod moves parallel to B, the emf is
quiz.why: A rod moving parallel to B cuts no field lines, so the induced emf is zero.

quiz.q: Eddy currents are reduced in transformer cores by
quiz.why: Laminated cores are made of thin insulated sheets, which break up the paths of eddy currents and reduce heating.

lessons.title: Self- and mutual inductance

scenes.text: Leela places her phone on a charging pad without plugging in any wire.
An alternating current in the pad's coil makes a changing field that threads a coil inside the phone.
That is mutual induction — two coils talking through a shared, changing magnetic flux.

steps.title: Mutual inductance
steps.body:
When current I₁ in coil 1 links flux N₂Φ₂ with coil 2: **N₂Φ₂ = M I₁** and ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt. Unit **henry (H)**. M₁₂ = M₂₁.

**Two long coaxial solenoids** (inner radius r₁, length l, turns per metre n₁ outer, n₂ inner): flux from the outer through the inner gives **M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l**. With a core: multiply by μᵣ.

steps.title: Self-inductance
steps.body:
A coil's own changing current changes its own flux: **NΦ = LI**, **ε = −L dI/dt** (back emf).

**Long solenoid** (n turns/m, area A, length l): NΦ = (nl)(μ₀nI)A ⇒ **L = μ₀n²Al = μ₀N²A/l**. L depends on geometry and core, not on current. L is the electrical analogue of mass (inertia against change of current).

steps.title: Energy stored in an inductor
steps.body: Work done against back emf while current rises from 0 to I: W = ∫LI dI = **½LI²**. For a solenoid this gives energy density **u = B²/(2μ₀)**, stored in the magnetic field.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A solenoid has 500 turns, length 0.5 m, area 1×10⁻³ m².
- L = μ₀N²A/l = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 2.5×10⁵ × 10⁻³/0.5 ≈ **6.3×10⁻⁴ H**.
- Energy at 2 A: ½ × 6.3×10⁻⁴ × 4 ≈ **1.26×10⁻³ J**.

**Ex 2.** A 0.2 H coil's current falls from 5 A to 1 A in 0.1 s.
- |ε| = L ΔI/Δt = 0.2 × 4/0.1 = **8 V**.

**Ex 3.** M = 1.5 H. Current in coil 1 rises from 0 to 20 A in 0.5 s.
- Flux-linkage change in coil 2 = MΔI = **30 Wb**; emf = 30/0.5 = **60 V**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using N instead of n (turns per metre) in L = μ₀n²Al.
- Thinking a large steady current through an inductor causes an emf.
- Forgetting that energy is ½LI², not LI².

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its formula.

quiz.why: The SI unit of inductance is the henry, equal to Wb/A.

quiz.q: Self-inductance of a solenoid is proportional to
quiz.why: For a solenoid L = μ₀n²Al, so L ∝ n².
Inductance opposes changes in current, just as mass opposes changes in motion, so it plays the role of inertia.

quiz.q: Energy stored in a 2 H inductor carrying 3 A is
quiz.why: U = ½LI² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

quiz.q: Inserting an iron core into a coil
quiz.why: L is proportional to the permeability of the core. An iron core has a large μᵣ, so L increases.

lessons.title: The AC generator

scenes.text: On a school trip to a hydroelectric dam, Ayaan watches water spin a giant turbine.
The turbine turns huge coils inside magnetic fields.
As each coil rotates, its flux rises and falls sinusoidally — and out comes alternating current at 50 Hz.

steps.title: Principle and parts
steps.body: A coil (armature) rotates in a uniform magnetic field; the angle between B and the coil's normal changes, so flux changes. Parts: armature coil, field magnets, slip rings and carbon brushes. Mechanical energy → electrical energy.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
At time t the angle is θ = ωt: Φ = BA cos ωt per turn.
ε = −N dΦ/dt = **NBAω sin ωt = ε₀ sin ωt**, with **peak emf ε₀ = NBAω** and ω = 2πν.
- ε is maximum when the coil's plane is parallel to B (flux zero but changing fastest).
- ε is zero when the plane is perpendicular to B (flux maximum).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 100-turn coil of area 0.1 m² rotates at 50 rev/s in B = 0.01 T.
- ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s
- ε₀ = NBAω = 100 × 0.01 × 0.1 × 314 = **31.4 V**.

**Ex 2.** A generator gives peak 200 V at 3000 rpm. At 1500 rpm with everything else unchanged, ε₀ = **100 V** (ε₀ ∝ ω), and the frequency halves to 25 Hz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying emf is maximum when the flux is maximum — it is maximum when flux is *zero* (fastest change).
- Forgetting to convert rpm to rad/s: ω = 2π × rpm/60.
- Confusing slip rings (AC output) with split rings (DC motor/commutator).

activity.label: Coil angle θ between B and the coil's normal

bands.text: θ = 0°: flux maximum (NBA), emf zero — flux is momentarily not changing.
θ = 30°–60°: flux decreasing, emf growing as sin θ.

lessons.title: AC through a resistor, rms values and phasors

scenes.text: Sneha reads '230 V AC' on a socket and wonders why the voltage is called constant if AC keeps changing direction.
On an oscilloscope the voltage swings between about +325 V and −325 V, fifty times a second.
'230 V' is the root-mean-square value — the steady DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally.

steps.title: AC voltage on a resistor
steps.body:
v = v_m sin ωt applied to R gives **i = (v_m/R) sin ωt = i_m sin ωt** — current and voltage are **in phase**. Average current over a cycle is zero, but average power is not:
p = i²R = i_m²R sin² ωt, and the average of sin² ωt is ½ ⇒ **P̄ = ½ i_m² R**.

steps.title: rms values
steps.body:
Define I (rms) so that P̄ = I²R:
**I = i_m/√2 ≈ 0.707 i_m**, **V = v_m/√2**.
AC meters read rms values. Indian mains: V_rms ≈ 230 V (often quoted as 220 V in problems), so v_m ≈ 1.414 × 230 ≈ 325 V.

steps.title: Phasors
steps.body: A phasor is a rotating vector of length v_m (or i_m) spinning anticlockwise at ω; its projection on the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value. Phase differences become angles between phasors — this makes adding sinusoidal voltages simple vector addition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using peak values in P = VI for heating — use rms.
- Saying the average AC current is i_m/√2 — the *mean* over a full cycle is zero; i_m/√2 is the rms.
- Reading ω as frequency: f = ω/2π.

activity.prompt: The peak voltage of an AC supply is 300 V. Find its rms voltage (V).

quiz.q: rms value of current i = i_m sin ωt is
quiz.why: The rms value is the peak divided by √2, from the average of sin²ωt being ½: i_rms = i_m/√2.

quiz.q: In a purely resistive AC circuit, current and voltage are
quiz.why: In a purely resistive circuit i = v/R at every instant, so the current and voltage are in phase.

quiz.q: Average value of AC over one full cycle is
quiz.why: Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel, so the average value is zero.
AC meters are calibrated to show the rms value, which gives the same heating effect as the equivalent DC.

lessons.title: AC through an inductor and a capacitor

scenes.text: Old fan regulators got hot; newer electronic ones stay cool.
Some regulators used a choke (an inductor) instead of a resistor to cut the current.
An ideal inductor opposes AC without wasting power as heat — current and voltage are 90° out of step.

steps.title: Pure inductor
steps.body:
v = v_m sin ωt across L: L di/dt = v ⇒ i = −(v_m/ωL) cos ωt = **i_m sin(ωt − π/2)**.
- **Current lags voltage by 90°.**
- **Inductive reactance X_L = ωL** (Ω), grows with frequency; at DC (ω = 0) X_L = 0.
- Average power over a cycle = **0**.

steps.title: Pure capacitor
steps.body:
v = v_m sin ωt across C: q = Cv, i = dq/dt = ωCv_m cos ωt = **i_m sin(ωt + π/2)**.
- **Current leads voltage by 90°.**
- **Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC)**, falls with frequency; at DC it is infinite (capacitor blocks DC).
- Average power = **0**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 44 mH inductor on 220 V, 50 Hz.
- X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.044 ≈ **13.8 Ω**.
- I_rms = 220/13.8 ≈ **15.9 A**.

**Ex 2.** A 60 μF capacitor on 110 V, 60 Hz.
- X_C = 1/(2π × 60 × 60×10⁻⁶) ≈ **44.2 Ω**.
- I_rms = 110/44.2 ≈ **2.49 A**.
- If the frequency is doubled, X_C halves and I doubles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping lead and lag. Memory aid **'CIVIL'**: in a C, I leads V; V leads I in an L.
- Writing X_C = ωC.
- Expecting a capacitor to pass DC current in steady state.

activity.prompt: Sort the property into the correct element.

quiz.why: The inductive reactance is X_L = ωL, which increases with frequency.

quiz.q: A capacitor offers infinite reactance to
quiz.why: X_C = 1/ωC. For DC, ω = 0, so X_C is infinite and no steady current flows through a capacitor.

quiz.q: In a pure capacitive circuit, current
quiz.why: In a capacitive circuit i = C dv/dt, so the current leads the voltage by 90°.

quiz.q: Average power in a purely inductive circuit is
quiz.why: With phase difference 90°, the average power is VI cos 90° = 0, so a pure inductor uses no power on average.
X_L = ωL = 2πfL is proportional to frequency, so doubling f doubles X_L.

lessons.title: Series LCR circuit and resonance

scenes.text: Grandma Shanti turns the knob of her radio to catch her favourite FM station.
Turning the knob changes a capacitor in an LCR circuit.
When the circuit's natural frequency equals the station's frequency, the current peaks — that is resonance.

steps.title: Phasor analysis
steps.body:
The same current i = i_m sin(ωt + φ) flows through R, L and C. Voltages: V_R in phase with I, V_L leading I by 90°, V_C lagging I by 90°. Adding phasors:
V_m² = V_Rm² + (V_Lm − V_Cm)²

**Impedance Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²)**, i_m = v_m/Z.

**Phase angle tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R**. If X_L > X_C the circuit is inductive (V leads I); if X_C > X_L, capacitive (I leads V).

steps.title: Resonance
steps.body:
Current is maximum when X_L = X_C, i.e. ωL = 1/(ωC):
**ω₀ = 1/√(LC)**, **f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC))**.
At resonance Z = R (minimum), φ = 0, and V_L and V_C can each be much larger than the source voltage (they cancel each other). Resonance needs both L and C; an RL or RC circuit cannot resonate.

**Sharpness (quality factor):** Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR). Smaller R ⇒ sharper peak ⇒ better tuning selectivity.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** R = 30 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω, X_C = 40 Ω on 200 V rms.
- Z = √(30² + 40²) = **50 Ω**; I = 200/50 = **4 A**.
- tan φ = 40/30 ⇒ **φ ≈ 53°**, voltage leads current (inductive).

**Ex 2.** L = 0.1 H, C = 10 μF.
- ω₀ = 1/√(0.1 × 10⁻⁵) = 1/√10⁻⁶ = **1000 rad/s**; f₀ ≈ **159 Hz**.
- With R = 20 Ω and 100 V source at resonance: I = 5 A; V_L = IX_L = 5 × 100 = **500 V** — far above the supply!

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding V_R + V_L + V_C arithmetically — they must be added as phasors.
- Forgetting that at resonance Z = R, not zero.
- Using f₀ = 1/√(LC) (that is ω₀).

activity.prompt: A series LCR circuit has R = 40 Ω, X_L = 60 Ω and X_C = 30 Ω. Find the impedance (Ω).

quiz.q: Impedance of a series LCR circuit is
quiz.why: The voltages across R and across (L − C) are at 90° to each other, so Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²).
At resonance X_L = X_C, so they cancel and the impedance falls to its minimum, Z = R.
Resonance occurs when ωL = 1/ωC, so ω₀ = 1/√(LC).

quiz.q: If X_C > X_L, the circuit is
quiz.why: If X_C > X_L the net reactance is capacitive and the current leads the voltage, so the circuit is capacitive.

quiz.q: A smaller resistance in an LCR circuit makes the resonance
quiz.why: The quality factor Q = ω₀L/R rises as R falls, so the resonance peak becomes sharper.
At resonance the net reactance is zero, so tan φ = 0 and the phase angle is 0°.

lessons.title: Power in AC circuits and power factor

scenes.text: Mr. Iyer's small factory gets a penalty on its electricity bill for a 'low power factor'.
Its many motors draw current that is out of phase with voltage — current flows but does little useful work.
Adding capacitor banks brings current back into phase and saves money.

steps.title: Average power
steps.body:
With v = v_m sin ωt and i = i_m sin(ωt + φ):
**P̄ = V I cos φ** (V, I rms). **cos φ = power factor = R/Z**.
- Pure R: cos φ = 1, P = VI.
- Pure L or C: cos φ = 0, P = 0.
- LCR at resonance: cos φ = 1.
Also P̄ = I²R — only the resistance dissipates power.

steps.title: Wattless current
steps.body: Resolve I into I cos φ (in phase with V) and I sin φ (90° to V). The component **I sin φ** contributes no average power — it is called the **wattless current**. Utilities want power factor close to 1 to avoid large I²R line losses for the same useful power.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** From the LCR example (200 V, 4 A, Z = 50 Ω, R = 30 Ω):
- cos φ = R/Z = **0.6**; P = 200 × 4 × 0.6 = **480 W**.
- Check: I²R = 16 × 30 = 480 W ✔

**Ex 2.** A motor takes 10 A at 230 V with power factor 0.8.
- P = 230 × 10 × 0.8 = **1840 W**.
- Wattless current = 10 × sin φ = 10 × 0.6 = **6 A**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P = VI in a reactive circuit — include cos φ.
- Using cos φ = X/Z instead of R/Z.
- Thinking a choke wastes as much power as a resistor would.

statements.s: Power factor of a purely resistive circuit is 1.
An ideal inductor dissipates average power I²X_L.
statements.why: Average power in a pure inductor is zero.

statements.s: Power factor equals R/Z.
Wattless current is the component of current in phase with voltage.
statements.why: It is the component 90° out of phase.

quiz.q: Average power in an AC circuit is
quiz.why: Only the component of current in phase with the voltage does work, so average power = VI cos φ.

quiz.q: Power factor of an LCR circuit at resonance is
quiz.why: At resonance Z = R, so the power factor cos φ = R/Z = 1.

quiz.q: Power factor of a pure capacitor is
quiz.why: A pure capacitor has φ = 90°, so the power factor cos 90° = 0.

quiz.q: The wattless component of current is
quiz.why: The component of current at 90° to the voltage, I sin φ, does no net work, so it is the wattless component.

quiz.q: A circuit has R = 6 Ω and Z = 10 Ω. Power factor:
quiz.why: Power factor = cos φ = R/Z = 6/10 = 0.6.

lessons.title: The transformer

story.title: From power station to your phone

scenes.text: Electricity leaves a power station at about 11 kV, then is stepped up to hundreds of kilovolts for long-distance lines.
Near the city, substations step it down again, finally to 230 V at home.
Your phone charger steps it down once more. Every step uses a transformer.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Two coils (primary Nₚ, secondary Nₛ) on a common soft-iron laminated core. AC in the primary sets up changing flux that links the secondary — **mutual induction**. Works only with AC (or changing current).

Ideal transformer (no flux leakage, no losses):
**Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = Iₚ/Iₛ**, and VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ.
- Step-up: Nₛ > Nₚ (voltage rises, current falls).
- Step-down: Nₛ < Nₚ.

steps.title: Energy losses
steps.body:
- **Flux leakage** — reduced by winding coils over each other.
- **Copper (I²R) loss** in windings — use thick wire.
- **Eddy currents** in the core — use laminated cores.
- **Hysteresis loss** — use soft iron with a low-loss magnetisation curve.
Efficiency of large transformers often exceeds 95%.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A transformer changes 220 V to 11 V. With 2000 primary turns, Nₛ = 2000 × 11/220 = **100 turns**. If the secondary delivers 5 A, the primary draws (ideal) **0.25 A**.

**Ex 2.** 800 kW is sent over lines of total resistance 10 Ω.
- At 11 kV: I = 800000/11000 ≈ 72.7 A; loss I²R ≈ **52.9 kW**.
- At 220 kV: I ≈ 3.64 A; loss ≈ **132 W**.
- Stepping up 20 times cuts the loss 400 times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a step-up transformer increases power — it increases voltage and decreases current; power at best stays equal.
- Using a transformer on DC.
- Inverting the current ratio: Iₛ/Iₚ = Nₚ/Nₛ.

activity.prompt: An ideal step-down transformer has 4000 primary turns and is connected to 240 V. How many secondary turns give 12 V?

quiz.q: Transformers work on the principle of
quiz.why: A transformer works on mutual induction: a changing current in the primary changes the flux through the secondary and induces an emf in it.
A step-up transformer raises the voltage. Since power is nearly conserved, the current decreases.
Laminated cores are made of thin insulated sheets, which break the paths of eddy currents and reduce eddy-current loss.

quiz.q: A transformer cannot work on DC because
quiz.why: DC gives a steady flux, with no change, so no emf is induced in the secondary.

quiz.q: For an ideal transformer, Vₛ/Vₚ equals
quiz.why: For an ideal transformer V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p, the ratio of the turns.

lessons.title: Displacement current

story.title: The puzzle of the capacitor gap

scenes.text: Neel's teacher draws a charging capacitor and asks: current flows in the wires, but what crosses the empty gap?
Ampère's law gives different answers depending on which surface you draw — a contradiction.
Maxwell fixed it: a changing electric field in the gap acts just like a current.

steps.title: The inconsistency
steps.body: Around a wire leading to a charging capacitor, take an Amperian loop. A flat surface pierced by the wire encloses current i; a pot-shaped surface passing between the plates encloses **no** conduction current. Ampère's law ∮B·dl = μ₀i would give two answers for the same loop.

steps.title: Maxwell's displacement current
steps.body:
Between the plates E = Q/(ε₀A), so the electric flux Φ_E = Q/ε₀ and dΦ_E/dt = i/ε₀. Define

**i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt**

Then the **Ampère–Maxwell law**: **∮B·dl = μ₀(i_c + i_d)**. Total current (conduction + displacement) is continuous everywhere. A changing E field produces B, just as a changing B produces E (Faraday) — together they allow self-sustaining EM waves.

steps.title: Maxwell's equations (in words)
steps.body:
1. Gauss (electricity): ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀.
2. Gauss (magnetism): ∮B·dA = 0.
3. Faraday: ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt.
4. Ampère–Maxwell: ∮B·dl = μ₀i_c + μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A capacitor is charged by a steady 0.15 A current. Displacement current between its plates = **0.15 A** (it equals the conduction current in the leads).

**Ex 2.** Plates of area 0.01 m²; E between them rises at 1×10¹² V m⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- i_d = ε₀A dE/dt = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 0.01 × 10¹² ≈ **0.089 A**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking charges physically jump across the gap — the displacement current is a changing field, not moving charge.
- Saying displacement current exists with a *steady* E field; it needs dE/dt ≠ 0.

activity.prompt: Complete the Ampère–Maxwell idea.
activity.text: Displacement current i_d = ε₀ × d(___)/dt. In a charging capacitor, i_d between the plates is ___ to the conduction current in the wires.

options: flow of electrons in the gap
quiz.why: Displacement current arises from a changing electric flux: i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt.
James Clerk Maxwell introduced the displacement current to make Ampère's law consistent.

quiz.q: In a charging capacitor, i_d between the plates compared with conduction current i is
quiz.why: Current is continuous overall. Between the plates the displacement current equals the conduction current in the wires.

quiz.q: Ampère–Maxwell law adds which term to Ampère's law?
quiz.why: Maxwell added the displacement current term μ₀ε₀ dΦ_E/dt to Ampère's law.
Displacement current is a current, so it is measured in amperes.

lessons.title: Nature and properties of EM waves

scenes.text: When ISRO's Mangalyaan sent pictures from Mars, the signals took several minutes to reach Earth.
Those radio signals crossed empty space — no air, no medium.
EM waves are self-sustaining oscillating electric and magnetic fields that need no medium at all.

steps.title: Source
steps.body: **Accelerated charges** radiate EM waves. A charge oscillating at frequency ν produces EM waves of the same frequency (e.g. an antenna; Hertz first produced and detected them in 1887–88; J.C. Bose and Marconi worked with shorter and longer waves). A charge moving uniformly does *not* radiate.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- E and B oscillate **in phase**, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel ⇒ **transverse**. Eₓ = E₀ sin(kz − ωt) with B_y = B₀ sin(kz − ωt) for travel along z.
- Speed in vacuum **c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s**; in a medium v = 1/√(με) = c/n.
- **E₀/B₀ = c** (also E/B = c at every instant).
- k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πν, c = νλ = ω/k.
- They carry **energy** (average energy density shared equally between E and B fields) and **momentum**: total energy U delivered to a surface with complete absorption carries momentum p = U/c ⇒ **radiation pressure**.
- They need no medium; frequency stays the same when entering a new medium, wavelength changes.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** In a plane EM wave B₀ = 1.6×10⁻⁷ T. Then E₀ = cB₀ = 3×10⁸ × 1.6×10⁻⁷ = **48 V/m**.

**Ex 2.** A radio station broadcasts at 30 MHz. λ = c/ν = 3×10⁸/3×10⁷ = **10 m**.

**Ex 3.** Light of 600 nm enters glass (n = 1.5). Frequency unchanged, = c/λ = **5×10¹⁴ Hz**; speed 2×10⁸ m/s; wavelength in glass = **400 nm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking EM waves are longitudinal.
- Saying E and B are 90° out of phase — they are in phase, though perpendicular in direction.
- Changing frequency on refraction — only speed and wavelength change.

statements.s: EM waves need a material medium to travel.
In an EM wave, E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.
E₀/B₀ equals the speed of light.
A charge moving with constant velocity radiates EM waves.

quiz.why: The speed of EM waves in vacuum is c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s.
The electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel, so EM waves are transverse.

lessons.title: The electromagnetic spectrum: radio to infrared

scenes.text: Ayesha warms dal in a microwave, changes the TV channel with the remote and hears the radio playing.
Three devices, three kinds of invisible waves.
All are the same thing — EM waves — differing only in wavelength and frequency.

steps.title: Radio waves (λ > 0.1 m; ν < ~10⁹ Hz)
steps.body:
Produced by accelerated charges in conducting wires (antennas).
- AM band 530 kHz – 1710 kHz; higher frequencies (up to ~54 MHz) for shortwave.
- TV waves 54 MHz – 890 MHz; FM radio 88 – 108 MHz.
- Cellular phones use ultra-high-frequency (UHF) bands.

steps.title: Microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm; ~10⁹–10¹¹ Hz)
steps.body:
Produced by special vacuum tubes (klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes).
- Radar for aircraft navigation and speed guns.
- **Microwave ovens:** frequency chosen to match a resonant frequency of water molecules, so energy goes into the food's water and heats it.

steps.title: Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm)
steps.body:
Produced by hot bodies and molecules — called **heat waves**.
- Absorbed by water, CO₂ and NH₃ in air; greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm.
- Infrared lamps in physiotherapy, TV remote controls (IR LEDs), night-vision and thermal cameras, earth-observation satellites.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** An FM station at 100 MHz: λ = 3×10⁸/10⁸ = **3 m** (radio band).

**Ex 2.** A microwave oven runs at 2.45 GHz: λ = 3×10⁸/2.45×10⁹ ≈ **12.2 cm** (microwave band).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling IR 'heat' as if it were not light — it is an EM wave, just invisible.
- Mixing up which has higher frequency: microwaves have higher ν (shorter λ) than radio waves.

activity.prompt: Match each wave to its use.

quiz.q: The wave used in radar is
quiz.why: Radar uses microwaves because their short wavelengths can be sent as narrow beams and reflect off objects.

quiz.q: Heat waves are another name for
quiz.why: Hot bodies emit infrared radiation, which is felt as heat, so infrared waves are called heat waves.
FM radio lies in the VHF band, about 88–108 MHz.

quiz.q: Microwave ovens heat food mainly by
quiz.why: Microwaves make water molecules in food rotate and vibrate, and the energy heats the food.
Frequency rises as wavelength falls. Radio has the longest wavelength, then microwaves, then infrared, so radio < microwave < IR.

lessons.title: The electromagnetic spectrum: visible to gamma rays

scenes.text: At the dentist, Farhan bites on a small card while a lead apron is placed on him.
X-rays pass through soft tissue but are stopped more by teeth and bone, revealing a cavity.
Higher-frequency waves carry more energy per photon — useful, but they must be handled with care.

steps.title: Visible light (≈ 700 nm – 400 nm)
steps.body: The narrow band our eyes detect: red (longest λ) to violet (shortest). Other animals see differently — bees see some UV, snakes detect IR.

steps.title: Ultraviolet (≈ 400 nm – 1 nm)
steps.body:
Produced by very hot bodies (the Sun) and special lamps.
- Most solar UV is absorbed by the **ozone layer** at 40–50 km.
- Too much UV causes sunburn and skin cancer; welders wear special goggles (glass absorbs some UV).
- Used in water purifiers and LASIK eye surgery (precisely focused UV).

steps.title: X-rays (≈ 10 nm – 10⁻⁴ nm) and gamma rays (< 10⁻³ nm)
steps.body:
- **X-rays:** produced by bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons. Uses: medical diagnosis, cancer treatment, crystal structure studies. Over-exposure damages tissue.
- **Gamma rays:** from nuclear reactions and radioactive nuclei; highest frequency. Used in medicine to destroy cancer cells and to sterilise equipment.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Which is more energetic per photon: 300 nm UV or 600 nm red? E ∝ 1/λ, so **UV is twice as energetic**.

**Ex 2.** A wave has ν = 3×10¹⁸ Hz. λ = 3×10⁸/3×10¹⁸ = **10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.1 nm** ⇒ **X-ray** region.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking X-rays and gamma rays are different because of wavelength alone — their bands overlap; they are named by *source* (electrons vs nuclei).
- Believing all UV is blocked by ozone — some reaches the ground, which is why sunscreen matters.

quiz.why: Arc welding produces strong ultraviolet light, which can damage the eyes, so welders use special goggles.
