lessons.title: Reflection by spherical mirrors

story.title: The shaving mirror and the car mirror

scenes.text: Kiran's father uses a concave mirror to shave — his face looks big and upright.
The car's side mirror is convex and warns 'objects are closer than they appear'.
One formula, with careful signs, explains both mirrors.

steps.title: Sign convention (New Cartesian)
steps.body:
- All distances are measured from the **pole**.
- Distances in the direction of the incident light are **positive**; against it **negative**.
- Heights above the principal axis positive, below negative.
With light coming from the left, the object distance u is negative. For a concave mirror f < 0; for a convex mirror f > 0. **f = R/2**.

steps.title: Mirror formula and magnification
steps.body:
**1/v + 1/u = 1/f**
**m = h'/h = −v/u**
- m negative ⇒ real, inverted image; m positive ⇒ virtual, erect.
- |m| > 1 magnified, |m| < 1 diminished.
- A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image (wide field of view).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Object 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of f = 15 cm.
- u = −10, f = −15: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/15 + 1/10 = 1/30 ⇒ **v = +30 cm** (behind mirror, virtual).
- m = −v/u = −30/(−10) = **+3** ⇒ erect, three times larger (shaving mirror).

**Ex 2.** A convex rear-view mirror has R = 2 m; a bus is 6 m behind.
- f = +1 m, u = −6 m: 1/v = 1 + 1/6 = 7/6 ⇒ **v ≈ 0.86 m**.
- m = −v/u = 0.86/6 ≈ **0.14** ⇒ upright and small.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the negative sign for u and for a concave mirror's f.
- Using m = v/u for mirrors (that is for lenses; mirrors use −v/u).
- Assuming a concave mirror always gives a real image — not when the object is inside F.

activity.prompt: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance v (cm, with sign).

quiz.q: Focal length of a spherical mirror equals
quiz.why: For a spherical mirror the focal length is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2.

quiz.q: In the New Cartesian convention, the object distance for a real object is
quiz.why: In the New Cartesian convention, distances are measured from the pole, and those against the direction of incident light are negative. A real object is in front, so u is negative.

quiz.q: A convex mirror always forms an image that is
quiz.why: A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image.

quiz.q: Magnification m = −2 means the image is
quiz.why: Negative magnification means the image is inverted, which for a mirror means real, and |m| = 2 means twice the size.

quiz.q: For an object at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror the image is at
quiz.why: An object at C of a concave mirror gives a real, inverted image of the same size, also at C (m = −1).

lessons.title: Refraction and total internal reflection

story.title: The bent pencil and the sparkling diamond

scenes.text: In a glass of water Tara's pencil looks bent at the surface.
Her aunt's diamond sparkles far more than glass cut in the same shape.
Both come from refraction — and, for the diamond, light being trapped by total internal reflection.

steps.title: Snell's law
steps.body:
**n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r**; refractive index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂. Absolute index n = c/v. Light bends towards the normal entering a denser medium.

**Apparent depth:** for viewing near-normally from air, apparent depth = real depth / n. The bottom of a tank seems raised by **h(1 − 1/n)**.

steps.title: Total internal reflection (TIR)
steps.body:
When light goes from **denser to rarer** medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the **critical angle i_c**, all light is reflected.
**sin i_c = n_rarer/n_denser** (= 1/n for glass–air).

Applications: sparkle of diamond (i_c ≈ 24°), totally reflecting prisms in binoculars and periscopes, **optical fibres** (core of higher n than cladding; light bounces along by repeated TIR — used in internet cables and endoscopes), mirages.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A tank holds water (n = 4/3) 12 cm deep. Apparent depth = 12/(4/3) = **9 cm**; the bottom appears raised by **3 cm**.

**Ex 2.** Critical angle for glass (n = 1.5) to air: sin i_c = 1/1.5 = 0.667 ⇒ **i_c ≈ 41.8°**.

**Ex 3.** For water to air: sin i_c = 3/4 ⇒ **i_c ≈ 48.6°**. A fish sees the whole sky through a circle of radius h tan i_c above it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trying TIR from rarer to denser medium — impossible.
- Using real depth × n instead of real depth / n.
- Writing sin i_c = n instead of 1/n.

statements.s: TIR can occur when light goes from air into glass.
A higher refractive index gives a smaller critical angle.
Optical fibres guide light by repeated total internal reflection.
Light bends away from the normal when entering a denser medium.

quiz.q: Refractive index n = c/v. If n = 1.5, v in glass is

quiz.why: The critical angle satisfies sin i_c = n₂/n₁, so it depends on the refractive indices of the two media.
Diamond has a very small critical angle (about 24°), so light entering it is totally internally reflected many times, which makes it sparkle.

quiz.q: A coin under 20 cm of liquid (n = 2) appears at depth
quiz.why: Apparent depth = real depth/n = 20/2 = 10 cm.

quiz.q: Mirages in deserts are due to
options: total internal reflection in hot air layers
quiz.why: Hot air near the ground is optically rarer. Light from the sky is totally internally reflected there, forming a mirage.

lessons.title: Refraction at spherical surfaces and lenses

scenes.text: Nani borrows Jai's magnifying glass to read the fine print on a medicine strip.
An optometrist later prescribes her +2.5 D lenses.
'Dioptre' is just 1 divided by focal length in metres — and the lens maker's formula tells how curved the glass must be.

steps.title: Refraction at one spherical surface
steps.body:
Medium n₁ (object side) to n₂, surface of radius R. For paraxial rays (using small angles and Snell's law):

**n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R**

(Use the same Cartesian signs; R positive if the centre of curvature is on the outgoing side.)

steps.title: Lens maker's and thin-lens formula
steps.body:
Apply the surface formula twice (the first image becomes the object for the second surface) for a thin lens of index n in air:

**1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)** — lens maker's formula
**1/v − 1/u = 1/f** — thin-lens formula
**m = v/u**

Convex (converging) lens: f > 0; concave: f < 0. In a medium of index n_m, replace (n − 1) by (n/n_m − 1).

steps.title: Power and combinations
steps.body:
**P = 1/f** (f in metres), unit **dioptre (D)**; converging lens positive.
Thin lenses in contact: **1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂**, **P = P₁ + P₂**; total magnification m = m₁m₂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the mirror formula (1/v + 1/u) for lenses — lenses use 1/v − 1/u.
- Using cm in P = 1/f: convert to metres.
- Forgetting that R₂ is negative for a biconvex lens.

quiz.why: The thin lens formula, with sign convention, is 1/v − 1/u = 1/f.

Lenses of +2 D and −0.5 D in contact have power
quiz.why: Powers of lenses in contact add: +2 + (−0.5) = +1.5 D.

lessons.title: Refraction through a prism

scenes.text: A glass crystal hanging at Ira's window throws a little rainbow on the wall every morning.
A prism bends light twice — at the entering and leaving faces.
The amount of bending has a minimum value from which the glass's refractive index can be measured exactly.

steps.title: Deviation by a prism
steps.body:
For a prism of angle A, with angles of incidence i and emergence e and internal refraction angles r₁, r₂:
- **r₁ + r₂ = A**
- **Deviation δ = i + e − A**
As i increases, δ first decreases, reaches a **minimum D_m**, then increases.

steps.title: Minimum deviation
steps.body:
At D_m the ray passes symmetrically: i = e, r₁ = r₂ = A/2, and i = (A + D_m)/2. Snell's law at the first face gives

**n = sin[(A + D_m)/2] / sin(A/2)**

**Thin prism** (small A): **δ = (n − 1)A**.

**Dispersion:** n depends on wavelength (higher for violet), so violet deviates most and red least — white light splits into a spectrum.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that at minimum deviation r = A/2.
- Using δ = (n − 1)A for large-angle prisms.
- Saying red deviates the most — violet does.

activity.prompt: A prism of angle 60° gives minimum deviation 38.9° (approx.). Using sin 49.45° ≈ 0.76, find n.

quiz.q: For a prism, r₁ + r₂ equals
quiz.why: For a prism the refraction angles inside add up to the prism angle: r₁ + r₂ = A.

quiz.q: At minimum deviation the ray inside the prism is
quiz.why: At minimum deviation i = e and r₁ = r₂, so the ray inside the prism runs parallel to the base.

quiz.q: Deviation by a thin prism is
quiz.why: For a thin prism the deviation is δ = (n − 1)A.

quiz.q: Which colour deviates most in a glass prism?
quiz.why: Violet has the highest refractive index in glass, so it is bent most.
The total deviation is the sum of the deviations at both faces: δ = i + e − A.

lessons.title: Optical instruments: microscopes and telescopes

story.title: Seeing the very small and the very far

scenes.text: In the biology lab, Rehan sees onion cells through a compound microscope.
That night at a star party he sees the rings of Saturn through a telescope.
Both use two lenses: one forms an image, the other magnifies it like a magnifying glass.

steps.title: Simple microscope (magnifying glass)
steps.body:
A convex lens of short focal length f, object inside f, eye close to the lens.
- Image at the near point (D = 25 cm): **m = 1 + D/f**.
- Image at infinity (relaxed eye): **m = D/f**.

steps.title: Compound microscope
steps.body:
Objective (small f_o) forms a real, magnified image; the eyepiece (f_e) acts as a simple microscope on it.
- **m = m_o × m_e**; for the final image at infinity **m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e)**, where L (tube length) is the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece.
- Near point: m ≈ (L/f_o)(1 + D/f_e).

steps.title: Telescopes
steps.body:
**Refracting (astronomical) telescope:** objective of *large* f_o and large aperture, eyepiece of small f_e.
- Normal adjustment (final image at infinity): **m = f_o/f_e**, tube length **f_o + f_e**; image inverted.
**Reflecting telescope (Cassegrain):** a concave primary mirror instead of a lens — no chromatic aberration, easier to support large mirrors, and parabolic mirrors avoid spherical aberration.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A magnifying glass of f = 5 cm: m = 1 + 25/5 = **6** (near point) or **5** (infinity).

**Ex 2.** Compound microscope: f_o = 2 cm, f_e = 5 cm, L = 20 cm, image at infinity.
- m ≈ (20/2)(25/5) = **50**.

**Ex 3.** Telescope: f_o = 100 cm, f_e = 5 cm in normal adjustment.
- m = 100/5 = **20**; length = **105 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a large focal length eyepiece for higher magnification — magnification needs *small* f_e.
- Swapping objective and eyepiece roles between microscope (small f_o) and telescope (large f_o).
- Forgetting that telescope magnification is angular, not linear size.

quiz.why: A telescope's objective has a large focal length (for large magnification) and a large aperture to collect more light.

quiz.why: In normal adjustment the angular magnification of a telescope is f_o/f_e.

quiz.why: In normal adjustment the focal points of the objective and eyepiece coincide, so the tube length is f_o + f_e.

quiz.q: A reflecting telescope is free from
quiz.why: Mirrors reflect all colours equally, so a reflecting telescope is free from chromatic aberration.

quiz.why: The least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye is 25 cm.

outcomes: Learners can use Huygens construction to derive the laws of reflection and refraction.
Learners can state conditions for constructive and destructive interference and the intensity formula.
Learners can derive and use fringe width β = λD/d.

lessons.title: Huygens principle and wavefronts

scenes.text: Aman drops a pebble into a still pond and watches circles spread outward.
Far away, the circles look almost like straight lines marching across the water.
Huygens imagined every point on a wave as a new tiny source — the idea that explains reflection and refraction.

steps.title: Wavefronts
steps.body:
A **wavefront** is the locus of points oscillating in the same phase. Rays are perpendicular to wavefronts.
- Point source nearby: **spherical** wavefront.
- Line source: cylindrical.
- Source very far away (Sun): **plane** wavefront.

steps.title: Huygens principle
steps.body:
1. Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of **secondary wavelets** spreading at the wave speed.
2. The new wavefront at a later time is the **forward envelope** (common tangent) of these wavelets. (Backwave is ignored.)

steps.title: Refraction by Huygens construction
steps.body:
A plane wavefront AB strikes the surface at angle i. While the wavelet from B travels BC = v₁τ in medium 1, the wavelet from A travels AE = v₂τ in medium 2. From triangles: sin i = BC/AC and sin r = AE/AC, so
**sin i / sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁** — Snell's law.
- If v₂ < v₁ the ray bends towards the normal. Frequency is unchanged; λ₂ = λ₁ v₂/v₁.
- Reflection: the reflected wavelet travels in the same medium, giving **i = r**.
- Lenses, prisms and mirrors change the *shape* of a wavefront (e.g. a convex lens turns a plane wavefront into a converging spherical one).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Light of 589 nm in air enters water (n = 1.33). (a) Frequency = 3×10⁸/589×10⁻⁹ ≈ **5.09×10¹⁴ Hz** (unchanged). (b) Speed = 3×10⁸/1.33 ≈ **2.26×10⁸ m/s**. (c) Wavelength in water = 589/1.33 ≈ **443 nm**.

**Ex 2.** Wavefronts from a distant star reaching a telescope are **plane**; after a convex lens they become **spherical converging** on the focus.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking frequency changes in refraction.
- Confusing rays with wavefronts — rays are normals to the wavefronts.
- The corpuscular (particle) model predicted light is *faster* in water; the wave model correctly predicts it is slower.

activity.prompt: Match the source to its wavefront shape.
pairs: After a convex lens (plane light incident)

quiz.q: A wavefront is a surface of
quiz.why: A wavefront is a surface on which all points are in the same phase.

quiz.q: Light from a very distant source has
quiz.why: A very distant source has a huge wavefront radius, so over a small region the wavefront is plane.

quiz.q: Huygens construction proves that sin i/sin r equals
quiz.why: Huygens's construction shows sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂, which is Snell's law.

quiz.q: When light enters a denser medium, its
quiz.why: In a denser medium the speed drops while the frequency stays the same, so the wavelength λ = v/ν decreases.

quiz.q: Rays are related to wavefronts as
quiz.why: Rays are the normals to wavefronts, so they are perpendicular to them.

lessons.title: Coherent sources and interference

scenes.text: Pihu blows soap bubbles and sees swirling colours on them.
There is no dye in soap water — the colours come from light waves reflected from the film's two surfaces overlapping.
Waves add up or cancel depending on their phase difference: that is interference.

steps.title: Superposition
steps.body:
The net displacement is the sum of individual displacements. For two waves of equal amplitude a with phase difference φ:
**I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2)** (I₀ = intensity of each).
- φ = 0, 2π, … (path difference Δ = nλ): **constructive**, I = 4I₀.
- φ = π, 3π, … (Δ = (n + ½)λ): **destructive**, I = 0.
In general I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cos φ. Energy is redistributed, not created or destroyed.

steps.title: Coherence
steps.body: Sustained interference needs **coherent sources** — same frequency and a **constant phase difference**. Two independent bulbs are incoherent: their phase changes randomly ~10⁻¹⁰ s, so intensities simply add (I = I₁ + I₂). Coherent sources are obtained by dividing light from one source (two slits, thin films) or by using lasers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Two coherent waves with intensities I and 4I meet.
- I_max = (√I + √4I)² = **9I**; I_min = (√4I − √I)² = **I**; ratio 9 : 1.

**Ex 2.** Path difference 2.5λ between two coherent equal waves ⇒ (n + ½)λ ⇒ **dark** (destructive).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding amplitudes of incoherent sources.
- Saying energy is destroyed at dark fringes — it reappears at bright fringes.
- Using path difference = nλ for dark fringes.

activity.prompt: Bright or dark? (equal coherent sources, in phase)

options: the same frequency and constant phase difference
quiz.why: Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, which gives a steady interference pattern.

quiz.q: For destructive interference the path difference is
quiz.why: Destructive interference needs a path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths, (n + ½)λ.

quiz.q: Two equal coherent waves interfere constructively; resultant intensity is
quiz.why: Amplitudes add to 2a, so the intensity is (2a)² ∝ 4I₀.

quiz.q: Light from two separate bulbs does not show interference because
quiz.why: Two separate bulbs emit light with random, rapidly changing phases, so they are not coherent and give no steady fringes.

quiz.q: Phase difference corresponding to path difference λ/2 is

lessons.title: Young's double-slit experiment

scenes.text: In 1801 Thomas Young let sunlight through a pinhole, then through two closely spaced slits.
On a screen appeared alternate bright and dark bands — impossible if light were only particles.
Measuring the band spacing even let him find the wavelength of light.

steps.title: Path difference derivation
steps.body:
Slits S₁ and S₂ separated by d, screen at distance D (D ≫ d). For a point P at height x from the centre:
S₂P² − S₁P² = [D² + (x + d/2)²] − [D² + (x − d/2)²] = 2xd
Since S₂P + S₁P ≈ 2D: **Δ = S₂P − S₁P = xd/D**.

steps.title: Fringe positions and width
steps.body:
- Bright: xd/D = nλ ⇒ **x_n = nλD/d**
- Dark: xd/D = (n + ½)λ ⇒ x = (n + ½)λD/d
- **Fringe width β = λD/d** (equal for bright and dark fringes).
- Angular fringe width θ = λ/d.
Effects: in a medium of index n, β becomes β/n. Larger d ⇒ narrower fringes. With white light, the central fringe is white and others are coloured (red outermost).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** λ = 600 nm, d = 0.5 mm, D = 1 m.
- β = 6×10⁻⁷ × 1 / 5×10⁻⁴ = **1.2 mm**.
- 3rd bright fringe from centre: 3β = **3.6 mm**.

**Ex 2.** The whole apparatus is immersed in water (n = 4/3).
- β' = 1.2/(4/3) = **0.9 mm**.

**Ex 3.** Two wavelengths 650 nm and 520 nm: the least distance from the centre where bright fringes coincide satisfies n₁ × 650 = n₂ × 520 ⇒ 4 × 650 = 5 × 520 ⇒ x = 4 × 650 nm × D/d.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using D in mm and d in m (or vice versa) — keep SI units.
- Expecting fringe width to change with slit width (it depends on separation d).
- Forgetting that the central fringe is bright (Δ = 0).

activity.prompt: In a YDSE, d = 0.2 mm, D = 1.2 m and fringe width is 3 mm. Find λ in nm.

quiz.why: The fringe width in Young's double slit experiment is β = λD/d.

quiz.q: If slit separation is doubled, fringe width
quiz.why: β = λD/d, so β ∝ 1/d. Doubling the separation halves the fringe width.

quiz.q: If the experiment is done in water, fringe width
quiz.why: In water λ is smaller (λ/n), so the fringe width λD/d decreases.

quiz.q: The central fringe in YDSE with white light is
quiz.why: At the centre the path difference is zero for every colour, so all colours overlap and the central fringe is white.

quiz.q: Path difference at a point x on the screen is
quiz.why: The path difference at a point a distance x from the centre is Δ = xd/D.

lessons.title: Diffraction at a single slit

scenes.text: Looking at a distant streetlight through a fine-weave umbrella, Gauri sees a pattern of spots and fringes.
Light bends around tiny obstacles and openings.
For a single narrow slit, it spreads into a bright central band with weaker bands on each side.

steps.title: Single-slit pattern
steps.body:
A slit of width a, parallel light of wavelength λ. Divide the slit into halves: wavelets from corresponding points of each half cancel when a sin θ = λ.
- **Minima: a sin θ = nλ** (n = ±1, ±2, …).
- Secondary maxima approximately at a sin θ = (n + ½)λ, much fainter.
- **Central maximum** spans from −λ/a to +λ/a: angular width **2λ/a**, linear width on a screen at D: **2λD/a**. It is twice as wide as other fringes and much brighter.

steps.title: Interference vs diffraction
steps.body:
| Interference: superposition of waves from two (or more) separate coherent sources; fringes equally spaced and equally bright.
| Diffraction: superposition of wavelets from different parts of one wavefront; central maximum twice as wide, intensity falling off rapidly.
In YDSE, each slit's diffraction envelope modulates the two-slit interference fringes.

**Fresnel distance** z_F = a²/λ — distance up to which ray optics is a good approximation for an aperture a.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** a = 0.2 mm, λ = 500 nm, D = 1 m.
- Width of central maximum = 2λD/a = 2 × 5×10⁻⁷/2×10⁻⁴ = **5 mm**.
- First minimum at 2.5 mm from centre.

**Ex 2.** For a = 3 mm and λ = 500 nm, Fresnel distance = (3×10⁻³)²/5×10⁻⁷ = **18 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a sin θ = nλ for maxima — that is the condition for *minima* in single-slit diffraction.
- Forgetting the factor 2 in the central maximum width.
- Thinking a wider slit gives a wider pattern — it gives a narrower one.

activity.label: Slit width a (μm) for λ = 500 nm

bands.text: a ≈ λ: light spreads almost everywhere — diffraction dominates.
Angular half-width λ/a is a few degrees: a clear, broad central maximum.
Wide slit: λ/a is tiny, the pattern shrinks and light travels almost in straight lines (ray optics).

quiz.q: First minimum of single-slit diffraction occurs at
quiz.why: The first minimum in single-slit diffraction occurs where a sin θ = λ.

quiz.q: Angular width of the central maximum is
quiz.why: The central maximum extends from −λ/a to +λ/a, so its angular width is 2λ/a.

quiz.q: If the slit is made narrower, the central maximum
quiz.why: The width of the central maximum is 2λ/a. A narrower slit (smaller a) makes it wider.

quiz.q: Compared with YDSE fringes, diffraction fringes
options: have a much brighter, wider central band
quiz.why: In diffraction, the central band is much brighter and wider than the others, which fall off in intensity. YDSE fringes are of nearly equal width and brightness.

quiz.q: Ray optics is valid for distances much less than
quiz.why: Ray optics applies for distances less than the Fresnel distance a²/λ. Beyond that, diffraction spreading is significant.

lessons.title: Polarisation

scenes.text: At the beach, Veer tilts his head while wearing polarising sunglasses and the glare off the sea fades and returns.
Light reflected from water is partly polarised.
Polaroid lenses block the vibration direction that carries the glare.

steps.title: What is polarisation
steps.body: Light is a transverse wave; in unpolarised light the E vector vibrates in all directions perpendicular to propagation. A **polaroid** transmits only the component along its pass axis, producing **plane-polarised** light. Only transverse waves can be polarised — so polarisation proves light is transverse (sound in air cannot be polarised).

steps.title: Malus's law
steps.body:
Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ through one polaroid: **I₀/2**.
Polarised light of intensity I₁ through a second polaroid (analyser) at angle θ to the first: **I = I₁ cos² θ**.
- θ = 0: full transmission; θ = 90° (crossed polaroids): zero.

steps.title: Polarisation by reflection: Brewster's law
steps.body: When the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, the reflected light is completely plane-polarised. The angle of incidence then is **Brewster's angle i_B**, with **tan i_B = n** (n of the reflecting medium relative to the first). Also i_B + r = 90°.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Unpolarised light I₀ passes through two polaroids at 60°.
- After the first: I₀/2. After the second: (I₀/2) cos² 60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = **I₀/8**.

**Ex 2.** Brewster angle for glass, n = 1.5: tan i_B = 1.5 ⇒ **i_B ≈ 56.3°**; angle of refraction = 90° − 56.3° = **33.7°**.

**Ex 3.** A third polaroid at 45° between two crossed polaroids: I = (I₀/2)cos²45° cos²45° = **I₀/8** — light now gets through!

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying cos² θ to unpolarised light (first polaroid always gives I₀/2).
- Using cos θ instead of cos² θ.
- Using sin i_B = n instead of tan i_B = n.

activity.prompt: Unpolarised light of intensity 32 W/m² passes through two polaroids whose axes are at 30°. Find the transmitted intensity (W/m²).

quiz.q: Polarisation shows that light waves are
quiz.why: Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation shows light is a transverse wave.

quiz.q: Unpolarised light through an ideal polaroid has intensity
quiz.why: An ideal polaroid passes half the intensity of unpolarised light: I₀/2.
Malus's law: the intensity of polarised light through an analyser at angle θ is I = I₀cos²θ.

quiz.q: At Brewster's angle the reflected and refracted rays are
quiz.why: At Brewster's angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other.
Brewster's law states tan i_B = n.

questions.why: A point source nearby emits wavefronts as expanding spheres, so the wavefront is spherical.

questions.q: Which phenomenon proves the transverse nature of light?
questions.why: Polarisation occurs only for transverse waves, so it proves that light is transverse.

questions.q: Interference requires sources that are
questions.why: A steady interference pattern needs coherent sources with a constant phase difference.

questions.q: Assertion: Fringes are not seen with two separate bulbs. Reason: Light from them is not coherent.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Light from two separate bulbs is not coherent, as the phase difference changes randomly, so no stable fringes appear.

questions.q: In YDSE β = 2 mm. If D is doubled and d halved, β becomes
questions.why: β ∝ D/d. Doubling D and halving d makes β four times: 8 mm.

questions.q: Ratio of maximum to minimum intensity when two coherent waves have amplitude ratio 3 : 1:
Light of 500 nm through a slit of 0.1 mm. Angular position of first minimum:
questions.why: First minimum at a sin θ = λ, so θ = λ/a = 500×10⁻⁹/10⁻⁴ = 5×10⁻³ rad.

questions.q: Case: Two polaroids are crossed. A third is inserted between them at 30° to the first. Fraction of the original unpolarised intensity transmitted:
questions.why: Unpolarised light through the first polaroid gives ½I₀. The middle polaroid at 30° passes cos²30° = 3/4. The last, crossed (60° to the middle), passes cos²60° = 1/4. So I = ½ × 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/32.

questions.q: Brewster's angle for a medium is 60°. Its refractive index is
questions.why: tan i_B = n, so n = tan 60° = √3.

questions.q: In YDSE with λ = 600 nm, the 4th bright fringe is at 4.8 mm. Fringe width:
questions.why: The 4th bright fringe is at 4β = 4.8 mm, so β = 1.2 mm.

questions.q: Assertion: The central maximum of single-slit diffraction is the widest. Reason: Its angular width is 2λ/a while others are λ/a.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. The central maximum spans −λ/a to +λ/a (2λ/a), while the other maxima have width λ/a, so it is widest.

questions.q: Light of 600 nm in air enters glass of n = 1.5. Wavelength and frequency in glass:
questions.why: In glass λ = 600/1.5 = 400 nm. Frequency does not change: ν = c/λ_air = 3×10⁸/600×10⁻⁹ = 5×10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.q: A thin transparent film of thickness t and index μ covers one slit of a YDSE. The central fringe shifts by
questions.why: The film adds an extra optical path of (μ − 1)t, so the pattern shifts by (μ − 1)t × D/d.

questions.q: Case: In a YDSE, 60 fringes are seen in the field of view with λ = 4000 Å. With λ = 6000 Å the number of fringes is
questions.why: β ∝ λ, so the same field of view holds fewer fringes at longer λ: 60 × 4000/6000 = 40.

questions.q: Two waves of equal intensity I₀ have phase difference π/2. Resultant intensity:
questions.why: I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2) = 4I₀cos²(π/4) = 4I₀ × ½ = 2I₀.

questions.q: The Fresnel distance for a 2 mm aperture with 400 nm light is
questions.why: The Fresnel distance is a²/λ = (2×10⁻³)²/(4×10⁻⁷) = 4×10⁻⁶/4×10⁻⁷ = 10 m.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
courses.summary: Electron emission, the photoelectric effect and its experimental laws, why the wave theory fails, Einstein's photoelectric equation and photons, and de Broglie's matter waves — with graphs and many numericals. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can describe the effect of intensity, frequency and potential on photoelectric current.
Learners can use Einstein's equation K_max = hν − φ₀ and interpret the V₀–ν graph.
Learners can calculate photon energy, momentum and photon flux.
Learners can find de Broglie wavelengths of electrons, protons and everyday objects.

lessons.title: Electron emission and the photoelectric effect

scenes.text: At the mall, the glass doors slide open the moment Sana walks in.
A light beam is interrupted; a photocell stops giving current and the control circuit acts.
The photocell works because light knocks electrons out of a metal — the photoelectric effect.

steps.title: Electron emission
steps.body: Free electrons in a metal are held by a minimum energy barrier: the **work function φ₀** (in eV; 1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J). Energy can be supplied by heat (thermionic emission), strong fields (field emission) or light (**photoelectric emission**). Hertz (1887) and Hallwachs and Lenard observed that UV light makes metals emit electrons.

steps.title: Experimental observations
steps.body:
With a photocell (emitter C, collector A, variable potential):
1. **Intensity:** photocurrent ∝ intensity (for ν above threshold).
2. **Collector potential:** current rises with positive potential to a **saturation** value; with negative potential it falls to zero at the **stopping potential V₀**. eV₀ = K_max.
3. V₀ is **independent of intensity** but **increases linearly with frequency**.
4. There is a **threshold frequency ν₀** below which no emission occurs, however intense the light.
5. Emission is **instantaneous** (< 10⁻⁹ s).

steps.title: Why the wave theory fails
steps.body: Wave theory predicts: brighter light ⇒ more energetic electrons; any frequency should eventually work; dim light should take time to 'fill up' energy. All three predictions contradict observations 3, 4 and 5.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Photoelectrons are stopped by V₀ = 1.5 V. K_max = eV₀ = **1.5 eV = 2.4×10⁻¹⁹ J**.

**Ex 2.** Max speed for K_max = 1.5 eV: v = √(2K/m) = √(2 × 2.4×10⁻¹⁹/9.1×10⁻³¹) ≈ **7.3×10⁵ m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying stopping potential depends on intensity — it does not.
- Saying more intense light below threshold will eventually eject electrons.
- Confusing saturation current (depends on intensity) with stopping potential (depends on frequency).

statements.s: Doubling intensity doubles saturation current.
Doubling intensity doubles the stopping potential.
statements.why: V₀ depends only on frequency and the metal.

statements.s: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted.
statements.why: Each photon has too little energy.

statements.s: There is a measurable delay before emission starts in dim light.

quiz.q: The minimum energy to free an electron from a metal surface is
quiz.why: The minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal is its work function φ₀.
Brighter light has more photons per second, so more electrons are ejected and the photocurrent rises.
eV₀ = hν − φ₀, so the stopping potential depends on the frequency of the light, not its intensity.
Photoelectric emission is instantaneous, in about 10⁻⁹ s, with no time delay.
The wave theory predicts that energy should build up with intensity, so it cannot explain a threshold frequency below which there is no emission.

lessons.title: Einstein's photoelectric equation and photons

scenes.text: Arjun's family installs solar panels and wonders why they still work weakly on a cloudy day.
Light arrives in packets — photons — each with energy hν.
Fewer photons on a cloudy day mean less current, but each photon still has enough energy to do its job.

steps.title: Einstein's equation (1905)
steps.body:
Light consists of **photons**, each of energy **E = hν** (h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J s). One photon is absorbed by one electron:

**K_max = hν − φ₀** or **eV₀ = hν − φ₀**, with **φ₀ = hν₀**.

So **V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e**: a straight line; slope **h/e** (same for all metals); x-intercept ν₀; y-intercept −φ₀/e. Millikan's experiments (1906–1916) confirmed this and measured h.

steps.title: Photon properties
steps.body:
- Energy E = hν = hc/λ; handy form **E (eV) = 1240/λ (nm)**.
- Momentum **p = h/λ = E/c**; zero rest mass; speed c in vacuum.
- Number of photons per second from a source of power P: **N = P/(hν) = Pλ/(hc)**.
- In photon–electron collisions, energy and momentum are conserved; photons can be created or absorbed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using λ in metres with the 1240 shortcut (it needs nm and gives eV).
- Forgetting to convert φ₀ from eV to joules before mixing with h in J s.
- Thinking the graph slope depends on the metal.

activity.prompt: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.5 eV. Find the stopping potential (V). Use E(eV) = 1240/λ(nm).

quiz.why: Einstein's photoelectric equation: K_max = hν − φ₀, energy conservation for one photon and one electron.

quiz.q: Slope of V₀ versus ν graph is
quiz.why: eV₀ = hν − φ₀, so V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ₀/e, a straight line with slope h/e.

quiz.q: Energy of a 620 nm photon is about

quiz.why: A photon's momentum is p = h/λ.

quiz.q: Threshold frequency is related to work function by
quiz.why: At the threshold the kinetic energy is zero, so hν₀ = φ₀.

quiz.q: If frequency of incident light doubles (above threshold), K_max
quiz.why: K₁ = hν − φ₀. After doubling, K₂ = 2hν − φ₀ = 2K₁ + φ₀, which is more than 2K₁.

lessons.title: Matter waves: de Broglie hypothesis

scenes.text: Doctors at a research lab image a virus far too small for any light microscope.
Their electron microscope uses electrons — which behave like waves with tiny wavelengths.
De Broglie's bold idea: if light can be particles, particles can be waves.

steps.title: de Broglie relation (1924)
steps.body:
Every moving particle has a wave associated with it:

**λ = h/p = h/(mv)**

In terms of kinetic energy K: **λ = h/√(2mK)**. For a charge q accelerated through V: K = qV ⇒ **λ = h/√(2mqV)**.

For an electron: **λ ≈ 1.227/√V nm** (V in volts).

steps.title: Why we do not see waves in daily life
steps.body:
Because h is so small, λ for everyday objects (large m) is absurdly tiny — far smaller than any aperture — so no diffraction can be seen. For electrons accelerated by ~100 V, λ ~ 0.1 nm, similar to atomic spacing in crystals, so crystals diffract electrons. (Davisson and Germer confirmed electron waves in 1927.)

The wave intensity |ψ|² at a point gives the **probability** of finding the particle there (Born). A localised particle corresponds to a *wave packet*, linked to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle Δx Δp ≈ h/(2π).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Electron accelerated through 100 V: λ = 1.227/√100 = **0.123 nm**.

**Ex 2.** A 0.12 kg ball at 20 m/s: λ = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/(0.12 × 20) ≈ **2.8×10⁻³⁴ m** — undetectable.

**Ex 3.** A proton and an electron have the same kinetic energy. λ ∝ 1/√m ⇒ **λₑ/λₚ = √(mₚ/mₑ) ≈ √1836 ≈ 43** (electron's is longer).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using λ = h/p with p of a photon formula mixed with rest mass of a particle.
- Using 1.227/√V nm for protons — it is only for electrons.
- Thinking matter waves are EM waves — they are not.

activity.prompt: Find the de Broglie wavelength (nm) of an electron accelerated through 400 V. Use λ = 1.227/√V nm.

quiz.why: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p = h/mv.

quiz.q: For the same speed, which has the smallest λ?
quiz.why: λ = h/mv. At the same speed, the heaviest particle, the α-particle, has the smallest wavelength.

quiz.q: An electron accelerated through V has λ proportional to
quiz.why: λ = h/√(2meV), so λ ∝ 1/√V.

quiz.q: If the kinetic energy of a particle becomes 4 times, λ becomes
quiz.why: λ = h/√(2mK). If K becomes 4 times, λ becomes half.

quiz.q: Matter waves of everyday objects are not observed because
quiz.why: For everyday objects the mass is huge compared with h, so λ = h/mv is extremely small and cannot be detected.

lessons.title: Photons and matter waves: mixed problem practice

scenes.text: At an olympiad training camp, Mira faces a problem combining photon energy, work function and de Broglie wavelength.
She breaks it into small steps: photon energy → kinetic energy → momentum → wavelength.
Chaining simple relations solves the toughest-looking problem.

steps.title: Problem-solving chain
steps.body:
1. Photon energy: E = hc/λ = 1240/λ(nm) eV.
2. K_max = E − φ₀ (and V₀ = K_max/e).
3. Electron momentum p = √(2mK).
4. Electron de Broglie λ = h/p (or 1.227/√V nm with V = K in eV numerically).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Light of 200 nm falls on a metal of φ₀ = 4.2 eV.
- E = 1240/200 = 6.2 eV
- K_max = 6.2 − 4.2 = **2.0 eV**; V₀ = **2.0 V**
- Electron de Broglie λ = 1.227/√2 ≈ **0.87 nm**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Two metals A (φ = 2 eV) and B (φ = 5 eV) are lit with 4 eV photons.
- A emits with K_max = **2 eV**.
- B emits **nothing** (4 eV < 5 eV), however intense the light.
- Threshold wavelength of B: 1240/5 = **248 nm**.

steps.title: Graph reading
steps.body: For K_max (or V₀) vs ν, parallel lines for different metals (slope h/e for V₀). For photocurrent vs collector potential: different intensities ⇒ same V₀, different saturation; different frequencies ⇒ different V₀, possibly the same saturation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the photon's wavelength as the electron's wavelength.
- Forgetting that K_max is a maximum — most electrons come out slower.

quiz.why: K_max = 5 − 3 = 2 eV, so the stopping potential is V₀ = 2 V.

quiz.why: The same stopping potential means the same frequency. Different saturation currents mean different numbers of photons per second, so the intensities differ.

quiz.q: A 1 mW laser at 633 nm emits about how many photons per second?
quiz.why: Photon energy = 1240/633 ≈ 1.96 eV = 3.14×10⁻¹⁹ J. Photons per second = 10⁻³/3.14×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.2×10¹⁵.

outcomes: Learners can describe the Geiger–Marsden experiment and its conclusions.

lessons.title: Alpha scattering and Rutherford's model

scenes.text: In 1909 Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at gold foil only about 0.1 μm thick.
Most went straight through, but about 1 in 8000 bounced back by more than 90°.
Rutherford said it was as if a shell fired at tissue paper came back and hit you — the atom must have a tiny, dense, positive core.

steps.title: The experiment and conclusions
steps.body:
5.5 MeV α-particles (from ²¹⁴Bi) hit a thin gold foil; a zinc-sulphide screen and microscope counted scattering at each angle.
- Most α-particles pass undeflected ⇒ the atom is mostly empty space.
- A few are scattered by large angles ⇒ the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in a tiny **nucleus** (~10⁻¹⁵ m, about 10⁻⁴–10⁻⁵ of the atom's size ~10⁻¹⁰ m).
- Electrons orbit the nucleus (planetary model), the electrostatic attraction providing the centripetal force.

steps.title: Impact parameter and closest approach
steps.body:
**Impact parameter b:** perpendicular distance of the initial velocity line from the nucleus. Small b ⇒ large scattering; b = 0 ⇒ head-on, α bounces straight back.

**Distance of closest approach (head-on):** all K converts to potential energy:
K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d ⇒ **d = 2kZe²/K**.
Useful: ke² = 1.44 eV nm = 1.44 MeV fm.

steps.title: Failure of Rutherford's model
steps.body: An orbiting electron accelerates and, by classical electromagnetism, should radiate energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus within ~10⁻⁸ s. Atoms would be unstable and would emit a *continuous* spectrum. Real atoms are stable and emit *line* spectra.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Closest approach of a 5 MeV α to gold (Z = 79):
- d = 2 × 79 × 1.44 MeV fm / 5 MeV ≈ **45.5 fm = 4.55×10⁻¹⁴ m**.

**Ex 2.** If the α energy is doubled to 10 MeV, d halves to **≈ 22.8 fm** (d ∝ 1/K).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using charge e for the α-particle instead of 2e.
- Forgetting to convert MeV to joules when using k = 9×10⁹ (or use 1.44 MeV fm consistently).
- Saying the nucleus is half the size of the atom — it is about 10⁵ times smaller.

activity.prompt: An α-particle of 7.2 MeV approaches a nucleus of Z = 50 head-on. Using ke² = 1.44 MeV fm, find the distance of closest approach (fm).

quiz.why: Most α-particles pass straight through the gold foil, which shows that the atom is mostly empty space.

options: positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
quiz.why: Some α-particles bounce back at large angles, which needs a strong force from a very small, concentrated positive charge, the nucleus.

quiz.q: Distance of closest approach varies as
quiz.why: At closest approach all the kinetic energy becomes potential energy: K = 2kZe²/d, so d ∝ 1/K.

quiz.q: For a head-on collision the impact parameter is
quiz.why: In a head-on collision the α-particle is aimed straight at the nucleus, so the impact parameter is zero.

options: stability of atoms and line spectra
quiz.why: By classical physics an orbiting electron should radiate and spiral into the nucleus. Rutherford's model cannot explain stable atoms and discrete line spectra.

lessons.title: Atomic spectra and spectral series

scenes.text: Astronomers can tell what a star is made of without going there.
Each element emits light at its own set of wavelengths, like a barcode.
Hydrogen's lines follow a simple formula found by Balmer in 1885 — a clue that led to Bohr's model.

steps.title: Emission and absorption spectra
steps.body: A gas excited electrically emits light only at specific wavelengths — a **line emission spectrum** unique to each element. White light passing through a cool gas shows dark lines at the same wavelengths — an **absorption spectrum**.

steps.title: Hydrogen series
steps.body:
**1/λ = R (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)**, R = 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹ (Rydberg constant), n₂ > n₁.
- **Lyman** (n₁ = 1): ultraviolet.
- **Balmer** (n₁ = 2): visible (Hα 656 nm red, Hβ 486 nm, Hγ 434 nm, Hδ 410 nm).
- **Paschen** (n₁ = 3), **Brackett** (n₁ = 4), **Pfund** (n₁ = 5): infrared.
The **series limit** (n₂ → ∞) gives the shortest wavelength: λ_min = n₁²/R.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Hα line (n = 3 → 2):
- 1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/9) = 5R/36
- λ = 36/(5 × 1.097×10⁷) ≈ **656 nm** (red).

**Ex 2.** Shortest wavelength of the Lyman series: λ = 1/R ≈ **91.2 nm**; longest Lyman line (2 → 1): λ = 4/(3R) ≈ **121.6 nm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the larger n first in (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), getting a negative λ.
- Saying Balmer is in the UV — most Balmer lines are visible.
- Mixing up longest wavelength (smallest energy jump) with shortest (series limit).

activity.prompt: Match the series to its lower level and region.

quiz.q: The Balmer series lies mainly in the
quiz.why: The Balmer series (transitions to n = 2) lies mainly in the visible region.
The Rydberg constant is R ≈ 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹.

quiz.q: Series limit of Lyman series is
quiz.why: The Lyman series limit has 1/λ = R, so λ = 1/R ≈ 91.2 nm.

quiz.q: Dark lines in a star's spectrum are
quiz.why: Dark lines on a continuous spectrum are absorption lines, made when cooler gas absorbs certain wavelengths.

quiz.q: The first line of a series corresponds to
quiz.why: The first (longest-wavelength) line of a series is the transition with the smallest energy gap, from n₁ + 1 to n₁.

lessons.title: Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom

scenes.text: Bohr pictured the electron like a person on a ladder: it can stand on the rungs, never between them.
Jumping down a rung releases a photon of exactly the energy difference.
With just three postulates he calculated hydrogen's spectrum almost perfectly.

steps.title: Bohr's postulates (1913)
steps.body:
1. Electrons revolve in certain **stationary orbits** without radiating energy.
2. Allowed orbits have angular momentum **L = mvr = nh/(2π)**, n = 1, 2, 3, … (quantisation).
3. When an electron jumps from a higher orbit to a lower one it emits a photon: **hν = E_i − E_f**.

steps.title: Radius, speed and energy (derivation)
steps.body:
Centripetal force = Coulomb force: mv²/r = ke²/r² and mvr = nh/2π. Solving:
- **r_n = n² h²ε₀/(πme²) = n² a₀**, a₀ = **0.529 Å** (Bohr radius).
- **v_n = e²/(2ε₀hn) = (c/137)/n ≈ 2.18×10⁶/n m/s**.
- K = ke²/2r, U = −ke²/r ⇒ **E_n = −ke²/2r_n = −13.6/n² eV**.
Note K = −E and U = 2E. For hydrogen-like ions (He⁺, Li²⁺): r_n = n²a₀/Z, E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV.

steps.title: Energy levels
steps.body:
n = 1: −13.6 eV (ground state); n = 2: −3.4 eV; n = 3: −1.51 eV; n = 4: −0.85 eV; n → ∞: 0.
- **Ionisation energy** of hydrogen = 13.6 eV.
- **Excitation energy** to n = 2 = 10.2 eV.
Photon energy for a jump: hν = 13.6(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²) eV — this reproduces the Rydberg formula with R = me⁴/(8ε₀²ch³).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Radius of the 3rd orbit: r₃ = 9 × 0.529 = **4.76 Å**.

**Ex 2.** Photon emitted for 4 → 2: ΔE = 13.6(1/4 − 1/16) = **2.55 eV**; λ = 1240/2.55 ≈ **486 nm** (Hβ, blue-green).

**Ex 3.** Energy to remove an electron from n = 2: **3.4 eV**.

**Ex 4.** In the ground state K = **13.6 eV**, U = **−27.2 eV**, total = −13.6 eV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the negative sign of energy (bound state).
- Using r ∝ n instead of n².
- Ignoring Z for hydrogen-like ions.

activity.prompt: Complete Bohr's results for hydrogen.
activity.text: Ground-state energy = ___ eV. Radius of the nth orbit varies as n to the power ___. Ionisation energy from n = 2 is ___ eV.

quiz.why: Bohr's quantisation condition is that angular momentum is an integer multiple of h/2π: mvr = nh/2π.

quiz.q: Energy of an electron in n = 3 of hydrogen is
Ratio of radii of 2nd and 1st orbits is
quiz.why: The radius is proportional to n², so r₂/r₁ = 4.

quiz.q: In a Bohr orbit, kinetic energy equals
quiz.why: In a Bohr orbit the kinetic energy equals the magnitude of the total energy, K = −E.
Energy ∝ Z². For He⁺, Z = 2, so E₁ = −13.6 × 4 = −54.4 eV.

quiz.q: Speed of the electron in the nth orbit varies as
quiz.why: The speed of the electron is proportional to 1/n, so it falls with higher orbits.

lessons.title: Line spectra and de Broglie's explanation

story.title: Standing waves on a sitar string

scenes.text: When Ustad-ji plucks a sitar string, only certain notes ring — those that fit a whole number of half-waves.
De Broglie suggested an electron's wave must wrap around its orbit and join itself smoothly.
Only whole numbers of wavelengths fit — which is exactly Bohr's mysterious rule.

steps.title: de Broglie's explanation of quantisation
steps.body:
For a stable orbit the electron wave must form a **standing wave**: circumference = whole number of wavelengths:
**2πr_n = nλ** and λ = h/(mv) ⇒ **mvr_n = nh/(2π)** — Bohr's second postulate follows naturally.

steps.title: Number of spectral lines
steps.body: An electron in level n can return to the ground state through various jumps. Maximum number of lines emitted = **n(n − 1)/2**. From n = 4: 6 lines.

steps.title: Limitations of Bohr's model
steps.body:
- Works only for hydrogen-like (one-electron) atoms; fails for helium and heavier atoms.
- Cannot explain relative intensities of lines or the fine structure.
- Mixes classical orbits with quantum rules; replaced by quantum mechanics where electrons are described by probability clouds.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Hydrogen atoms are excited to n = 5. Maximum lines = 5 × 4/2 = **10**.

**Ex 2.** In which orbit is the electron's de Broglie wavelength equal to 4 × 0.33 nm (λ₁ ≈ 0.33 nm, n = 1)? Since λ ∝ n (λ = 2πr/n with r ∝ n²): **n = 4**.

**Ex 3.** Does a 12.1 eV photon get absorbed by ground-state hydrogen? E₃ − E₁ = 13.6 − 1.51 = **12.09 eV** ⇒ yes, to n = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the direct jump to ground state when asked for 'possible lines'.
- Assuming any photon above 10.2 eV is absorbed — only exact level differences (or > 13.6 eV for ionisation).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the wavelength of a hydrogen spectral line.
items: Identify the initial and final levels nᵢ and n_f

quiz.why: For a stable orbit the circumference must hold a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths: 2πr = nλ.

quiz.q: Maximum number of lines from n = 4 is
quiz.why: From n = 4 the possible transitions are n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6 lines.
Bohr's model works only for one-electron systems, and fails for multi-electron atoms such as neutral helium.

De Broglie wavelength of the electron in the nth Bohr orbit is proportional to
quiz.why: λ = h/mv = 2πr/n. In the nth orbit the circumference is n wavelengths, so λ = 2πrₙ/n, and rₙ ∝ n², giving λ ∝ n.

courses.summary: Atomic masses and nuclear composition, isotopes, isobars and isotones, nuclear size and density, mass–energy equivalence, mass defect and binding energy, the binding-energy curve, nuclear force, and nuclear energy from fission and fusion — plus radioactive decay as a JEE/NEET extension. outcomes: Learners can describe nuclear composition and use R = R₀A^(1/3).
Learners can compute mass defect and binding energy per nucleon using 1 u = 931.5 MeV.

lessons.title: Composition and size of the nucleus

scenes.text: Scientists measure atomic masses with mass spectrometers to six or more decimal places.
Chlorine shows two peaks: masses near 35 and 37 — same element, different nuclei.
Nuclei are built from protons and neutrons, and their sizes follow a beautifully simple rule.

steps.title: Atomic mass unit and composition
steps.body:
**1 u** = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = **1.660539×10⁻²⁷ kg**.
- Proton m_p = 1.007276 u; neutron m_n = 1.008665 u (Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932).
- Nucleus ᴬ_Z X: **Z** protons (atomic number), **N = A − Z** neutrons, **A** nucleons (mass number).
- **Isotopes:** same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl).
- **Isobars:** same A, different Z (³H and ³He).
- **Isotones:** same N (¹⁹⁸Hg and ¹⁹⁷Au both have N = 118).

steps.title: Nuclear size and density
steps.body: Scattering experiments show **R = R₀A^(1/3)**, R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m). So volume ∝ A and **nuclear density is the same for all nuclei**: ρ ≈ m_u/((4/3)πR₀³) ≈ **2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³** — about 10¹⁴ times the density of water (similar to neutron stars).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Radius of ²⁷Al: R = 1.2 × 27^(1/3) = 1.2 × 3 = **3.6 fm**.

**Ex 2.** Ratio of radii of ²¹⁶X and ²⁷Al: (216/27)^(1/3) = 8^(1/3) = **2**.

**Ex 3.** Neutrons in ²³⁵₉₂U: N = 235 − 92 = **143**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking heavier nuclei are denser — density is roughly constant.
- Writing R ∝ A instead of A^(1/3).
- Confusing isobars (same A) and isotones (same N).

activity.prompt: Classify each pair.

quiz.why: One atomic mass unit is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), proportional to the cube root of the mass number.
Volume ∝ A and mass ∝ A, so the density is nearly the same for all nuclei.

quiz.q: Number of neutrons in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe is
quiz.why: Number of neutrons = A − Z = 56 − 26 = 30.
³H and ³He have the same mass number (3) but different atomic numbers, so they are isobars.

lessons.title: Mass–energy, mass defect and binding energy

scenes.text: Kabir adds the masses of 2 protons and 2 neutrons and compares with a helium-4 nucleus.
The nucleus is lighter by about 0.03 u!
That missing mass became binding energy, via Einstein's E = mc².

steps.title: Mass–energy equivalence
steps.body: **E = mc²**; 1 u × c² = **931.5 MeV**. Mass and energy are interconvertible; in nuclear reactions total (mass + energy) is conserved.

steps.title: Mass defect and binding energy
steps.body:
**ΔM = [Z m_p + (A − Z) m_n] − M_nucleus** (using atomic masses: Z m_H + N m_n − M_atom, the electron masses cancel).

**Binding energy E_b = ΔM c²** — energy needed to split the nucleus into free nucleons (or released when it forms).

**Binding energy per nucleon E_bn = E_b/A** measures stability.

steps.title: The binding-energy curve
steps.body:
Plot E_bn against A:
- Rises steeply for light nuclei, has a broad maximum ≈ **8.75 MeV at A ≈ 56 (Fe)**, and is nearly constant (~8 MeV) for 30 < A < 170 — showing nuclear forces are **short-range and saturate** (each nucleon binds only its neighbours).
- Falls to ~7.6 MeV for A ≈ 238.
- Heavy nuclei splitting into medium ones (**fission**) and light nuclei joining (**fusion**) both move towards higher E_bn and therefore **release energy**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing atomic and nuclear masses (use m_H with atomic mass, or m_p with nuclear mass).
- Thinking higher total binding energy means more stable — compare binding energy *per nucleon*.
- Forgetting the 931.5 factor or using 931 inconsistently.

activity.prompt: A nucleus has a mass defect of 0.0989 u and A = 12. Find binding energy per nucleon in MeV (1 u = 931.5 MeV).

quiz.why: 1 u × c² is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy.

quiz.q: Binding energy per nucleon is maximum near
quiz.why: The binding energy per nucleon peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 (the iron region), the most stable nuclei.
The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons. The difference is the mass defect.

quiz.q: Constant E_bn over a wide range of A shows that nuclear force
quiz.why: A nearly constant binding energy per nucleon shows that the nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates, so each nucleon interacts only with near neighbours.

quiz.q: Energy is released in fission because
quiz.why: In fission, heavy nuclei split into medium ones with higher binding energy per nucleon. The extra binding energy is released.

lessons.title: Nuclear force and nuclear energy

scenes.text: The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium deep in its core at about 1.5×10⁷ K.
India's nuclear power plants, like those at Tarapur and Kudankulam, split uranium nuclei instead.
Opposite processes, same reason: both move nuclei towards the peak of the binding-energy curve.

steps.title: Nuclear force
steps.body:
- **Strongest** of the fundamental forces in its range (much stronger than Coulomb repulsion between protons).
- **Short range** (a few fm); attractive above ~0.8 fm, strongly repulsive below.
- **Charge-independent:** p–p, n–n and p–n forces are about equal.
- Saturating, non-central in general.

steps.title: Fission
steps.body:
A slow neutron is absorbed by ²³⁵U, forming unstable ²³⁶U which splits, e.g.
¹n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3 ¹n (other fragment pairs also occur)
Energy released ≈ **200 MeV per fission**. Extra neutrons can sustain a **chain reaction**. In reactors: **moderator** (heavy water, graphite) slows neutrons; **control rods** (cadmium, boron) absorb neutrons to keep the multiplication factor K = 1; coolant carries heat to turbines.

steps.title: Fusion
steps.body:
Light nuclei combine at very high temperatures (thermonuclear fusion) so they can overcome Coulomb repulsion:
¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν + 0.42 MeV, and ultimately 4 ¹H → ⁴He + … releasing about 26.7 MeV in the proton–proton cycle. Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission; controlled fusion on Earth is still under development (e.g. the international ITER project, in which India participates).

steps.title: Q-value
steps.body: **Q = (Σ masses of reactants − Σ masses of products) × 931.5 MeV/u**. Q > 0: energy released (exoergic).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Energy from fissioning 1 g of ²³⁵U at 200 MeV each:
- N = 6.02×10²³/235 ≈ 2.56×10²¹ nuclei
- E = 2.56×10²¹ × 200 MeV = 5.1×10²³ MeV ≈ **8.2×10¹⁰ J** (about 23 MWh).

**Ex 2.** D–T fusion ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n with masses 2.014102, 3.016049, 4.002603 and 1.008665 u.
- Δm = 5.030151 − 5.011268 = 0.018883 u ⇒ **Q ≈ 17.6 MeV**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking control rods slow neutrons — moderators slow; control rods absorb.
- Saying fusion needs high temperature for chemical reasons — it is to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
- Getting the sign of Q wrong (reactants minus products).

The correct answer is “cadmium or boron”. Reasoning: Good neutron absorbers. A choice like “graphite” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “fusion”. Reasoning: Hydrogen to helium. A choice like “radioactive decay only” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “energy released”. Reasoning: Products are lighter. A choice like “mass increases” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Radioactivity (JEE/NEET extension)

scenes.text: Archaeologists date ancient bones from a site using carbon-14.
Half the ¹⁴C in a sample decays every 5730 years, like clockwork.
The decay law lets them read the clock — the same law medical physicists use for radioactive tracers.

steps.title: Types of decay
steps.body:
- **α-decay:** ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−2) Y + ⁴₂He.
- **β⁻-decay:** n → p + e⁻ + ν̄: Z increases by 1, A unchanged.
- **β⁺-decay:** p → n + e⁺ + ν: Z decreases by 1.
- **γ-decay:** an excited nucleus emits a photon; Z and A unchanged.
Penetrating power: γ > β > α; ionising power: α > β > γ.

steps.title: Decay law
steps.body:
Rate ∝ number present: dN/dt = −λN ⇒ **N = N₀e^(−λt)**.
- **Half-life T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ**; after n half-lives N = N₀/2ⁿ.
- **Mean life τ = 1/λ = 1.44 T½**.
- **Activity R = λN** (becquerel, 1 Bq = 1 decay/s; 1 Ci = 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A sample's half-life is 10 days. Fraction left after 30 days = (1/2)³ = **1/8**.

**Ex 2.** ²³⁸U → ²⁰⁶Pb: number of α and β decays?
- ΔA = 32 ⇒ **8 α**; Z falls by 16 from α, but net fall is 92 − 82 = 10 ⇒ **6 β⁻**.

**Ex 3.** λ = 0.0231 per day ⇒ T½ = 0.693/0.0231 = **30 days**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking that after two half-lives everything has decayed (1/4 remains).
- Forgetting that β⁻ decay leaves A unchanged.
- Mixing mean life and half-life.

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Recent rationalised NCERT editions trimmed radioactivity from this chapter, but it remains important for competitive exams; check your current syllabus.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
courses.summary: Classification of metals, semiconductors and insulators by conductivity and energy bands, intrinsic and extrinsic (n- and p-type) semiconductors, formation of the p-n junction, the diode under forward and reverse bias, and the diode as a half-wave and full-wave rectifier — plus special diodes and logic gates as a JEE extension. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can classify solids using energy bands and band gap.
Learners can explain doping and use nₑnₕ = nᵢ².
Learners can describe depletion layer, barrier potential and diode V–I characteristics.
Learners can explain half-wave and full-wave rectification and filtering.

lessons.title: Energy bands and intrinsic semiconductors

scenes.text: Zara's phone contains billions of transistors made from silicon.
Silicon comes from ordinary sand, yet with a little help it can be made to conduct exactly as engineers want.
The secret is the energy band gap — just right, not too wide, not too narrow.

steps.title: Classification by conductivity
steps.body:
- **Metals:** ρ ≈ 10⁻²–10⁻⁸ Ω m.
- **Semiconductors:** ρ ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁶ Ω m (Si, Ge; compounds like GaAs, CdS; organic semiconductors).
- **Insulators:** ρ ≈ 10¹¹–10¹⁹ Ω m.

steps.title: Energy bands
steps.body:
In a crystal, atomic energy levels spread into bands. The **valence band** (filled at 0 K) and the **conduction band** are separated by the **band gap E_g**.
- **Metals:** bands overlap or conduction band partly filled — E_g ≈ 0.
- **Insulators:** E_g > 3 eV (diamond ≈ 5.4 eV) — electrons cannot jump at room temperature.
- **Semiconductors:** E_g small — Si ≈ **1.1 eV**, Ge ≈ **0.7 eV**; some electrons are thermally excited at room temperature.

steps.title: Intrinsic semiconductors
steps.body: Pure Si or Ge: each atom shares four covalent bonds. Thermal energy breaks a few bonds, creating a **free electron** and a **hole** (vacancy with effective +e charge). In pure material **nₑ = nₕ = nᵢ**. Current I = Iₑ + Iₕ (holes move as neighbouring electrons fill them). At 0 K an intrinsic semiconductor is an insulator; conductivity rises with temperature.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Can red light (700 nm) create electron–hole pairs in Si (E_g = 1.1 eV)? E = 1240/700 ≈ 1.77 eV > 1.1 eV ⇒ **yes**.

**Ex 2.** Longest wavelength that can excite carriers in Si: λ = 1240/1.1 ≈ **1127 nm** (near infrared).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking holes are positrons — a hole is an absence of an electron.
- Saying semiconductors conduct better when cold — resistance falls when they are heated.
- Confusing band gap of Si (1.1 eV) and Ge (0.7 eV).

activity.prompt: Classify by band gap.

quiz.q: Band gap of silicon is about
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1.1 eV”. Reasoning: Si ≈ 1.1 eV. A choice like “0 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “nₑ = nₕ”. Reasoning: Pairs are created together. A choice like “nₑ = 0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: At 0 K a pure semiconductor behaves as
quiz.why: The correct answer is “an insulator”. Reasoning: No thermally excited carriers. A choice like “a superconductor” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “a positive charge”. Reasoning: Missing electron. A choice like “a photon” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Resistance of a semiconductor on heating
quiz.why: The correct answer is “decreases”. Reasoning: More carriers. A choice like “becomes infinite” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Extrinsic semiconductors: n-type and p-type

story.title: A pinch of salt in the soup

scenes.text: A cook adds just a pinch of salt to a huge pot and the taste changes completely.
Adding one impurity atom per million silicon atoms raises conductivity enormously.
This controlled impurity — doping — makes n-type and p-type materials.

steps.title: n-type (pentavalent dopant)
steps.body:
Dopants: **P, As, Sb** (group 15). Four electrons bond, the fifth is loosely held (~0.01–0.05 eV) and freed easily ⇒ **donor**.
- **Majority carriers: electrons**; minority: holes.
- The material stays electrically **neutral** (the donor ion is positive and fixed).

steps.title: p-type (trivalent dopant)
steps.body:
Dopants: **B, Al, In, Ga** (group 13). One bond is incomplete ⇒ a hole ⇒ **acceptor**.
- **Majority carriers: holes**; minority: electrons.
- Also electrically neutral overall.

steps.title: Mass-action law
steps.body: In thermal equilibrium: **nₑ nₕ = nᵢ²**. Doping raises one carrier density and lowers the other. Donor and acceptor levels lie just below the conduction band and just above the valence band respectively.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Si with nᵢ = 1.5×10¹⁶ m⁻³ is doped with arsenic at 5×10²² m⁻³.
- nₑ ≈ **5×10²² m⁻³** (each As gives one electron)
- nₕ = nᵢ²/nₑ = 2.25×10³²/5×10²² = **4.5×10⁹ m⁻³**.
- It is **n-type**.

**Ex 2.** Ge doped with indium becomes **p-type** (In is trivalent).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying n-type is negatively charged — it is neutral.
- Mixing up donor (pentavalent) and acceptor (trivalent) elements.
- Adding nᵢ to the donor density (it is negligible).

activity.prompt: Which type results from each dopant in silicon?

quiz.q: Majority carriers in p-type silicon are
quiz.why: The correct answer is “holes”. Reasoning: Acceptor doping. A choice like “protons” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “As”. Reasoning: Pentavalent. A choice like “B” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “electrically neutral”. Reasoning: Every free electron leaves a fixed + ion. A choice like “magnetic” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “nₑnₕ = nᵢ²”. Reasoning: Equilibrium relation. A choice like “nₑ = nₕ²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “10¹⁰ m⁻³”. Reasoning: 10³²/10²². A choice like “10¹⁶ m⁻³” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: The p-n junction and the diode

scenes.text: Kabir connects an LED backwards in his school project and it refuses to glow.
He flips it and it lights up instantly.
A p-n junction lets current flow easily one way and blocks it the other way.

steps.title: Formation of the junction
steps.body: When p and n regions are joined: electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n (**diffusion current**). They leave behind fixed ions: + on the n side, − on the p side, forming the **depletion region** (≈ 1 μm wide, no free carriers). Its field drives minority carriers back (**drift current**). Equilibrium: diffusion = drift. The resulting **barrier potential** is ≈ 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge.

steps.title: Forward and reverse bias
steps.body:
- **Forward bias** (p to +, n to −): barrier lowered, depletion layer narrows. Current is very small until the **threshold (knee/cut-in) voltage** (≈ 0.7 V Si, 0.2–0.3 V Ge), then rises steeply (exponentially) — milliamperes.
- **Reverse bias** (p to −, n to +): barrier raised, depletion layer widens; only a tiny **reverse saturation current** (μA) of minority carriers, nearly independent of voltage, until **breakdown** at a large reverse voltage.
- Dynamic resistance r_d = ΔV/ΔI (small in forward bias).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A Si diode (0.7 V drop) in series with 1 kΩ and a 5.7 V battery, forward biased.
- I = (5.7 − 0.7)/1000 = **5 mA**.
- If reversed: I ≈ **0** (only μA leakage).

**Ex 2.** On the forward curve, V rises from 0.70 V to 0.80 V while I rises from 10 mA to 20 mA.
- r_d = 0.1 V/10 mA = **10 Ω**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a diode conducts at any forward voltage — it needs to exceed the knee voltage.
- Calling the depletion region 'empty space' — it contains fixed ions, just no mobile carriers.
- Saying reverse current is zero — it is tiny but non-zero.

statements.s: In forward bias the depletion layer becomes narrower.
Reverse saturation current is due to majority carriers.
statements.why: It is due to minority carriers.

statements.s: The barrier potential of silicon is about 0.7 V.
In equilibrium, diffusion current is greater than drift current.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “immobile ions”. Reasoning: No mobile carriers. A choice like “free electrons” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “widens”. Reasoning: Barrier increases. A choice like “stays the same” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “0.7 V”. Reasoning: Si threshold. A choice like “1.1 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “majority carriers (diffusion)”. Reasoning: Lowered barrier. A choice like “minority carriers” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: The diode as a rectifier

scenes.text: The wall socket gives AC that reverses 100 times a second, but Riya's phone battery needs steady DC.
Inside the charger, diodes let only one direction through.
A capacitor smooths the bumps — and out comes DC.

steps.title: Half-wave rectifier
steps.body: One diode in series with the load (via a transformer). During the positive half-cycle the diode is forward biased and conducts; during the negative half it blocks. Output: pulsating DC with **one pulse per cycle** — output frequency = input frequency (50 Hz).

steps.title: Full-wave rectifier (centre-tap)
steps.body: Two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer. In each half-cycle one diode conducts, and current through the load is always in the same direction. Output: **two pulses per cycle** — ripple frequency = **2 × input frequency (100 Hz)**. More efficient than half-wave. (A bridge rectifier with four diodes avoids the centre tap.)

steps.title: Filtering
steps.body: A **capacitor in parallel with the load** charges to near the peak voltage and discharges slowly through the load between peaks, smoothing the output. Larger C (and larger load R) ⇒ smaller ripple; time constant RC should be much greater than the time between peaks.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Input 50 Hz AC. Ripple frequency: half-wave **50 Hz**, full-wave **100 Hz**.

**Ex 2.** A full-wave rectifier gives a peak output of 12 V (ideal diodes). With a large filter capacitor the DC output is close to **12 V**; without it the average of the pulsating output is 2V_m/π ≈ **7.6 V**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying full-wave output frequency equals input frequency.
- Putting the filter capacitor in series with the load.
- Forgetting that each diode in a centre-tap rectifier conducts only for half the cycle.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “50 Hz”. Reasoning: One pulse per cycle. A choice like “0 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Special diodes and logic gates (JEE extension)

scenes.text: Modern traffic signals use LEDs that last for years and use little power.
The calculator on Neha's desk runs on a tiny solar cell.
Inside, logic gates add numbers using only 0s and 1s.

steps.title: Special-purpose diodes
steps.body:
- **Zener diode:** heavily doped, used in **reverse breakdown**; voltage across it stays almost constant ⇒ **voltage regulator**.
- **Photodiode:** reverse-biased; light creates e–h pairs and increases reverse current ⇒ light detection.
- **LED:** forward-biased; electrons and holes recombine and emit light; colour depends on band gap (E_g ≈ hc/λ). Low power, long life.
- **Solar cell:** no external bias; light creates e–h pairs and the junction field separates them, giving an emf (~0.5–0.6 V for Si).

steps.title: Logic gates
steps.body:
Digital signals: 0 (low) and 1 (high).
- **NOT:** Y = Ā.
- **OR:** Y = A + B (1 if any input is 1).
- **AND:** Y = A·B (1 only if both are 1).
- **NAND:** NOT of AND; **NOR:** NOT of OR. NAND and NOR are **universal gates** — any gate can be built from them.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** An LED emits 620 nm light. Approximate band gap: 1240/620 = **2.0 eV**.

**Ex 2.** A NAND gate with both inputs tied together acts as a **NOT gate** (Y = (A·A)′ = Ā).

**Ex 3.** For A = 1, B = 0: AND = 0, OR = 1, NAND = 1, NOR = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a Zener in forward bias as a regulator.
- Confusing photodiode (reverse bias) and LED (forward bias).
- Thinking NOR(1, 0) = 1.

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Recent rationalised NCERT editions trimmed special diodes, transistors and logic gates from this chapter, but they still appear in some competitive-exam syllabi; check the latest official syllabus.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “voltage regulator”. Reasoning: Constant voltage in breakdown. A choice like “oscillator” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “both inputs are 0”. Reasoning: NOT of OR. A choice like “both inputs are 1” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “NAND and NOR”. Reasoning: Any logic can be built from them. A choice like “XOR and AND” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
