questions.why: The correct answer is “decreases”. Reasoning: Applied voltage opposes it. A choice like “is unchanged” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The width of the depletion layer increases when
questions.why: The correct answer is “reverse bias increases”. Reasoning: Barrier increases. A choice like “doping increases” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Si (nᵢ = 1.5×10¹⁶ m⁻³) is doped so that nₕ = 4.5×10²² m⁻³. Then nₑ is
questions.why: The correct answer is “5×10⁹ m⁻³”. Reasoning: nᵢ²/nₕ = 2.25×10³²/4.5×10²². A choice like “4.5×10²² m⁻³” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A Si diode (0.7 V) and a 500 Ω resistor are in series with a 3.2 V battery (forward). Current:
questions.why: The correct answer is “5 mA”. Reasoning: (3.2 − 0.7)/500. A choice like “6.4 mA” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Same circuit with the diode reversed. Current is
questions.why: The correct answer is “approximately zero”. Reasoning: Reverse bias blocks. A choice like “infinite” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The maximum wavelength absorbed to create e–h pairs in a material with E_g = 2.48 eV:
questions.why: The correct answer is “500 nm”. Reasoning: 1240/2.48. A choice like “620 nm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: The ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier is twice the input frequency. Reason: Both half-cycles are used to produce output pulses.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: Two pulses per cycle. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: On a diode's forward curve, V changes 0.65 → 0.75 V and I changes 2 → 7 mA. Dynamic resistance:
questions.why: The correct answer is “20 Ω”. Reasoning: 0.1/0.005. A choice like “14 Ω” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Which is NOT true for a p-n junction in equilibrium?
options: Mobile carriers fill the depletion region
Fixed ions sit on both sides
questions.why: The correct answer is “Mobile carriers fill the depletion region”. Reasoning: The depletion region has no mobile carriers. A choice like “Diffusion and drift currents balance” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: Two identical Si diodes D₁ (forward) and D₂ (reverse) are in parallel branches each with 1 kΩ across a 5.7 V source. Total current is about
questions.why: The correct answer is “5 mA”. Reasoning: Only D₁'s branch conducts: (5.7 − 0.7)/1000. A choice like “0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: (Extension) For a NAND gate with inputs A = 1 and B = 1, output is
questions.why: The correct answer is “0”. Reasoning: AND = 1 ⇒ NAND = 0. A choice like “A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: (Extension) A Zener diode of 6 V is used with series R = 100 Ω on a 10 V supply, no load. Current through the Zener is
questions.why: The correct answer is “40 mA”. Reasoning: (10 − 6)/100. A choice like “100 mA” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Resistivity of a semiconductor at room temperature lies around
questions.why: The correct answer is “10⁻⁵–10⁶ Ω m”. Reasoning: Between metals and insulators. A choice like “10¹⁵ Ω m” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 12 Physics
courses.summary: Complete formula sheets for all 14 chapters, exam strategy for boards and JEE/NEET, two mock papers with fully explained answers, and a 25-question final mock test with difficulty spread 1–5. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can recall every key formula of Class 12 Physics with units.
Learners can plan time and avoid common traps in board and entrance exams.
Learners can solve mixed-chapter questions under time pressure.
Learners can identify their weak chapters from mock-paper results.

lessons.title: Formula sheet I: Electrostatics and current electricity

scenes.text: It is the night before the board exam and Rahul has no time to reread 3 chapters.
He opens one sheet with every formula, its unit and when to use it.
Twenty minutes later he is confident — he knows which tool fits which problem.

steps.title: Ch 1 · Charges and fields
steps.body:
- F = kq₁q₂/r², k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻²; medium: ÷K
- E = kq/r²; dipole p = q(2a); E_axial = 2kp/r³; E_eq = kp/r³
- τ = pE sin θ; flux Φ = EA cos θ; Gauss: Φ = q_enc/ε₀
- Line λ: E = λ/2πε₀r; sheet: σ/2ε₀; between plates σ/ε₀; shell: kq/r² outside, 0 inside

steps.title: Ch 2 · Potential and capacitance
steps.body:
- V = kq/r; dipole V = kp cos θ/r²; E = −dV/dr
- U = kq₁q₂/r; dipole U = −pE cos θ
- C = Q/V; parallel plate C = ε₀A/d; dielectric KC₀; slab ε₀A/(d − t + t/K)
- Series 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ; parallel C = ΣCᵢ
- U = ½CV² = Q²/2C; u = ½ε₀E²; loss on sharing C₁C₂(V₁ − V₂)²/2(C₁ + C₂)

steps.title: Ch 3 · Current electricity
steps.body:
- I = neAv_d; v_d = eEτ/m; ρ = m/ne²τ; μ = v_d/E
- R = ρl/A; stretched n times ⇒ n²R; R_T = R₀(1 + αΔT)
- P = VI = I²R = V²/R; 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J
- V = ε − Ir; series cells nε, nr; parallel ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂)
- Kirchhoff: ΣI = 0, ΣΔV = 0; bridge P/Q = R/S

steps.title: How to use the sheet
steps.body: Before solving, write the *given* quantities with units, choose the formula that links them, and convert to SI first. Most lost marks come from μ, m and c prefixes.

cards.front: Energy lost when capacitors share charge

quiz.q: Field outside a charged spherical shell at distance r is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “kq/r²”. Reasoning: As if at the centre. A choice like “zero” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor with K = 4 filling it is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4C₀”. Reasoning: KC₀. A choice like “C₀” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Resistance of a wire stretched to twice its length becomes
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4R”. Reasoning: n²R. A choice like “R” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is based on conservation of
quiz.why: The correct answer is “energy”. A choice like “charge” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.

quiz.q: Unit of electric dipole moment is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “C m”. Reasoning: q × distance. A choice like “N/C” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Energy stored in a capacitor is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “½CV²”. Reasoning: Standard. A choice like “½QV²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Formula sheet II: Magnetism, EMI, AC and EM waves

scenes.text: Isha notices that magnetism formulas look like electrostatics with p → m and 1/ε₀ → μ₀.
Remembering one family lets her rebuild the other.
Pattern-spotting halves the memorising load.

steps.title: Ch 4–5 · Magnetism
steps.body:
- F = q(v × B); r = mv/qB; T = 2πm/qB; pitch = 2πmv cos θ/qB; v = E/B (selector)
- Loop centre μ₀NI/2R; axis μ₀IR²/2(R² + x²)^(3/2); wire μ₀I/2πr; solenoid μ₀nI
- Parallel wires f = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd; τ = NIAB sin θ; m = NIA
- Ammeter shunt S = I_gG/(I − I_g); voltmeter R = V/I_g − G
- Bar magnet: B_axial = μ₀2m/4πr³; τ = mB sin θ; U = −mB cos θ; T = 2π√(I/mB)
- B = μ₀(H + M); χ = M/H; μᵣ = 1 + χ; Curie χ ∝ 1/T

steps.title: Ch 6–7 · EMI and AC
steps.body:
- Φ = BA cos θ; ε = −N dΦ/dt; Δq = NΔΦ/R; ε = Blv; rotating rod ½Bωl²
- L = μ₀n²Al; M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l; U = ½LI²; u = B²/2μ₀; generator ε₀ = NBAω
- I_rms = i_m/√2; X_L = ωL; X_C = 1/ωC; Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R
- ω₀ = 1/√(LC); Q = ω₀L/R; P = VI cos φ; cos φ = R/Z
- Transformer Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = Iₚ/Iₛ

steps.title: Ch 8 · EM waves
steps.body:
- i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt; c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀); E₀ = cB₀; p = U/c
- Spectrum (long → short λ): radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X, γ

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- Angle in τ = NIAB sin θ is with the *normal*.
- AC heating uses rms values.
- At resonance Z = R, not zero.

activity.prompt: Match the electric formula with its magnetic twin.

quiz.q: Radius of a charged particle's circular path is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “mv/qB”. Reasoning: Balance qvB = mv²/r. A choice like “v/qB” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Self-inductance of a solenoid depends on n as
quiz.why: The correct answer is “n²”. Reasoning: μ₀n²Al. A choice like “1/n” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
At resonance X_L = X_C, so Z = R and φ = 0. Power factor = cos 0 = 1.

quiz.q: Peak emf of a generator is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “NBAω”. Reasoning: Standard. A choice like “NBA/ω” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: E₀/B₀ for an EM wave equals
quiz.why: The correct answer is “c”. Reasoning: E₀ = cB₀. A choice like “c²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Paramagnetic susceptibility varies with temperature as
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1/T”. Reasoning: Curie's law. A choice like “T²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Formula sheet III: Optics and modern physics

scenes.text: With a week left, Fatima splits her revision: two days optics, two days modern physics, three days of mock papers.
She times every paper and marks errors in red.
By the last mock her score has jumped — practice under time pressure works.

steps.title: Ch 9 · Ray optics
steps.body:
- Mirror 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, m = −v/u, f = R/2
- Snell n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r; apparent depth = real/n; sin i_c = 1/n
- Surface n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R; lens maker 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
- Lens 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u; P = 1/f (m); P = P₁ + P₂
- Prism δ = i + e − A; n = sin((A + D_m)/2)/sin(A/2); thin δ = (n − 1)A
- Simple microscope 1 + D/f; compound (L/f_o)(D/f_e); telescope f_o/f_e, length f_o + f_e

steps.title: Ch 10 · Wave optics
steps.body:
- I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2); I_max/I_min = ((√I₁ + √I₂)/(√I₁ − √I₂))²
- YDSE Δ = xd/D; β = λD/d; in medium β/n
- Single slit minima a sin θ = nλ; central width 2λD/a; Fresnel distance a²/λ
- Malus I = I₀ cos² θ; unpolarised → I₀/2; Brewster tan i_B = n

steps.title: Ch 11–14 · Modern physics and electronics
steps.body:
- E = hν = 1240/λ(nm) eV; K_max = hν − φ₀ = eV₀; p = h/λ
- de Broglie λ = h/mv = h/√(2mK); electron 1.227/√V nm
- Closest approach d = 2kZe²/K; Bohr r = 0.529n²/Z Å; E = −13.6Z²/n² eV; v ∝ Z/n
- 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²); lines n(n − 1)/2
- R = 1.2A^(1/3) fm; 1 u = 931.5 MeV; E_b = ΔM c²; N = N₀e^(−λt); T½ = 0.693/λ
- nₑnₕ = nᵢ²; Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV; half-wave ripple ν, full-wave 2ν

steps.title: Units cheat-sheet
steps.body: Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m · nm = 10⁻⁹ m · fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m · eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J · MeV = 1.6×10⁻¹³ J · μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m/A · ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m · h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s

quiz.q: Magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “f_o/f_e”. Reasoning: Angular magnification. A choice like “f_e/f_o” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: YDSE fringe width in water (n = 4/3) compared with air is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “smaller”. Reasoning: β/n. A choice like “larger” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “1 eV”. Reasoning: 1240/1240. A choice like “12.4 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Radius of the 2nd Bohr orbit of hydrogen is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2.12 Å”. Reasoning: 4 × 0.529. A choice like “4.76 Å” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “931.5 MeV”. Reasoning: Energy equivalent. A choice like “1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “100 Hz”. Reasoning: 2ν. A choice like “200 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Mock paper 1 (mixed chapters)

scenes.text: Saturday morning: Ankit sits a timed mock paper at home with the phone in another room.
He gives 1 minute per MCQ, skips any that take longer, and returns later.
He checks answers only after finishing — and learns more from his mistakes than from his correct answers.

steps.title: How to use this mock
steps.body: Attempt the 8 questions below in 12 minutes without notes. Then read every explanation, including for the questions you got right. Mark each wrong answer as: concept gap, formula slip, unit error or careless reading.

steps.title: Board exam strategy
steps.body:
- Read the whole paper in the first 10–15 minutes; start with sections you are strongest in.
- For derivations, draw a labelled diagram, state assumptions, then derive step by step — marks are given per step.
- Box the final answer with units.
- For numericals, write the formula first (it earns marks even if arithmetic slips).

steps.title: JEE/NEET strategy
steps.body:
- Use elimination: check units/dimensions and limiting cases (what if θ = 0? r → ∞?).
- NEET penalises wrong answers: guess only when you can rule out two options.
- Keep 10% of time to recheck marked questions.

steps.title: Avoid these
steps.body:
- Not converting cm/μC/mA to SI.
- Copying the sign convention halfway through optics problems.
- Reading 'NOT' or 'incorrect' in the question too fast.

steps.title: Disclaimer
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by CBSE, NTA or any exam provider. Check the official syllabus and exam guide for the current pattern.

activity.prompt: Mock-paper discipline checklist
items: Every wrong answer categorised (concept / formula / unit / careless)
Formula sheet re-read for those chapters

quiz.q: Two point charges repel with 9 N at 1 m. At 3 m the force is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1 N”. Reasoning: 9/9. A choice like “27 N” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor in parallel are in series with 2 Ω across 8 V. Current from the source:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2 A”. Reasoning: R = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. A choice like “1 A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A proton enters B = 0.5 T at 10⁶ m/s perpendicular. Radius (m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg):
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2.1 cm”. Reasoning: r = 1.67×10⁻²¹/(0.8×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 0.021 m. A choice like “0.21 m” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 200-turn coil of area 0.01 m² rotates at 50 rad/s in B = 0.2 T. Peak emf:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “20 V”. Reasoning: 200 × 0.2 × 0.01 × 50. A choice like “40 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A convex lens of f = 10 cm forms a real image at 30 cm. Object distance:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “15 cm”. Reasoning: 1/30 − 1/u = 1/10 ⇒ u = −15 cm. A choice like “30 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: In YDSE, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m, λ = 500 nm. Fringe width:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “0.5 mm”. Reasoning: λD/d. A choice like “1 mm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Light of 248 nm on a metal of φ₀ = 3 eV. Stopping potential:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2 V”. Reasoning: 5 eV − 3 eV. A choice like “8 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Binding energy per nucleon of a nucleus with ΔM = 0.5 u and A = 60:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “7.76 MeV”. Reasoning: 0.5 × 931.5/60. A choice like “465.8 MeV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Mock paper 2 (mixed chapters)

scenes.text: In her first mock, Pooja scored 52%. Optics and EMI were her weakest.
She revised those formula sheets and redid every wrong question.
This second mock is her chance to see the improvement.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: 8 questions, 12 minutes, no notes. Several questions are assertion–reason and case-based, as in recent board papers. Then study the explanations.

steps.title: Assertion–reason method
steps.body:
1. Judge the assertion alone: true or false?
2. Judge the reason alone.
3. Only if both are true, ask: does the reason *explain* the assertion (does 'because' make sense)?

steps.title: Case-based questions
steps.body: Read the case once fully, underline numbers and units, then answer each sub-question independently — one mistake should not cascade.

steps.title: Last-minute warnings
steps.body:
- In AC questions check whether a value is rms or peak.
- In modern physics check eV vs J.
- In capacitor questions check whether the battery stays connected.

activity.prompt: Compare your two mock scores. Which chapter improved most, and which still needs work? Write your three-day plan.
activity.hint: Be specific: chapter, topic, and how many questions you will practise each day.

quiz.q: Assertion: Inside a charged conducting shell E = 0. Reason: All charge resides on the outer surface.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: Gauss's law with zero enclosed charge. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V stores energy
quiz.why: The correct answer is “0.05 J”. Reasoning: ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 10⁴. A choice like “5 J” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Case: An LCR circuit has L = 0.4 H and C = 10 μF. Resonant angular frequency:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “500 rad/s”. Reasoning: 1/√(4×10⁻⁶) = 500. A choice like “1000 rad/s” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A transformer with Nₚ : Nₛ = 1 : 20 is fed 230 V. Output voltage:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4600 V”. Reasoning: × 20. A choice like “230 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “45°”. Reasoning: sin i_c = 1/√2. A choice like “60°” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Unpolarised light through two polaroids at 45°: fraction transmitted
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1/4”. Reasoning: ½ × cos²45°. A choice like “0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Energy of an electron in the 3rd orbit of hydrogen:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “−1.51 eV”. Reasoning: −13.6/9. A choice like “−0.85 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A full-wave rectifier's output on 60 Hz mains has ripple frequency
quiz.why: The correct answer is “120 Hz”. Reasoning: Twice input. A choice like “60 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: SI unit of electric flux is
questions.why: The correct answer is “N m²/C”. Reasoning: E × area. A choice like “V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Unit of inductance is
questions.why: The correct answer is “henry”. A choice like “tesla” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.

questions.q: Which EM wave has the highest frequency?
questions.why: The correct answer is “gamma rays”. Reasoning: Shortest wavelength. A choice like “X-rays” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Majority carriers in n-type Ge are
questions.why: The correct answer is “electrons”. Reasoning: Donor electrons. A choice like “holes” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The potential at the centre of a charged conducting sphere (radius R, charge Q) is
questions.why: The correct answer is “kQ/R”. Reasoning: Same as surface. A choice like “kQ/R²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A cell of 2 V, r = 0.5 Ω gives what current through 3.5 Ω?
questions.why: The correct answer is “0.5 A”. Reasoning: 2/4. A choice like “0.57 A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Field at the centre of a 50-turn coil of radius 5 cm carrying 2 A:
questions.why: The correct answer is “1.26×10⁻³ T”. Reasoning: μ₀NI/2R = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 100/0.1. A choice like “2.5×10⁻³ T” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Image by a plane mirror is
questions.why: The correct answer is “virtual, erect, same size”. Reasoning: Basic property. A choice like “real, inverted” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: A capacitor blocks DC but passes AC. Reason: X_C = 1/ωC decreases with frequency.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: At ω = 0, X_C → ∞. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Equivalent of 3 μF, 6 μF in series, in parallel with 4 μF:
questions.why: The correct answer is “6 μF”. Reasoning: 2 + 4. A choice like “13 μF” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron at 25 V is
questions.why: The correct answer is “0.245 nm”. Reasoning: 1.227/5. A choice like “0.049 nm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A 2 m rod moves at 5 m/s perpendicular to 0.3 T on rails with R = 6 Ω. Power dissipated:
questions.why: The correct answer is “1.5 W”. Reasoning: ε = 3 V; P = ε²/R = 1.5 W. A choice like “9 W” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A prism of 60° and n = √2 gives minimum deviation
questions.why: The correct answer is “30°”. Reasoning: sin((60 + D)/2) = √2 × 0.5 ⇒ 45° ⇒ D = 30°. A choice like “60°” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Two coherent sources with intensity ratio 1 : 9. I_max : I_min =
questions.why: The correct answer is “4 : 1”. Reasoning: (1 + 3)²/(3 − 1)² = 16/4 = 4. A choice like “9 : 1” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Work function 2 eV; light of 4 eV. If intensity doubles, K_max
questions.why: The correct answer is “stays 2 eV”. Reasoning: Intensity does not affect K_max. A choice like “halves” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Series LCR: R = 3 Ω, X_L = 8 Ω, X_C = 4 Ω on 10 V. Current:
questions.why: The correct answer is “2 A”. Reasoning: Z = 5 Ω. A choice like “0.67 A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Ratio of radii of nuclei ⁸Be and ⁶⁴Cu:
questions.why: The correct answer is “1 : 2”. Reasoning: (8/64)^(1/3) = 1/2. A choice like “2 : 1” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A galvanometer of 20 Ω, full scale 5 mA, converted to 0–5 V needs series resistance
questions.why: The correct answer is “980 Ω”. Reasoning: 5/0.005 − 20. A choice like “1000 Ω” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A charge q is at the centre of a cube; another charge q is outside it. Flux through the cube:
questions.why: The correct answer is “q/ε₀”. Reasoning: Only enclosed charge counts. A choice like “2q/ε₀” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Two long wires 4 cm apart carry 20 A and 10 A in opposite directions. Force per metre on each:
questions.why: The correct answer is “1×10⁻³ N, repulsive”. Reasoning: 2×10⁻⁷ × 200/0.04 = 10⁻³ N; opposite currents repel. A choice like “1×10⁻³ N, attractive” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: An electron in hydrogen jumps 3 → 2. Wavelength emitted:
questions.why: The correct answer is “656 nm”. Reasoning: 1.89 eV ⇒ 656 nm. A choice like “103 nm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “0.024 J”. Reasoning: C₁C₂V²/2(C₁ + C₂) = 6×10⁻¹² × 4×10⁴/(2 × 5×10⁻⁶) = 0.024 J. A choice like “0.04 J” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “75 cm”. Reasoning: (1.5 − 1)/(1.5/1.25 − 1) = 0.5/0.2 = 2.5 ⇒ 75 cm. A choice like “60 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “30 min”. Reasoning: 4 half-lives in 120 min. A choice like “15 min” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “45°”. Reasoning: I = (I₀/8) sin² 2θ, maximum at 45°. A choice like “60°” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

courses.title: Contemporary World Politics · The End of Bipolarity
courses.summary: The Soviet system, Gorbachev's reforms, the disintegration of the USSR in 1991, consequences for world politics, shock therapy in post-communist states, tensions after disintegration and India's relations with Russia.
outcomes: Learners can describe features of the Soviet system
Learners can explain causes of the Soviet disintegration
Learners can evaluate shock therapy
Learners can describe India–Russia relations
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: The Soviet system and the Berlin Wall

scenes.text: Crowds in Berlin climb the wall that had divided their city since 1961.
Within two years, the Soviet Union itself would cease to exist.

steps.title: The Soviet system
steps.body: The **USSR** emerged after the **1917** socialist revolution in Russia and was formed in **1922**. Features: **one-party** rule by the Communist Party; state ownership and **planned economy**; developed industry, space and defence; minimum standard of living — no unemployment, subsidised health and education. Weaknesses: **bureaucratic and authoritarian**; lack of democracy and freedom of speech; Russia dominated other republics; arms race drained resources; lagged in technology and consumer goods.

steps.title: Second World
steps.body: After World War II, East European countries liberated by the Soviet army formed the 'socialist bloc' (the **Second World**), bound by the **Warsaw Pact** (1955) military alliance. The **Berlin Wall** (built **1961**) symbolised the divide between capitalist and communist worlds; it fell on **9 November 1989**; Germany unified on **3 October 1990**.

steps.title: Solved: strengths vs weaknesses
steps.body: Strengths: industrial base, universal education/health, nuclear and space power. Weaknesses: stagnant economy, shortages of consumer goods, lack of political freedom, costly Afghanistan intervention (1979).

steps.title: Solved: date gap
steps.body: Wall built 1961 → fell 1989: **28 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The USSR was formed in 1922, not 1917 (1917 was the revolution).

activity.prompt: Order these events

quiz.why: Planned.

options: Military alliance of the socialist bloc
quiz.why: Alliance.

quiz.q: A weakness of the Soviet system:
quiz.why: Authoritarian.

scenes.text: On 25 December 1991, Gorbachev resigns and the Soviet flag is lowered over the Kremlin.
Fifteen independent countries now appear on the map.

steps.title: Gorbachev's reforms
steps.body: **Mikhail Gorbachev** became General Secretary in **1985**. **Perestroika** (restructuring) and **glasnost** (openness) aimed to reform the system; he normalised relations with the West, withdrew from Afghanistan, and did not intervene as East European regimes collapsed (1989).

steps.title: Disintegration (1991)
steps.body: Reforms raised expectations; people wanted faster change, while conservatives resisted. **August 1991**: a coup by hardliners failed; **Boris Yeltsin** (Russia) emerged as a hero resisting it. The **Baltic republics** (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) pressed independence. **December 1991**: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared the USSR dissolved and formed the **Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS)**; Gorbachev resigned on **25 December 1991**. Russia became the **successor state** (took the UN Security Council seat).

steps.title: Why did it collapse?
steps.body: 1) Internal weaknesses of economic and political institutions. 2) Huge resources on arms race and satellite states. 3) Information about Western progress shocked people. 4) Gorbachev's reforms unleashed forces he could not control. 5) **Nationalism** and desire for sovereignty in republics (Baltics, Ukraine, Georgia).

steps.title: Solved: consequences
steps.body: 1) **End of the Cold War** confrontations. 2) Change in balance of power — the US became the sole superpower (**unipolar** world). 3) Emergence of many new countries. 4) Capitalist economy and liberal democracy became dominant models; IMF and World Bank more powerful.

steps.title: Solved: count
steps.body: USSR had **15** republics → all became independent states.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The CIS was founded by Russia, Ukraine and Belarus — not by the Baltic states.

activity.prompt: Put the collapse in sequence
items: Gorbachev becomes General Secretary and starts perestroika and glasnost
Russia, Ukraine and Belarus form the CIS (December 1991)
Gorbachev resigns; USSR ends on 25 December 1991

quiz.why: Openness.
Gorbachev resigned.
Three Slavic republics.
UNSC seat.

lessons.title: Shock therapy, tensions and India–Russia ties

scenes.text: In 1992, a state factory in Russia is sold to private buyers at a fraction of its value.
Pensioners see their savings wiped out by inflation.

steps.title: Shock therapy
steps.body: Post-communist transition to a capitalist economy and democracy, pushed by the World Bank and IMF: **privatisation** of state assets, private property, collective farms replaced by private farming, free trade, currency convertibility, opening to the West; rejected gradual change.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body: Economic ruin: the value of the **ruble** fell sharply, high inflation wiped out savings; collective farms disintegrated, food security suffered; about **90%** of industries sold — described as **'the largest garage sale in history'**; social welfare dismantled; rise of an oligarchy (mafia); widening inequality. Constitutions were drafted in haste; strong presidencies emerged. Some recovery in the 2000s from oil and gas exports.

steps.title: Tensions
steps.body: Conflicts: **Chechnya** and **Dagestan** secession movements in Russia; civil war in **Tajikistan** (~10 years, till 2001); Azerbaijan's province of Nagorno-Karabakh; Georgia's regions; Central Asian resources attracted outside powers. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into Czech Republic and Slovakia; Yugoslavia broke up violently (Bosnia).

steps.title: India and Russia
steps.body: Long friendship: **Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (1971)**; Soviet support on Kashmir at the UN, help in steel plants (Bhilai, Bokaro), defence supplies, oil. Post-1991: shared vision of a **multipolar** world; strategic partnership; cooperation in defence, energy, space, nuclear energy.

steps.title: Solved: evaluate shock therapy
steps.body: Aim: quick transition. Result: collapse of industry, inequality, poverty. Lesson: rapid privatisation without institutions and safety nets causes social damage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Shock therapy was **not** gradual reform — its defining feature was speed.

statements.s: Shock therapy meant gradual, slow reforms.
About 90% of Russian industries were sold to private buyers.
The Indo-Soviet Treaty was signed in 1971.
Czechoslovakia split through a long civil war.
India and Russia share a vision of a multipolar world.

quiz.q: 'Largest garage sale in history' refers to:
quiz.why: Privatisation.
Western institutions.
Chechnya.

quiz.why: Bhilai.

steps.title: Map in words

courses.title: Contemporary World Politics · International Organisations
courses.summary: Why international organisations exist, the making of the United Nations, its principal organs, the Security Council and veto, the reform debate and India's case, and other organisations (IMF, World Bank, WTO, IAEA, NGOs).
outcomes: Learners can explain the need for international organisations
Learners can narrate the founding of the UN with dates
Learners can analyse Security Council reform and India's claim
Learners can describe other major international organisations
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: The United Nations: origin and organs

scenes.text: After a devastating war, delegates from 50 countries meet to draft a charter for peace.
On 24 October 1945, the United Nations is born.

steps.title: Why international organisations?
steps.body: They help countries cooperate on war and peace, climate, disease, trade; resolve disputes; share information; and reduce mistrust. They are not a world government — they depend on members' consent.

steps.title: Making of the UN
steps.body:
- **League of Nations** (after WWI) failed to prevent WWII.
- **Atlantic Charter** (Aug 1941, Roosevelt & Churchill).
- **Declaration by United Nations** (Jan 1942).
- **Yalta Conference** (Feb 1945).
- **San Francisco conference** (April–June 1945) drafted the **UN Charter**, signed **26 June 1945** by 50 nations (Poland signed later → **51** original members).
- UN founded **24 October 1945** (UN Day). Today **193** member states.

steps.title: Principal organs
steps.body: **General Assembly** (all members, one vote each), **Security Council**, **Economic and Social Council**, **International Court of Justice** (The Hague), **Secretariat** headed by the **Secretary-General** (first: Trygve Lie of Norway; current since 2017: António Guterres of Portugal), and the Trusteeship Council (suspended after 1994). Agencies: WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR, FAO, ILO.

steps.title: Solved: why did the League fail?
steps.body: 1) Major powers absent or left (USA never joined). 2) No effective enforcement. 3) Aggression in the 1930s went unpunished. The UN tried to fix these with a stronger Security Council.

steps.title: Solved: membership growth
steps.body: 51 founding members → 193 today: an increase of **142** countries, mostly due to decolonisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: UN Charter signed 26 June 1945; UN came into existence 24 October 1945.

activity.prompt: Order the founding of the UN

quiz.why: Trygve Lie.
The Hague.

scenes.text: Fourteen members vote for a resolution; one permanent member votes no.
The resolution fails — the power of the veto.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body: **15** members: **5 permanent (P5)** — USA, Russia, UK, France, China — and **10 non-permanent** elected by the General Assembly for **2-year** terms (not immediately re-electable). Decisions on substantive matters need **9 votes** with no negative vote from a P5 — the **veto**.

steps.title: Reform debate
steps.body: Since the end of the Cold War, changes: Soviet collapse, US dominance, rise of China, India, Brazil, Germany, Japan; growing membership from Asia, Africa, Latin America. In **1992** the General Assembly adopted a resolution on reform. Proposed criteria for new permanent members: major economic power, military power, substantial contributor to UN budget, big nation by population, respects democracy and human rights, representative of geography/culture. Debate on veto: some say abolish it; others say great powers need it to stay engaged.

steps.title: India's claim
steps.body: India is a founding member; one of the largest contributors of troops to **UN peacekeeping**; second most populous country (now the most populous); world's largest democracy; a major economy; pursued peace, disarmament and decolonisation. Objections raised by some: nuclear weapons, relations with Pakistan, concerns about regional balance.

steps.title: Solved: votes needed
steps.body: A resolution gets 10 yes votes, 4 no votes from non-permanent members, 1 abstention by a P5 → passes (≥ 9 yes, no P5 negative vote; abstention is not a veto by practice).

steps.title: Solved: case
steps.body: 14 yes, 1 no from China → fails (veto).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Non-permanent members don't have a veto.

statements.s: The Security Council has 15 members.
Non-permanent members serve 5-year terms.
An abstention by a P5 member counts as a veto in practice.
India is a major contributor to UN peacekeeping.
A UNSC reform resolution was adopted by the General Assembly in 1992.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a P5 member?
quiz.why: India is not.

quiz.q: Case: 12 yes, 3 no (one from the USA). Result?
quiz.why: US veto.

lessons.title: IMF, World Bank, WTO, IAEA and NGOs

scenes.text: In 1991, India faces a balance-of-payments crisis and turns to the IMF.
Economic reforms follow, changing India's economy.

steps.title: Bretton Woods twins
steps.body:
Created at **Bretton Woods (1944)**: 
- **IMF** — oversees financial institutions and regulations at the international level; voting weighted by contributions (rich countries have more votes).
- **World Bank** (IBRD) — loans and grants for human development (health, education), agriculture and rural development, environment, infrastructure and governance; criticised for conditions imposed on borrowers.

steps.title: WTO and IAEA
steps.body:
- **WTO** (set up **1995**, successor to **GATT** created after WWII) — sets rules for global trade; decisions by consensus, though major economic powers dominate.
- **IAEA** (established **1957**) — promotes peaceful use of nuclear energy and prevents its military use; inspectors visit nuclear facilities.

steps.title: NGOs
steps.body: **Amnesty International** — campaigns for human rights, publishes reports; **Human Rights Watch** — research and advocacy on human rights, draws media attention. They are not government bodies but influence global debates.

steps.title: Solved: why is IMF voting criticised?
steps.body: Votes are proportional to contributions; the G-7 and the US hold large shares — developing countries have less say in decisions affecting them.

steps.title: Solved: GATT → WTO
steps.body: GATT (1948) was an agreement; WTO (1995) is a permanent organisation with dispute settlement covering goods, services and intellectual property.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The WTO is not a UN principal organ; IMF and World Bank are separate from the Security Council.

courses.title: Politics in India · Challenges of Nation Building
courses.summary: Challenges at independence, Partition and its consequences, integration of princely states (Junagadh, Hyderabad, Manipur, Kashmir) and the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines.
outcomes: Learners can state the three challenges facing independent India
Learners can explain the process and consequences of Partition
Learners can describe the integration of princely states with cases
Learners can analyse linguistic reorganisation of states
courses.guardianNote: Covers the violence of Partition in 1947 factually and without graphic detail, as required by the Class 12 political science syllabus. Suitable for ages 16–18.
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Nehru speaks of India's 'tryst with destiny' to the Constituent Assembly.
At the same time, trains full of refugees cross the new borders in Punjab and Bengal.

steps.title: Three challenges
steps.body: 1) **Shape a nation** that is united yet accommodates diversity. 2) **Establish democracy** — representative democracy based on the parliamentary form. 3) **Ensure development and well-being** of all, especially the poor and marginalised (DPSP guidance).

steps.title: Process of Partition
steps.body: Based on the **two-nation theory** advanced by the Muslim League. Principle: Muslim-majority areas to Pakistan. Problems: 1) No single Muslim-majority belt — **West and East Pakistan** separated by Indian territory. 2) Not all Muslim-majority areas wanted Pakistan — **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan** (North-West Frontier Province) opposed. 3) **Punjab and Bengal** had to be divided district by district. 4) Minorities on both sides faced fear and violence.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body: One of the largest, most abrupt, unplanned and tragic population transfers in history. About **80 lakh** people migrated across the new border; estimates of those killed range from **5 to 10 lakh**. Women faced abduction and violence; families divided; property lost. Cities like Lahore, Amritsar, Kolkata became 'communal zones'. Division of financial assets, army and government staff. India's leaders chose a **secular state** — Gandhi worked for communal harmony until his assassination on **30 January 1948**.

steps.title: Solved: why secular?
steps.body: 1) India's diversity of religions. 2) Commitment of the national movement. 3) Fear of majoritarianism. 4) Constitution guarantees equality and freedom of religion to all.

steps.title: Solved: geography of Partition
steps.body: West Pakistan: West Punjab, Sindh, NWFP, Baluchistan. East Pakistan: East Bengal (became **Bangladesh in 1971**). India retained East Punjab and West Bengal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not all Muslim-majority areas were enthusiastic about Pakistan — NWFP under Ghaffar Khan is a key example.

statements.s: Pakistan was formed as two territories separated by India.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan supported the two-nation theory.
About 80 lakh people migrated across the new borders.
India chose to become a theocratic state.
Punjab and Bengal were divided.

quiz.why: Nehru.
League.
Ghaffar Khan.

scenes.text: Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon persuade ruler after ruler to sign the Instrument of Accession.
Hundreds of states join India — but a few hold out.

steps.title: The problem
steps.body: British India had **about 565 princely states** covering about one-third of the land. With British paramountcy ending, they were technically free to join India, Pakistan, or stay independent — a threat to unity.

steps.title: Government's approach
steps.body: **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** (Deputy PM and Home Minister) led with firm diplomacy. Three considerations: people of most states wanted to join India; government was flexible on autonomy; integration was essential for territorial unity. Most rulers signed the **Instrument of Accession** before 15 August 1947.

steps.title: Difficult cases
steps.body:
- **Junagadh** (Gujarat): Nawab wanted Pakistan; people protested; a **plebiscite** (Feb 1948) confirmed joining India.
- **Hyderabad**: largest state; **Nizam** wanted independence; signed Standstill Agreement (Nov 1947); peasant movement in Telangana and Razakar violence; Indian army action (**September 1948**) → Nizam surrendered.
- **Manipur**: Maharaja **Bodhachandra Singh** signed accession; held elections under universal adult franchise in **June 1948** with a constitutional monarchy; pressured to sign a merger agreement in **September 1949** without consulting the elected assembly — resentment still felt.
- **Kashmir**: Maharaja Hari Singh signed accession after tribal invasion from Pakistan (October 1947).

steps.title: Solved: why was Manipur's merger controversial?
steps.body: Manipur already had an elected legislature; the merger agreement was signed without its consent — raising questions of democratic legitimacy.

steps.title: Solved: three methods used
steps.body: Persuasion and diplomacy (most states), plebiscite (Junagadh), military action (Hyderabad).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hyderabad action was in **1948**, not 1947.

activity.prompt: Match the princely state to how it joined India

quiz.why: Patel.
Nizam.

quiz.q: Manipur held elections under universal adult franchise in:
quiz.why: June 1948.

quiz.q: Document signed by rulers to join India:
quiz.why: Accession.

scenes.text: In 1952, Potti Sriramulu fasts for a separate Telugu-speaking state.
His death after 56 days leads to the creation of Andhra state.

steps.title: Linguistic demand
steps.body: The Congress (Nagpur session, 1920) had accepted linguistic provinces. After Partition, leaders feared further division. Telugu-speaking areas of Madras province demanded Vishalandhra; **Potti Sriramulu** fasted and died in **December 1952** after 56 days; protests followed; **Andhra state** was formed on **1 October 1953**.

steps.title: States Reorganisation Commission
steps.body: Appointed in **1953**: **Justice Fazl Ali**, **K.M. Panikkar**, **H.N. Kunzru**. Report accepted that boundaries should reflect languages. **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**: **14 states and 6 union territories**.

steps.title: Later states
steps.body:
- **Gujarat and Maharashtra** from Bombay state (**1960**).
- **Nagaland** (**1963**).
- **Punjab and Haryana** (**1966**); Himachal Pradesh got some areas.
- **Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura** (**1972**); Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (1987).
- **Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand** (**2000**); **Telangana** (**2014**).

steps.title: Solved: did linguistic states weaken unity?
steps.body: Fears proved largely unfounded: 1) Democracy became more accessible in local languages. 2) Regional aspirations were accommodated. 3) Diversity was recognised as strength. Unity was strengthened by accommodation.

steps.title: Solved: date gap
steps.body: SRC appointed 1953 → Act 1956: 3 years. Andhra 1953 → Telangana 2014: 61 years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The 1956 Act created 14 states and 6 UTs — not 28 states.

story.title: A ballot box for each candidate

scenes.text: In 1952, a first-time voter in a village drops her ballot paper into the box marked with a symbol.
Election officials had trained lakhs of staff to manage India's first general election.

steps.title: Challenges
steps.body: The **Election Commission** was set up in **January 1950**; **Sukumar Sen** was the first Chief Election Commissioner. Tasks: delimit constituencies, prepare electoral rolls (about **17 crore** eligible voters), train **3 lakh** officers and polling staff; most voters were not literate — so special methods: each candidate had a separate ballot box with a **symbol**.

steps.title: Conduct and result
steps.body: Elections held from **October 1951 to February 1952** (commonly called the 1952 election). Turnout was a little under half of eligible voters — remarkable for a first election. Critics had doubted that democracy could work in a poor, largely illiterate country — the election proved them wrong. **Congress** won **364 of 489** Lok Sabha seats; the **CPI** came second with **16** seats.

steps.title: Solved: seat share
steps.body: 364/489 = **74.4%** of seats. Congress's vote share was about 45% — FPTP magnified its seats.

steps.title: Solved: methods of voting
steps.body: 1952 & 1957: separate box per candidate with symbol. From 1962: a single ballot paper listing candidates and symbols. From the late 1990s: **EVMs**, used across the country by 2004.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The first election ran from Oct 1951 to Feb 1952 — it wasn't a single-day poll.

activity.prompt: Congress won 364 of 489 seats in 1952. What percentage of seats is that (one decimal)?

quiz.why: Sukumar Sen.
CPI.
17 crore.

story.title: A party like a big tent

scenes.text: Inside the Congress were industrialists and peasants, socialists and conservatives.
Factions argued openly — yet stayed in one party.

steps.title: Why Congress dominated
steps.body: 1) **Legacy of the national movement**. 2) Only party with an organisation across the country. 3) Popular leaders like **Nehru**. 4) FPTP gave it a larger share of seats than votes. 5) Accommodated diverse groups.

steps.title: Social and ideological coalition
steps.body: Congress brought together diverse social groups — peasants and industrialists, urban and rural, upper castes, Dalits, Adivasis, minorities — and **ideologies** from revolutionary and pacifist to conservative and radical, moderate and extremist. It tolerated **factions** — groups inside the party with different views. This internal competition meant even opposition views found space inside Congress — hence dominance did not mean lack of democracy.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body: Unlike one-party rule in countries like the former USSR or China, India's dominance came through **free and fair elections**; other parties competed freely. Similar 'dominant party' systems: e.g. long-dominant parties elsewhere (Mexico's PRI was cited as a case of dominance with less free competition).

steps.title: Solved: Kerala 1957
steps.body: In **1957**, the **CPI** won the assembly election in **Kerala** and **E.M.S. Namboodiripad** became Chief Minister — one of the first democratically elected communist governments. It was dismissed in **1959** under **Article 356** — a controversial use of central power.

steps.title: Solved: factions as strength
steps.body: Factions allowed bargaining and representation within the party, kept dissatisfied groups inside and made Congress responsive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'One-party dominance' ≠ 'one-party state'. India had multiple parties.

scenes.text: Opposition MPs in the first Lok Sabha were few, but they questioned the government sharply.
Their criticism kept Congress responsive.

steps.title: Communist Party of India
steps.body: Formed in the early 1920s, inspired by the Bolshevik revolution; worked within the Congress until 1941; supported British war effort against Nazi Germany then. Initially thought 1947 independence was not true freedom; supported violent uprisings in Telangana; then took part in 1952 elections. Leaders: **A.K. Gopalan, S.A. Dange, E.M.S. Namboodiripad, P.C. Joshi, Ajoy Ghosh, P. Sundarraya**. Split in **1964** (CPI and CPI(M)).

steps.title: Bharatiya Jana Sangh
steps.body: Formed in **1951** with **Syama Prasad Mukherjee** as founder-president. Ideas: 'one country, one culture, one nation'; emphasised Indian culture and traditions; advocated Hindi as official language; argued for India developing atomic weapons after China's 1964 test. Leaders: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya, Balraj Madhok. The BJP traces its roots to it.

steps.title: Swatantra and Socialist parties
steps.body:
- **Swatantra Party** (**1959**) after Congress's Nagpur resolution on land ceilings and cooperatives; leaders **C. Rajagopalachari**, K.M. Munshi, N.G. Ranga, Minoo Masani; favoured free market, less state control, closer ties with the USA.
- **Socialist Party**: origins in the **Congress Socialist Party** (1934); left Congress in 1948; leaders **Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia**, Asoka Mehta; split into several parties over time.

steps.title: Solved: role of opposition
steps.body: 1) Criticised government policies, kept it accountable. 2) Prepared alternatives. 3) Kept democratic competition alive. 4) Leaders were respected — Nehru included some opposition leaders in his first cabinet (e.g. Ambedkar, Syama Prasad Mukherjee).

steps.title: Solved: identify party
steps.body: Free market, less licence-permit raj, oppose land ceilings → **Swatantra**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

courses.title: Ch 1 · Variations in Psychological Attributes
courses.summary: Individual differences, intelligence theories, IQ computation, assessment and creativity.
outcomes: Define intelligence and compare Spearman, Thurstone, Gardner, Sternberg and PASS
Compute ratio IQ and deviation IQ
Interpret IQ classification
Distinguish intelligence from creativity

scenes.text: Isha solves maths puzzles quickly; her friend Zoya reads people's moods and leads the team.
Is intelligence one thing or many?

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Spearman:** general factor *g* plus specific factors *s* (two-factor).
- **Thurstone:** seven primary mental abilities (verbal comprehension, numerical, spatial, perceptual speed, word fluency, memory, reasoning).
- **Gardner:** multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic).
- **Sternberg triarchic:** analytical, creative, practical.
- **PASS (Das, Naglieri):** Planning, Attention-arousal, Simultaneous and Successive processing.

steps.title: Solved example · who said it?
steps.body:
1. 'One general ability underlies all tasks' → Spearman.
2. 'A street-smart businessperson shows practical intelligence' → Sternberg.
3. 'A dancer's body control is a distinct intelligence' → Gardner.
Use the *number and nature of abilities* as the clue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Gardner's intelligences as learning styles.
- Writing 'Thurstone: 8 abilities' — it is seven primary mental abilities.

activity.prompt: Match theorist to idea

quiz.why: Analytical, creative, practical.
General and specific.
Added by Gardner.

scenes.text: In the early 1900s Alfred Binet was asked to identify children needing extra help in Paris schools.
With Simon he created the first practical intelligence scale, using mental age.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**Ratio IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100** (MA = mental age, CA = chronological age).
IQ of 100 = average. **Deviation IQ** compares a person with others of the same age using mean 100 and SD 15 (or 16 in some tests).
Typical classification: below 70 low, 90–109 average, 130+ very superior.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A child with CA = 8 years and MA = 10 years.
- IQ = (10 ÷ 8) × 100 = **125**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using months and years together; convert both to the same unit.
- Believing IQ is fixed forever or measures every human quality; tests are culture-sensitive and should be used by trained examiners.

activity.prompt: A child has MA 9 years and CA 12 years. Find the ratio IQ.

quiz.why: By design.

quiz.q: Who made the first practical intelligence test?
quiz.why: Binet–Simon scale.

scenes.text: Two students score alike on an IQ test, but only one invents new uses for a paper cup.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Intellectual disability:** IQ roughly below 70 plus limits in adaptive behaviour, appearing in the developmental period; levels mild to profound.
- **Giftedness:** very high IQ (around 130+) or high talent; needs enrichment.
- **Creativity:** producing original and useful ideas. **Divergent thinking** (many solutions: fluency, flexibility, originality) vs **convergent** (single correct answer — IQ-type).
- Guilford emphasised divergent thinking; creativity needs motivation and an enabling environment.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Task: 'List uses of a brick.' Student A lists 12 uses in 3 categories; Student B lists 5. A shows higher **fluency** (12) and **flexibility** (3 categories).

steps.title: Respectful language
steps.body: Use person-first language and focus on support. Disability assessment requires qualified professionals.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Self and Personality
courses.summary: Self-concept, self-esteem, self-regulation, personality theories (type, trait, psychodynamic, humanistic) and assessment.
outcomes: Distinguish self-concept, self-esteem and self-efficacy
Compare type and trait approaches
Explain Freud's id, ego, superego and psychosexual stages
Describe Big Five and assessment methods

scenes.text: Arjun describes himself as a cricketer, a good listener and poor at maths.
He feels confident about his bowling and believes he can improve in maths with practice.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Self-concept:** organised beliefs about oneself.
- **Self-esteem:** overall evaluation of self-worth (high/low).
- **Self-efficacy** (Bandura): belief that I can perform a task.
- **Self-regulation:** controlling own behaviour through self-observation, goal setting and self-reinforcement.
- Indian view: self as embedded in relationships; ideas like *atman* in traditional thought.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: 'I am good at maths' → self-concept. 'I like who I am' → self-esteem. 'I can solve this sum if I try' → self-efficacy. Delaying a game until homework is done → self-regulation.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Equating self-esteem with arrogance; healthy self-esteem is realistic and stable.

quiz.why: Bandura.

lessons.title: Personality: type, trait and psychodynamic approaches

scenes.text: At a party one friend talks to everyone, another prefers a quiet corner.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Approaches
steps.body:
**Personality** = relatively stable pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviour that makes a person unique.
- **Type:** Hippocrates (humours), Sheldon (endomorph, mesomorph, ectomorph), Jung (introvert/extrovert), Friedman–Rosenman (Type A/B), Indian *gunas* (sattva, rajas, tamas).
- **Trait:** Allport (cardinal, central, secondary), Cattell (16PF), Eysenck (extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism), **Big Five** (OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism).
- **Psychodynamic (Freud):** **id** (pleasure principle), **ego** (reality principle), **superego** (morality). Stages: oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital. Defence mechanisms: repression, denial, projection, rationalisation, displacement, sublimation.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A student angry with the teacher shouts at a younger sibling → **displacement**. A person who failed says the exam was unfair → **rationalisation**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving ID as 'reality principle' (that's ego).
- Treating types as strict boxes; most people lie on a continuum.

quiz.why: Five-factor model.

quiz.why: Displacement.

scenes.text: A counsellor shows Neha an ambiguous picture and asks her to tell a story.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Rogers:** self, ideal self, congruence, unconditional positive regard.
- **Maslow:** self-actualisation at the top of the hierarchy.
- **Assessment:** self-report inventories (e.g. 16PF, Big Five questionnaires); **projective techniques** — Rorschach inkblot, **TAT** (Thematic Apperception Test), sentence completion; **behavioural** methods and interviews.
- Good tests are standardised, reliable and valid; interpretation needs trained professionals.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A large gap between real self and ideal self → low congruence → distress in Rogers' view. Counselling aims to increase congruence through unconditional positive regard.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Projective tests presume that unconscious conflicts are expressed in how one interprets ambiguous stimuli; they have lower objectivity than inventories.

lessons.title: What is stress? Sources and effects

scenes.text: Sana's heart races and she cannot sleep the night before her board exam.
Her body is reacting to a perceived demand.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body:
**Stress** is a pattern of responses to events (stressors) that tax or exceed one's coping resources. Lazarus: **primary appraisal** (is it a threat?) and **secondary appraisal** (can I cope?).
- **Eustress** = positive, motivating; **distress** = harmful.
- Sources: life events, daily hassles, traumatic events, environmental (noise, crowding), social (conflict), frustration/conflict.
- Effects: physiological (heart rate, sleep), emotional (anxiety, irritability), cognitive (poor concentration), behavioural (withdrawal), burnout.

steps.title: Solved example · GAS
steps.body:
Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome:
1. **Alarm** (fight-or-flight, adrenaline rises)
2. **Resistance** (body adapts, stays vigilant)
3. **Exhaustion** (resources depleted → illness risk).
Exam month: nervousness in week 1 = alarm; continued revision with tension = resistance; constant fatigue and illness = exhaustion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all stress is harmful; moderate eustress can improve performance.
- Placing exhaustion before resistance.

activity.prompt: Order the GAS stages

quiz.why: Hans Selye.

scenes.text: Rohan makes a revision plan; Dia talks to a friend; Karan avoids the topic and plays games.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Coping strategies
steps.body:
- **Task-oriented / problem-focused** (plan, seek information).
- **Emotion-oriented** (venting, relaxation) — useful when the situation cannot be changed.
- **Avoidance-oriented** (denial, distraction) — brief use only.
Management techniques: relaxation (deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation), meditation/yoga, exercise, time management, cognitive restructuring, social support, adequate sleep.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Classify: Rohan = task-oriented; Dia = emotion-oriented with social support; Karan = avoidance. Best long-term approach: combine planning with support, using relaxation to calm the body first.

steps.title: When to seek help
steps.body: If stress causes persistent sleeplessness, panic, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm, talk to a trusted adult, school counsellor or doctor. India: Tele-MANAS 14416; emergency 112.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Positive health:** more than absence of disease — includes well-being, resilience, strong relationships.
- **Resilience** and **hardiness** (commitment, control, challenge) protect against stress.
- **Life skills (WHO):** self-awareness, empathy, critical and creative thinking, decision-making, problem-solving, effective communication, interpersonal relationships, coping with stress and emotions.
- Healthy diet, exercise, sleep; avoiding tobacco, alcohol and drugs.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A student with a clash of two events uses decision-making: list options, weigh consequences, choose, review. This applies WHO life skills.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Listing only physical health under positive health; psychological and social wellbeing are included.

courses.summary: Concepts of abnormality, classification (DSM/ICD), anxiety, mood, schizophrenia and other disorders; stigma and help-seeking.
outcomes: Explain the criteria for abnormality
Describe major categories of disorders
Differentiate anxiety, depressive and psychotic symptoms
Reduce stigma and know where to seek help
courses.guardianNote: Describes mental-health conditions in factual, non-graphic terms for exam study. It is not a diagnostic tool; if you or someone you know is struggling, talk to a trusted adult or call Tele-MANAS 14416; emergency 112.

story.title: Is that unusual or a disorder?

scenes.text: Some people talk to themselves while solving sums; others have a fear that stops them leaving the house.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Four Ds
steps.body:
Abnormality is judged by the **4 Ds**: **Deviance** (from social norms), **Distress**, **Dysfunction** (impaired daily life) and **Danger** (to self/others). Being unusual alone is not a disorder.
- Classification: **DSM** (American Psychiatric Association) and **ICD** (WHO). ICD-11 is current.
- Historical views: supernatural, biological, psychological; today **biopsychosocial** model and diathesis–stress.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A student prefers solitude but is happy and functions well → not a disorder (no distress/dysfunction). A person who avoids all social contact from fear and cannot attend school → distress + dysfunction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating mental illness as weakness or possession.
- Self-diagnosing from a checklist; diagnosis requires a trained clinician.

activity.prompt: Which 'D' is it?

quiz.why: World Health Organization.
Multiple causes.
Need distress/dysfunction.

scenes.text: Ravi has felt constantly tense for months and cannot control his worry, which affects sleep and studies.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Categories
steps.body:
- **Generalised anxiety disorder:** persistent, excessive worry plus restlessness and tension.
- **Panic disorder:** sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms.
- **Phobias:** irrational fear of a specific object/situation; **social anxiety**.
- **OCD:** obsessions (intrusive thoughts) and compulsions (repetitive acts).
- **Depression:** persistent low mood, loss of interest, sleep/appetite change, low energy, worthlessness for at least two weeks.
- **Bipolar:** episodes of mania/hypomania and depression.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Repeated handwashing because of fear of contamination, taking hours → compulsion linked to obsession (OCD). Fear only of heights → specific phobia.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: These are treatable (psychotherapy such as CBT, medication when prescribed by a doctor). Tele-MANAS 14416 offers free support; emergencies 112.

scenes.text: A young adult hears voices no one else hears and believes strangers are plotting against him; his family fears he is possessed.
A psychiatrist explains this is an illness and treatment helps.

steps.title: Key points
steps.body:
- **Schizophrenia:** psychotic disorder; positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganised speech), negative symptoms (flat affect, social withdrawal). Not 'split personality'.
- **Neurodevelopmental:** ADHD, autism spectrum, specific learning disorders.
- **Substance-related disorders** and addiction.
- **Dissociative** disorders (identity/memory disruption).
- **Stigma:** myths cause delay in help. Early treatment, family support and rehabilitation improve outcomes. India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017 recognises the right to access care.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Hallucination = perception without stimulus (hearing voices). Delusion = false fixed belief (being persecuted). Flat affect = reduced emotion → negative symptom.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing schizophrenia with multiple personality.
- Treating hallucination and delusion as the same.

school-c12-sociology.title: Class 12 Sociology (NCERT-based)
school-c12-sociology.description: Original, exam-ready chapter notes for Class 12 Indian Society and Social Change and Development in India: demography, inequality and exclusion, cultural diversity and social movements, with demographic numericals.

courses.title: Ch 2 · The Demographic Structure of the Indian Society
courses.summary: Population theories, demographic concepts and formulas, India's census trends, age structure and the sex ratio.
outcomes: Compare Malthus, Marx and demographic transition
Compute birth rate, death rate, natural growth rate and sex ratio
Explain age structure, dependency ratio and demographic dividend
Interpret Census 2011 trends

scenes.text: A village's population doubled in 30 years while its farmland stayed the same.
Villagers and planners debate whether food will run short.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Malthus:** population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8…), food arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4…); checks: preventive (late marriage) and positive (famine, disease, war).
- **Marx and others:** poverty is a result of social structure and capitalism, not population alone.
- **Demographic transition:** societies move from high birth and death rates to low ones in stages; population growth peaks when death rates fall before birth rates.
- **Demography** = scientific study of population; **census** = decennial count (India since 1881).

steps.title: Solved example · Malthusian arithmetic
steps.body: Population 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 (geometric) while food 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 (arithmetic). After 5 steps population is 16 vs food 5 — a gap of 11 units, which Malthus said checks would close.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing geometric and arithmetic.
- Ignoring that technology (Green Revolution) can raise food production faster than Malthus assumed.

scenes.text: A district office records 30,000 births and 12,000 deaths in a year for a population of 1,000,000.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Birth rate (CBR)** = (births ÷ mid-year population) × 1000.
- **Death rate (CDR)** = (deaths ÷ population) × 1000.
- **Natural growth rate** = birth rate − death rate (per 1000; divide by 10 for %).
- **Sex ratio** = females per 1000 males.
- **Infant mortality rate** = infant deaths (under 1 year) per 1000 live births.
- **Dependency ratio** = (population 0–14 + 60+) ÷ (population 15–59) × 100 (as used in the NCERT frame).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A town has 52,000 males and 49,400 females.
- Sex ratio = 49,400 ÷ 52,000 × 1000 = **950** females per 1000 males.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 100 instead of 1000.
- Inverting the sex ratio (males per female).
- Forgetting to convert per 1000 to percent.

lessons.title: India's population: age structure, sex ratio and dividend

scenes.text: A large share of India's people are of working age.
Jobs and skills decide whether this becomes a gain or a strain.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body:
- Census 2011: population about 121 crore (1.21 billion); decadal growth 17.7% (2001–11), lowest since the 1991–2001 trend began to slow.
- Sex ratio 943 females per 1000 males; **child sex ratio (0–6) 919** — the decline reflects son preference and sex-selective abortion, which is illegal under the PCPNDT Act 1994.
- Literacy: 74% (males about 82%, females about 65%).
- **Age structure:** share of children, working-age (15–59) and elderly (60+).
- **Demographic dividend:** economic gain when working-age people form a large share; needs education, health and jobs.
- Fertility varies: lower in states such as Kerala and Tamil Nadu, higher in some northern states.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Population 100: ages 0–14 = 30, 15–59 = 60, 60+ = 10. Dependency ratio = (30 + 10) ÷ 60 × 100 = **66.7**. A lower ratio gives a stronger dividend.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing overall and child sex ratio.
- Assuming dividend is automatic; unemployment can turn it into a burden.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Patterns of Social Inequality and Exclusion
courses.summary: Caste, untouchability, Scheduled Tribes, OBCs, gender and disability: forms of inequality and state and social responses.
outcomes: Distinguish social inequality, exclusion and discrimination
Explain caste discrimination and constitutional safeguards

courses.guardianNote: Discusses caste discrimination, untouchability and exclusion factually for exam study; content is respectful and focuses on rights and remedies.

scenes.text: In some places people from certain castes were not allowed to draw water from the common well.
The Constitution of India now forbids this.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Social inequality:** unequal access to resources and opportunities (income, education, status).
- **Social exclusion:** being shut out of full participation, often by group identity.
- **Prejudice** is an attitude; **discrimination** is unequal treatment in practice.
- **Caste:** hierarchical, hereditary, endogamous; untouchability imposed ritual and social segregation.
- **Constitutional safeguards:** Article 15 (no discrimination), **Article 17 abolishes untouchability**, reservation in education and jobs, **SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989**, Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955.
- Reformers: Jotirao Phule, Periyar, B.R. Ambedkar.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Q: Distinguish prejudice and discrimination.
- Prejudice: believing a group is less capable (attitude).
- Discrimination: refusing a job to that group (action).
A person can be prejudiced without acting, but discrimination is an action.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that caste is a purely ancient system; its forms have changed but persist in marriage, work and politics.
- Equating reservation with charity; it is a remedy for historic exclusion.

lessons.title: Scheduled Tribes, OBCs and the minority question

scenes.text: Tribal communities depend on forests, but displacement for mines and dams threatens their livelihoods.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body:
- **Scheduled Tribes (Adivasis):** about 8.6% of India's population (Census 2011), often in hilly, forest regions; issues: land alienation, displacement, poor health and education. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest dwellers' rights; Fifth and Sixth Schedules protect tribal areas.
- **OBCs:** socially and educationally backward classes; Mandal Commission (1980) recommended 27% reservation; implemented in central jobs in 1990 and upheld in the Indra Sawhney case (1992) with the creamy-layer exclusion.
- Tribal identity is diverse; 'tribe' includes communities with different languages and livelihoods.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Case: A dam will submerge a forest village. Rights-based response: environmental and social impact assessment, consent, compensation and rehabilitation under law, recognising Forest Rights Act claims.

steps.title: Exam hint
steps.body: Quote one law and one concrete issue per group to earn full marks.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Gender inequality:** unequal literacy, workforce participation, safety and political representation. The 73rd/74th Amendments reserve one-third seats for women in panchayats and urban local bodies; constitution allows special provisions (Article 15(3)). The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 and POSH Act 2013 protect women.
- **Disability:** social model — barriers in society disable people. The **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016** recognises 21 disabilities and mandates accessibility and reservation.
- Words matter: say 'persons with disabilities'.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Medical vs social model. Medical: the person's impairment is the problem. Social: the ramp-less building is the problem; remove the barrier and participation improves.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying disability is only a health matter; it is also a matter of rights and access.

courses.title: Ch 6 · The Challenges of Cultural Diversity
courses.summary: Cultural diversity, community identity, nation-state, regionalism, communalism and secularism.
outcomes: Define cultural diversity and unity in diversity

lessons.title: Diversity, community identity and the nation-state

scenes.text: A train journey from Kashmir to Kanyakumari passes through changing languages, food and dress.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Cultural diversity:** variety of languages, religions, castes, customs. India has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule and many more mother tongues.
- **Community identity:** based on birth and belonging, not achievement, ascribed rather than chosen; gives a sense of security and meaning but may produce exclusion.
- **Nation:** a community with a sense of shared identity; **state:** political institution with territory and sovereignty; **nation-state** joins both.
- India's approach: **unity in diversity**, a multicultural federal state.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: How can diversity become a challenge? When identity groups feel excluded or compete for resources, tension arises; inclusive policy (language rights, federalism) reduces it.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Believing one language or religion is needed for national unity; the Constitution recognises plural identities.

scenes.text: Two states disagree about sharing river water, and political leaders appeal to regional pride.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Regionalism:** attachment to a region based on language, culture or economic grievances; may be accommodated through states' reorganisation (1956 on linguistic lines) and federalism.
- **Communalism:** using religious identity for political ends and claiming hostility among communities; distinct from religious faith.
- **Secularism in India:** the state treats all religions equally (principled distance); freedom of religion under Articles 25–28; minorities' cultural and educational rights under Articles 29–30. The word 'secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
- Remedies: rule of law, impartial policing, education, inter-community dialogue.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Is communalism the same as religiosity? No. Religiosity is personal faith; communalism makes religion a basis for political mobilisation and opposition to other communities.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Defining Indian secularism as hostility to religion; it means equal respect and state neutrality.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Social Movements
courses.summary: Concept, types and examples of social movements: peasant, environmental, women's, caste and tribal.
outcomes: Define a social movement and its features
Classify redemptive, reformist and revolutionary movements
Describe Chipko, Narmada Bachao Andolan, Bhoodan and Tebhaga/Telangana
Explain why movements matter for change

scenes.text: In 1973 women of villages in Uttarakhand embraced trees to stop commercial felling.
The protest drew national attention to forests and livelihoods.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body:
A **social movement** is a collective, organised and sustained effort to bring about or resist change, usually outside regular institutions. Features: collective action, shared goals, leadership and ideology, continuity over time, strategies (petitions, marches, media).
- **Types by aim:** **redemptive** (change individuals), **reformist** (gradual change in structure), **revolutionary** (radical transformation).
- **Stages:** emergence, coalescence, bureaucratisation, decline/success.
- Distinct from a one-time protest.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Classify: temperance movement to make people give up alcohol → redemptive; movement for right to information → reformist; peasant armed uprising to overthrow landlords → revolutionary (in aim).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Equating a movement with a political party or a single riot.

scenes.text: Vinoba Bhave walked from village to village asking landlords to donate land.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Bhoodan** (1951, Vinoba Bhave): voluntary land gifts for the landless; later Gramdan.
- **Tebhaga** (Bengal, 1946–47): sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of the crop; **Telangana** (1946–51) armed peasant struggle against feudal landlords.
- **Chipko:** led by communities with leaders like Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt; principle of non-violent forest protection.
- **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (from the 1980s, Medha Patkar): resistance to large dams and displacement; raised rehabilitation and development questions.
- Debates: development vs displacement, rights of local people.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: Why is the Narmada movement both environmental and social? It questions ecological loss and also unfair burden on displaced tribal and rural families.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling Chipko a movement of men only; women were central participants.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Women's movements:** 19th-century reform (Sati abolition 1829, widow remarriage 1856); 20th-century mobilisation; later campaigns on dowry, domestic violence and workplace harassment (Vishakha guidelines 1997 led to the POSH Act 2013).
- **Caste movements:** Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj, Self-Respect Movement of Periyar, Ambedkar's Mahad satyagraha (1927) and conversion; Dalit movements seek dignity and equality.
- **Tribal movements:** Jharkhand struggle culminating in a separate state in 2000; Birsa Munda's earlier uprising.
- Role of **media** and **legal activism** (public interest litigation).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Q: How did the women's movement change law? Sustained campaigns led to Vishakha guidelines (1997) and the POSH Act (2013) on workplace sexual harassment.

steps.title: Answer pattern
steps.body: Cause → leaders → methods → outcomes.
